docs.text:
• Dragging single fixes, which comes after this.
  • Jump removal and smoothing, the rest of tidying tracks, and the legacy OTG and DR modes.
  • Stretching and shearing, which belong with TMA solutions (CAP-21).
  • Choosing which track wins where merged tracks overlap.

docs.title: Shear and stretch
docs.text:
A track, or its fixes in the time window, can now be sheared: hold one end, drag the other, and every fix in between moves in proportion to its time from the end you held. A straight leg stays a straight leg, with a new course and speed, and the map tells you both as you drag. Stretch does the same with the speed alone. Each release is one step, and the keyboard and two small forms do it too.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the pointer and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By the time they reach RED ONE and BLUE ONE, earlier steps of the tests have moved and turned both.

docs.title: Why shear first
docs.text:
When an analyst works up a target motion analysis (TMA), the solution is a set of legs: straight lines, each run at a steady speed. The bearings pin one end of a leg reasonably well; what's uncertain is where the target went from there. Legacy Debrief's answer was to shear the leg: keep one end where it is and drag the other, so the course and speed change together. The product owner told us yesterday that this is the drag analysts use most with TMA legs, so it comes before the rest of the track tidying (jump removal, smoothing, dragging single fixes).

The live bearing residuals that make this a full TMA tool belong to the TMA module, which comes later. What arrives today is the drag itself, on any track, so it can be tried, tested and argued about now.

docs.title: Two diamonds
docs.text:
Select a track on its own and, beside the move and rotate handles from the last post, two diamonds appear: one beside its first fix and one beside its last. Here RED ONE's leg between 09:40 and 10:20, a straight run at a steady 4 knots, with Time window chosen on the map so only that leg changes:

Drag the diamond at the end. The start stays exactly where it is, the end follows the pointer, and every fix in between moves part of the way: a third of the way for a fix a third of the way through the leg in time, and so on. The note at the top gives the new course and speed, and how far the end has gone: RED ONE: shearing to 258.6°T 4.4 kn; end moved 1.16 nmi 324.8°T.

Let go, and it's one step in the History view, named by what the leg now makes good: RED ONE part sheared: 258.6°T 4.4 kn, with Held at the start, 09:40:00Z and the course and speed it made good before as its notes. Only the fixes in the window changed, so the track jumps where they meet the rest of it, just as a move does.

Choose Stretch under Drag the ends on the map and the diamonds get a double edge. Now only how far you drag along the leg counts: the course stays, and the note gives the new speed against the old, RED ONE: stretching to 5.5 kn (was 4.0 kn).

docs.title: The geometry, on a curved earth
docs.text:
The obvious way to shear on a chart is to slide each fix by a fraction of the end's move: a third of the distance, along the same bearing. On the earth that isn't quite right. Meridians close in towards the poles, so "the same bearing" points in slightly different directions at different fixes, and a sheared leg would come out very slightly bent: tens of metres over a 10 nmi leg at 50° north, more further north.

So Debrief works from the end you're holding. Every fix is placed by its range and true bearing from that end, measured along geodesics as everything in Debrief is (see Measuring on the real Earth). Seen that way, any geodesic through the held end is a straight line, and ranges from it are exact. The shear is done there, so a straight leg at a steady speed comes out exactly straight and steady, at 50° north, at 84° north or across the antimeridian; the tests check all three. A stretch keeps each fix's bearing from the held end and scales its range, so a leg stays on its own line.

The courses and speeds recorded with each fix aren't thrown away and worked out again from the new positions, which would replace what the log recorded with the jitter of the fixes. They're carried through the same change instead: a shear adds the leg's change of velocity to each fix's own, so a fix that the log says was steering 000 at 10 knots, on a leg that has just gained 10 knots east, now says 045 at 14.1 knots. On a clean straight leg, every fix ends up with exactly the leg's new course and speed.

docs.title: Keyboard and forms
docs.text:
Tab to a diamond. Shearing, the arrow keys move it 5 pixels at a time (25 with Shift). Stretching, Up makes the leg 0.1 knots faster and Down 0.1 knots slower (1 knot with Shift). As with every handle, a run of presses is one step, not one per press.

For an exact answer there's Shear track… on the outline's menu (Shear… under Track, below the outline, in the playground): which end stays, then the course and speed you want the leg to make good, offered as what it makes good now. Stretch track… asks only for the speed. Speeds can be typed in knots, metres per second or kilometres an hour.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: The same map, diamonds and steps. The integration test shears BLUE ONE as its end would, then through Shear track… and Stretch track… with values given, as an agent does through debrief/edit_track, and opens the form.

docs.title: Every step has its reasons
docs.text: Each shear or stretch records which end was held and when, how far and which way the other end went, and the course and speed the leg then made good. An agent doing the same through the tool service leaves the same record, and Ctrl+Z takes any of it back.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select RED ONE, narrow the time window to one of its legs, choose Time window on the map, and drag the diamond at the leg's end. Then choose Stretch and drag again, or try Shear… under Track, below the outline:

docs.text:

  • Shearing one leg of a multi-leg solution while its neighbours follow.
  • Dragging single fixes, jump removal and smoothing.

docs.title: Dragging a fix, and dead reckoning
docs.text:
The last of the track operations has arrived. Zoom in on a track and each fix has a small ring of its own: drag one, and only that fix moves. Its time stays, its neighbours stay, and the map tells you, as you drag, how fast the platform would now have to go to reach it and to carry on. And the legacy OTG and DR modes are back, the legacy way: import a REP file and Debrief asks, for each track, whether it is plotted over the ground or dead reckoned from its courses and speeds, and you can tell it to use that choice for future imports. Each change to a plot is one step, and Ctrl+Z takes it back.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the mouse, a finger and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By then, earlier steps of the tests have moved, split and cleaned the tracks.

docs.title: One fix, the legacy way
docs.text:
We asked the product owner how a single-fix drag should behave, and the answer was: as legacy Debrief did, unless there's a reason not to. So only the fix you grab moves. Nothing either side of it is stretched or smoothed to meet it, its time is unchanged, and if it carries a colour, a label or a comment of its own, that stays with it (marks are found by their fix's time, as the last post explained).

The one real question was the fix's course and speed. A plot holds, for each fix, the course and speed the platform logged. When you move a fix, should Debrief work them out again from the new positions? We decided not to, for the same reason a move of the whole track keeps them: they are what the platform's compass and log (or its GPS) said, not something Debrief derived from where the fix was plotted, and a fix plotted in the wrong place doesn't change what the ship was doing. Recomputing them would quietly swap logged data for guesses.

What the new position implies is still worth knowing, though, so Debrief says it: the speed needed to reach the fix from the one before, and to get from it to the one after, each along the geodesic. Pull a fix too far and the note says so: faster than 15.0 kn, as a jump would be, using the same threshold jump removal offers.

Let go, and that's one step in the history: RED ONE fix at 09:43:00Z moved 0.31 nmi 056.5°T, with notes giving the new position and the speeds before and after.

docs.title: Rings only when you can grab one
docs.text:
A track of 241 fixes, seen whole, is a line of dots a pixel or two apart; rings on all of them would bury it, and you'd grab the wrong one. So the rings appear only when you've zoomed in far enough that the fixes are apart on the screen (at least 14 pixels, and no more than 60 in view). Until then, the note at the top says Zoom in to move a single fix.

We considered a single ring that follows the pointer to the nearest fix instead. We chose rings that are simply there, once you're close enough, because they work the same with a finger (a tablet has no pointer to hover) and from the keyboard: Tab reaches each ring after the track's other handles, the arrow keys nudge it, and a run of presses is one step. The rings sit beneath the move, rotate and pivot handles and the shear diamonds, so those keep working as before; where one shares a fix, drag the pivot off it, or Tab to the fix.

docs.title: Or type where it goes
docs.text: Move a fix… (on the outline's menu in VS Code, or Move… in the playground's fix list, or right-click a ring) asks where the fix goes. Type a position in any notation Debrief reads, and the field tells you what it understood, how far and which way that moves the fix, and the speeds it would imply, before you commit.

docs.title: Over the ground, or dead reckoned
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief could plot a track two ways. Over the ground (OTG) puts each fix where it was logged. Dead reckoning (DR) starts from the first fix and places each one after it by the course and speed logged at the fix before, the way a navigator plots a DR track. As each track came in, legacy asked which you wanted, with a checkbox: Use this choice for future track imports. The product owner told us that worked well, because a community tends to stick with one or the other, so we've done the same.

Import a REP file and Debrief asks, track by track: How is NELSON plotted? (1 of 3). Choose over the ground or dead reckoning and, as in legacy, tick Use this choice for future track imports if you'd like Debrief to stop asking. The import's notes say how each track was plotted, and, when your remembered choice was used, how to change it.

VS Code asks in a list. A VS Code list has no check box, so the box is the list's last line, an empty or a ticked circle that says off or on: choose it to tick it, and the list stays open for your answer. That's one question per track, the same with the keyboard, the mouse or a screen reader, rather than a second question after each.

Where that remembered choice lives matters. It's yours, not the plot's: a colleague you send a plot to shouldn't inherit it, and it mustn't change what's in a catalogue. So it is kept with your own Debrief settings (the same file VS Code and the Python services both read), never in a catalogue or a plot file. In VS Code it's an ordinary setting, Debrief: Track import mode (ask, OTG or DR), and Debrief: Ask again whether imported tracks are OTG or DR puts it back to asking; in the playground, Ask again sits under Import. The importer itself is simply told the answer, which is also how an agent says which it wants.

What is the plot's is how each track is plotted: the mode is kept on the track, like its colour, and changing it later (Plot over the ground or by dead reckoning…) is one step. A track plotted by dead reckoning keeps its positions as logged beside the dead-reckoned ones, so switching back puts them back exactly; and the track's line is always the positions as plotted, so any other GeoJSON tool draws what Debrief draws. It's tagged DR beside its name, in the outline and in its label on the map; its line is drawn as any track's.

docs.title: Editing a dead-reckoned track
docs.text:
What does dragging a fix mean on a track plotted by dead reckoning? Its positions aren't data in their own right: they're worked out from where the track starts and each fix's course and speed. The product owner decided that's where edits go. Move the whole track and you move where it starts. Do anything else and you change courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again: a rotation turns the courses, a stretch scales the speeds, a shear adds one set and drift to every leg (so a straight leg steers exactly the course and speed the map shows, and a leg with a turn in it keeps its turn), and smoothing averages courses and speeds rather than positions.

Drag a single fix and Debrief changes the course and speed of the leg into it, so dead reckoning puts it where you let go, and every fix after it follows, as it must on a DR plot. The map shows that as you drag, the later fixes and their rings moving with the pointer, and says what the leg has become: RED ONE (DR) fix at 11:38:00Z: moving 0.35 nmi 056.5°T; leg into it now 068.8°T 18.3 kn. Let go and the step is named the same way: RED ONE (DR) leg into 11:38:00Z now 068.8°T 18.3 kn. Over the ground nothing changes: only the fix you grab moves.

The same thinking settles jump removal. On a DR track a position can only jump if a logged speed is wild, so Debrief offers the fixes whose logged speed is implausible, and removing one lets the leg before it carry on to the fix after. And the positions, courses and speeds as logged are all kept beside the track, untouched by any edit.

Switching back does lose something, though: if you've moved the track, dragged a fix or turned it while it was plotted by dead reckoning, its fixes, courses and speeds go back to those logged and those changes go. So Debrief asks first, saying what changed (where it starts, or the first course and speed that isn't as logged; comparing courses and speeds is what catches a rotation); it's still one step, and Ctrl+Z brings the changes back.

We checked our dead reckoning against legacy's. Legacy plot files save a DR leg's worked-out positions, and placing each fix from the one before, by that fix's course and speed, along the geodesic, puts every fix of the legacy sample plots back within 0.1 m of them. Those plots aren't asked about at all: they say how each leg was plotted, and come in that way, with a note saying so.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: The same through the tool service: debrief/edit_track with {"action": "move_fix", "fix_time": …, "distance": …, "bearing": …} (or a position), and {"action": "set_plotting_mode", "plotting_mode": "dr"}, each one step with what was asked in its record (back over the ground after a change made while plotted by dead reckoning is refused, saying why, unless the change says "discard_dr_changes": true); and debrief/import_rep takes the mode for each track.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select RED ONE, zoom in until its fixes have rings, and drag one. Then try Tab and the arrow keys, Move… in Fixes…, or OTG/DR… under Track, below the outline, and drag a fix again to see the fixes after it follow; and import a REP file of your own to be asked how its tracks are plotted:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• How often fixes are labelled, given a symbol and a direction arrow, set for several tracks at once, every second to every 24 hours: a new requirement from the product owner, planned but not yet scheduled.
  • A ring on the fix nearest the pointer when zoomed out.

docs.title: The Tote
docs.text:
The Tote is back. Choose a primary track, usually your own ship, and add the secondaries you want to watch: for each one the Tote gives the range, the true bearing, the relative bearing, the angle on the bow and the bearing rate from the primary, and its own course, speed and depth, at current time. On the map, a thin line joins the primary to each secondary. Drag current time, step it or press play, and the values keep pace. It's in VS Code's sidebar under Time, and in the playground under the time controller. In the playground every panel down the side now folds away by its heading, as the Tote's does, and your browser remembers which you folded.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the mouse, a finger and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief's Tote listed, for the primary and each secondary, the same few measures, and that is the core of the new one, with legacy's two optional ones, angle on the bow and bearing rate, in it from the start:

Measure From Written Range primary to secondary in your length unit: 3.49 nmi; close in, in yards: 1070 yd Bearing primary to secondary true, three figures: 322.5°T Relative bearing primary to secondary, from its head red to port, green to starboard: R081.3°, G108.0° Angle on the bow the secondary, as the primary sees it red or green, as relative bearing: G135.0° Bearing rate primary to secondary, how fast the bearing changes degrees a minute, right positive: -0.8°/min Course, speed, depth each track 226.1°T, 5.0 kn, 20.0 m

It's laid out as legacy Debrief's Tote was: a row for each measure, a column for each track. The row headings carry the units, Range nmi, Brg °T, Spd kn, so the cells hold just the figures, right-aligned and lined up. The primary's column comes first, its name in bold, with its own course, speed and depth; then a column for each secondary, its colour, name and × at the top. Units and decimals are your display settings, the same as everywhere else in Debrief, with one exception the product owner asked for: if your lengths are in nautical miles, a range under a mile is in whole yards, 60 yd rather than 0.03 nmi, as analysts call close ranges, and back to 1.00 nmi from a mile out. A close range is the one cell that shows a unit, since it isn't the heading's. Bearing rate keeps your angle decimals, one by default. A track with no depth recorded shows a dash, not a zero.

A sidebar, a demo's side column or a phone hasn't room for every track, so the tracks scroll sideways inside the table while the row headings stay put; the page itself never does. Long names are cut short, in full on hover. We first had a layout that fitted each secondary into three short lines with labelled values; the product owner looked at it on a phone, called it ugly, and pointed out that with table headings you don't need labelled fields. Fair point, and legacy Debrief had got it right all along.

docs.title: Where a track is, now
docs.text:
A Tote is only useful if its numbers agree with the map. Each track's square on the map at current time sits on the geodesic between the fixes either side, in proportion to time; the Tote places each track in exactly the same way, and a shared set of test cases holds the map's code and the Python to the same positions, in the Arctic and across the antimeridian included. The range you read is the range between the two squares.

Course, speed and depth are what the platform recorded at the fixes either side, interpolated the same way, with course going the shorter way round through north (from 350° to 010° passes 000°, not 180°). A reversal has no shorter way round: between fixes at 000° and 180°, half way is neither 090° nor 270°, and the ship never steered either, so the Tote gives the course of whichever fix is nearer in time. A track with no recorded courses, such as a sketched one, gets its course and speed from its positions instead.

When a track has no data at current time, its column is dashes and the Tote says why under the table rather than leaving you guessing: Starts 08:28:48Z, or Ended 10:35:17Z.

docs.title: On the map
docs.text: The map shows which tracks the Tote is comparing: a thin dashed line, in a muted colour from your theme, from the primary's square to each secondary's at current time. The lines move as current time does, and follow the geodesic, so each is exactly the range the Tote gives. Lines on the map, under Add, turns them off, for the plot, the same way the tracks are chosen: saved with it, never a step.

docs.title: Choosing tracks
docs.text: Primary is a list at the top of the Tote; Add is a list beneath it, and each secondary has a × at the top of its column to remove it; from the keyboard, Tab to it and press Enter or Delete. From the outline, a track's menu has Set as Tote primary, Add to Tote and Remove from Tote: right-click it, press and hold it on a tablet, or press Shift+F10. In VS Code those act on every track you've selected, so adding five AIS tracks is one menu choice.

docs.title: Saved with the plot, but not a step
docs.text: Which tracks the Tote compares is a choice about how you're looking at the plot, not a change to it. We put it where the product owner put the time window: in the plot file's island, the part that travels with the plot but sits outside its history. Send the plot to a colleague and they open the same Tote. But choosing tracks is never a step in History, Ctrl+Z never changes it, and it can never conflict with a change to the plot's content. If a colleague changes the Tote's tracks while you do, Debrief shows theirs and tells you, rather than overwriting either. Legacy Debrief, as it happens, made the same call: it kept its Tote's tracks in the GUI part of a plot file, beside the data.

docs.title: Fast enough to play
docs.text:
A Tote has to keep pace with current time: the requirement says within 100 ms. The values are worked out in Python, where all of Debrief's measurement lives, so each change of current time is a request to Python. In the first phase we measured that architecture and found it fast enough; now we've measured the real thing:

Where Typical 95% within VS Code, through the tool service 5 ms 10 ms The playground, Python in your browser 7 ms 15 to 20 ms

Two things keep it there. The tracks are prepared once and kept until the plot changes, so a request does a few interpolations and geodesics, not a read of the plot. And the Tote never queues: it sends one request, and when the answer comes, one more for wherever current time has got to by then. Playing at 3600× can't build a backlog, and the table is never more than one answer behind. Those numbers come from checks that run with every change, so if the Tote ever slows down, we'll see it.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: The Tote view sits below Time in the Debrief sidebar, folded until you first use it; the outline's menu opens it.

docs.title: Measure groups
docs.text: The SRD says the Tote is a view onto a measure group: a named set of measures for a mode of analysis, which a study's lead analyst defines and keeps in the study catalogue, so every plot in the study shows the same Tote. This post's Tote shows the core group. The schema and the tool service already describe groups and their measures, and the Tote shows whatever group it is given, so the next part adds study groups, and measures beyond the core, without changing the view.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/tote with a time (and, if you like, the tracks) returns the values, in metres, degrees and metres per second; debrief/measure_groups lists what can be measured; and debrief/set_view with a tote member chooses the tracks, as the Tote view does.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Choose BLUE ONE as the primary, add RED ONE and a cargo ship, and press play:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Study measure groups, kept in the study catalogue, and measures beyond the core.
  • A heading separate from course, for relative bearing when a platform crabs across a current.
  • A depth setting. Depths are in metres (feet where your lengths are), to one decimal.

docs.title: Narrative in the Timeline
docs.text:
Every platform in an exercise keeps a log, and reconstructing what happened means reading them side by side, against the tracks. Debrief now holds narrative properly: each entry has its time, who wrote it, what kind of entry it is and its text, and every platform's entries sit on one Zulu time axis. You read them in the Timeline, with notes and periods of interest, and it follows current time as you play, without ever fighting your own scrolling. Choose an entry and current time moves to it. Filter by source or type, search the text, add and correct entries, and see the current one beside its track on the map. It copes with sixty thousand entries.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the mouse, a finger and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service.

docs.title: One list, not two views
docs.text:
We started building a Narrative view of its own, beside the Timeline. The product owner stopped us: the Timeline already listed notes and periods in time order, and choosing one already moved current time; a second list in time order, a few centimetres below the first, would only make you choose which to read. So narrative went into the Timeline, which became one list of narrative entries, notes, periods and the comments on fixes, and is where data coverage will join them when collation arrives.

It reads as a table, because it is one: the headings Time, Source and Type once at the top, then a row an entry, with nothing labelled in the rows. (We'd learned that one from the Tote.) Times are monospaced so they line up; the source carries its track's colour where it has one; the type is quieter; the text wraps. A day's date heads its first entry. In a sidebar or on a phone the text goes under the time, source and type, so the times run down the left like a log's margin. Entries outside the time window are fainter, still there to read and choose.

docs.title: Reading along with the replay
docs.text:
Press play and the list keeps the entry current time is at in sight. It doesn't scroll every time an entry passes: it waits until the current entry is about to leave the middle of the view, then puts it a third of the way down, so you can see what's coming. It never moves the keyboard, and it never animates.

The moment you scroll the list yourself, or move through it with the arrow keys, it stops following, so it never drags you away from what you're reading. Follow time appears in the bar, with an arrow pointing to where current time has got to; press it, choose an entry, or press Play again, and it follows again.

Choose an entry (click it, tap it, or Enter) and current time moves to it; if it's outside the time window, the window widens to take it in, without saving, exactly as when a tool moves time. When several entries share a second, the one you chose is the one marked. And the entry current time is at, if it belongs to a track, is shown on the map beside that track's square: its source and the start of its text, gone once ten minutes of plot time have passed without another. Narrative on the map, under the list, turns that off for the plot, and on again; like the Tote's lines, it's kept in the plot, not in your undo history.

docs.title: Finding things
docs.text: Filter opens a list of every kind, source and type in the plot, each with how many entries it has; untick what you don't want. The search box finds words in an entry's text, its source or its type, and highlights them. Under the list, 5 entries of 36 reminds you that you're not seeing everything. Your filter is yours: it's kept in the page, not the plot, because two analysts reading the same narrative want different filters, and filtering doesn't change what the plot says.

docs.title: One step at a time
docs.text:
+ opens a short form above the list: the time (starting at current time, typed any way you'd write it, 09:30Z or 150930Z JUN 23), the source, the type, the track it belongs to (which follows the source's name until you choose one) and the entry. Edit and Delete appear on the entry you're working with, so the rest of the list stays quiet. Each change is one step in History, named like Narrative entry by BLUE ONE at 17:31:00Z added, and Ctrl+Z undoes it like any other, from the Timeline itself too (in its search box and form, Ctrl+Z undoes your typing instead).

Each entry is a feature of its own in the plot, with no position, like a note. That matters for the history: changing one entry records just that entry. If a whole platform's log were one feature, every correction to it would put the whole log into the history again.

docs.title: Where narrative comes from
docs.text:
• REP files. ;NARRATIVE: and ;NARRATIVE2: lines are read the way legacy Debrief read them, quirks included: on a plain ;NARRATIVE: line an unquoted two-word platform is read as its first word, and the rest is text, because that's what an analyst's old files mean. We ported legacy's test cases, on lines we made up. A REP file of narrative alone now makes a plot.
  • A second platform's log, into the plot you have open. Read narrative into this plot (REP)… adds its entries as one step, keeping the file as a source of the plot, so it can be checked later and undone in one go.
  • Legacy plots. A .dpf file's narrative comes in with its types, which the first .dpf import had to leave out.
  • The sample. The sample exercise's scripted log was a set of notes; it's narrative entries now, each with a kind (Course, Sonar, CPA and so on), and BLUE ONE's and RED ONE's belong to their tracks. A note you add is still a note: your own annotation, with a name and a style.

Each entry belongs to the plot's track of its source's name, if there's one. Every source's entries go in one order, the same in Python and in the views: by time, then by source, then in the order the log gave them. Two platforms logging the same second always come out in the same order, whichever you imported first, and one platform's entries at one second stay in the order it wrote them. (Legacy Debrief sorted entries at one second by their text, which could put Contact lost before Contact gained.)

docs.title: Sixty thousand entries
docs.text:
Most narratives are a few hundred entries. At two thousand, changing an entry takes Python about 20 ms, and reading a 2,000-line log into a plot in your browser under a second.

The requirement says Debrief must cope with the legacy sample's 12,000 narrative entries scaled by three to five, so we tested that too, with 60,000 made-up entries from five sources over a day:

Where What Time Python Reading all 60,000 into a plot, as one step 1.4 to 2.5 s Python Changing one entry; undoing it under a second; about half a second The playground Reading a 60,000-line log into a plot, in your browser 8 to 30 s The playground Building the list under a tenth of a second The playground Scrolling: time between frames 16.7 ms, 60 a second The playground Searching all of them 30 to 60 ms

The list only ever draws the rows you can see, measuring each one as it's drawn and estimating the rest from the length of their text, so scrolling through 60,000 is as smooth as through 36. The Python side needed one change to get there: checking each feature against the schema for its own kind first, rather than trying every kind of feature in turn, which took reading 20,000 entries from 37 seconds to one.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text:
The Timeline view in the Debrief sidebar is the same list, now a webview rather than a plain tree, because a tree couldn't search, filter, follow time without stealing the keyboard, or hold sixty thousand rows. Its title bar has Add narrative entry…, Add annotation… and Read narrative into this plot (REP)….

On a phone it's the same list, one column for the text, and the page never scrolls sideways.

docs.title: From the keyboard
docs.text: With the list focused, Up and Down (and Page Up, Page Down, Home, End) move through it without moving time; Enter moves current time to the entry; F2 changes it, Delete deletes it, N adds one, and / jumps to the search box. Screen readers hear each entry's full date and time, its source, type and text.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/narrative returns the narrative in its one order, filtered by sources, types, text and a period, a page at a time, and which entry a given time is at. debrief/add_narrative, debrief/edit_narrative, debrief/delete_narrative and debrief/import_narrative change it, each one step, exactly as the Timeline does.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Press play under Time and watch the Timeline follow; scroll it and choose Follow time; filter out a source; add an entry with +:

docs.title: Next: Word and PDF
docs.text: Most narrative arrives as Word documents and PDFs, in several house styles that legacy Debrief's parsers know. That's part B: porting those parsers and their tests (with made-up documents), and asking the questions legacy asked, such as which types to bring in and which track an unknown platform is. The entries they produce are exactly what Debrief now holds, so they'll appear in the Timeline with everything else. Fire-control solutions logged in the narrative will wait for TMA in the data model, later.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Word and PDF narrative (part B).
  • Data coverage in the Timeline, which comes with collation.
  • Legacy's Narrative viewer extras: highlighted phrases, an off switch for choosing an entry moving current time, text size and wrapping, and choosing the columns shown.
  • Plain-text and CSV logs; for now a log can be read in as REP ;NARRATIVE: lines.

docs.title: Narrative from Word and PDF
docs.text:
Most of an exercise's narrative doesn't arrive as REP lines. It arrives as Word documents and PDFs: a ship's log typed up with its metadata hidden in the text, a rider's table of times, bearings and remarks, a printout of either. Legacy Debrief read four of these house styles, and Debrief now reads them too, on the desktop and in your browser, asking the questions legacy Debrief asked before it reads anything in. And the Timeline has gained legacy's Narrative viewer extras: words highlighted wherever they appear, choosing an entry without moving time, text size and wrapping, and the columns shown, all tucked into one small menu so the list stays quiet.

The pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser, and shows VS Code's Timeline view as VS Code does. The log in them is made up for the sample exercise, as the exercise is.

docs.title: Four house styles
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief's Word parsers, ImportNarrativeDocument and its relatives, are ported to Python with the cases of their tests. We didn't copy their test documents, or a line of their text: the tests build made-up documents that exercise the same cases. Where a checkout of legacy Debrief is at hand, a separate test reads its sample documents and checks we get the same counts its own tests expected, entry for entry: 13, 5, 18, 364, 350, 371, 285, 15 and 28.

Style Debrief knows it by What it holds A narrative log anything else An entry a paragraph: a DTG, then day, month, year, platform and type, comma-separated and usually hidden in Word, then the text. Short entries take the date and platform from the one before; text alone continues the entry above; 12 Mar 20 starts a new day. A Rider's narrative a table that starts DTG Start A row an entry: time of day, bearing, beam, remarks. ASW data lines starting TMPOS Positions of one platform: a track, not narrative. Import it as a plot and you're asked what to call the track. Dated lines 2023,06,15,17:22,… Type, platform and text after a full date.

You never say which: Debrief looks at the document. It doesn't trust the name either; legacy Debrief met .docx files called .doc, and so will we.

Legacy Debrief also corrected the mistakes these logs are prone to, and so do we, saying so in the import's record each time: a day that goes backwards with no new month (a cut and paste gone wrong) keeps the day before; an entry at 23:45 whose hidden date is the next day, because it was typed in just after midnight, goes back to the evening it describes. A few things we do differently, on purpose. Every time is UTC; legacy Debrief read some in the computer's own time zone. 31 April is reported rather than quietly read as 1 May. A bad line is listed with its number and why, and reading carries on; legacy stopped some imports at the first. A rider's log that runs past midnight goes on into the next day. And an entry keeps every line that follows it, up to the next entry: legacy Debrief joined six, dropped the seventh and carried on, which in a PDF, where every printed line is a paragraph, lost the ends of long entries.

One more, from the product owner. A line that starts with four figures was, to legacy Debrief, a new entry at that time, so 2000 yds, closing. in the middle of an afternoon's log became an entry at 20:00. Now a number at the start of a line is only a time when it fits: an entry more than an hour before the one above it, or more than an hour after the ones that follow, is read as text of the entry above, and the import's record lists each line it treated that way. Late entries written within the hour, and logs running past midnight, stay entries. Legacy Debrief's own sample logs read exactly as before.

docs.title: Asked first, as before
docs.text:
Before a document goes into the open plot you're asked what legacy Debrief asked: which types of entry to read, with how many of each; all of them, or only those within the plot's period; and which track a platform belongs to when none has its name. (HMS BLUE ONE still finds BLUE ONE on its own: the prefixes legacy skipped are skipped.) An entry matched to a track takes the track's name, and so its colour, in the Timeline; the name as the document wrote it stays in the import's record.

Your answers are remembered for that house style, as your own setting, never in the plot: next time the questions come filled in, said in a line, and one key reads the document as last time.

Then it's one step, like a REP file's narrative: the document is kept with the plot as its source, untouched; the step's record names the importer, the document, the style it was read in and what you chose, and lists what wasn't read and why. Undo takes the whole document out again.

These documents come from elsewhere, so each reader has firm limits: a file that would take too much memory or too long to read, a zip bomb or a PDF that draws millions of operations, is refused with a reason, rather than tying up Debrief or your browser tab.

docs.title: Read it twice?
docs.text:
Logs get passed around, renamed and read in again. Debrief knows a document it has read into the plot by its content, whatever it's called now, and says so before asking anything else: when it was read in, by whom, as which step, and how many of its entries are still there. You can Skip entries already in the plot, reading only what's new, or Cancel. The same goes for a different file that repeats some entries already in the plot: an entry is the same when its time, source and text are.

In VS Code it's Read narrative into this plot (REP, Word, PDF)… on the Timeline's title bar, and the questions are a few quick picks. Import plot file (REP, .dpf, Word, PDF)… makes a plot of a document's narrative alone.

docs.title: What waits for later
docs.text: Fire-control solutions (FCS entries: bearing, range, course, speed, classification) are read exactly as legacy Debrief read them, but they stay narrative: turning them into TMA solution positions on the platform's track waits for TMA solutions in the data model. A rider's bearings, which legacy Debrief also drew as sensor cuts, stay in the entry's text until sensor data arrives. The import's record says how many of each there were, so nothing is lost on the way.

docs.title: Word and PDF in your browser
docs.text:
Everything above runs in the playground too, in your browser, nothing uploaded. That came down to choosing readers written in pure Python: the standard library for .docx, olefile and a small reader of Word 97's insides for .doc, and pypdf for PDF. The Pyodide check reads the same documents in the browser and on the desktop and compares the answers; they match.

A PDF of a log is the one case that needs a little help: the metadata that was hidden in Word isn't printed, so the entries have times and text but no platform. They're given the plot's one track, as legacy Debrief did, or the document's name, which you can change.

docs.title: The Timeline's extras
docs.text:
The product owner kept legacy's Narrative viewer extras, with one condition: the Timeline mustn't get busy. So they live in one small menu, ⋯ beside Filter, and the bar stays as it was.

  • Highlight. Type words or phrases in the box labelled Highlight, separated by commas, and they're marked wherever they appear in an entry's text: bold and underlined, so they're told apart from what the search finds (shaded) without relying on colour.
  • Choosing an entry moves current time. On, as before. Turn it off to read back through a log while the replay holds its place: choosing an entry just puts you on it.
  • Wrap long entries. Off, each entry is one line, cut short.
  • Text size, from 11 to 18 pixels, with A− and A+.
  • Columns: time, source and type, each on or off. The entry's text is always there.

Like your filter, these are yours: kept with your view, never in the plot, so two analysts reading the same narrative see it their own way. ⋯ is drawn like Filter (2) when you've changed anything. Nothing ever scrolls sideways, at any size, in a sidebar 210 pixels wide or on a phone.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/preview_narrative says what a file holds before anything is read: its style, its types and platforms with counts, the track each platform would go to, and how many entries fall outside the plot's period. debrief/import_narrative takes the answers (types, within_period, tracks, platform), or reads everything. The preview also says whether the file was read in before and how many of its entries are in the plot; an import of such a file is refused, with a message saying so, until the agent says duplicates: "skip" or "add".

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Download a made-up Word log for RED ONE, then under Import your own read it into serial 3 as A narrative into the open plot. Open ⋯ in the Timeline and highlight contact:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• FCS entries as TMA solution positions, with TMA solutions in the data model (Phase 4).
  • Rider bearings as sensor cuts, with sensor data (Phase 4).
  • Word 6 and Word 95 documents, and password-protected ones: saved again as .docx, they read. Scanned PDFs, which are pictures of text, need text recognition first.
  • Data coverage in the Timeline, which comes with collation.

docs.title: Labels, symbols and arrows
docs.text:
A track on a chart is more use with the times written along it. Legacy Debrief let you label a track's fixes every so often, mark them with its symbol, and put direction arrows along it, each at its own frequency. Debrief now does the same: select one or more tracks, say how often, and the map labels the times on the clock's round numbers, beside each track, thinning them as you zoom out so it never turns into a smudge.

The pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser, and from VS Code's own test. The tracks are the sample exercise's, made up as the exercise is.

docs.title: Before and after
docs.text:
BLUE ONE and RED ONE as the map drew them before: a few arrows along each, a dot at each end.

Select both (Ctrl-click the second, in the outline or on the map) and choose Frequencies… under Track. The form is three choosers: Labels, Symbols, Arrows. Labels every 10 min and arrows every 5 min:

One step for both tracks, named Labels every 10 min, arrows every 5 min on BLUE ONE and RED ONE, and undone as one. The map then labels each track at 0820, 0830, 0840 and so on, beside it, and puts an arrow on the line every five minutes:

docs.title: As legacy Debrief did, mostly
docs.text:
• On the clock's round numbers. Every 10 min is 0900, 0910, 0920, wherever the track starts, as legacy Debrief aligned its frequencies: it rounded each track's start up to a multiple of the interval. Every 24 h is midnight Zulu, every day; UTC has no daylight saving to shift it.
  • Legacy's labels. The time as HHmm, legacy's default fix label; with seconds where the interval has them, 0930.05; and with the day first, 150800, on the first label of each day, so a long deployment's labels never leave the day in doubt.
  • To port. Legacy Debrief put a fix's label on the port side of its course, so labels keep to one side of a track instead of sitting on it. So do we, at the end of a short leader in the track's colour. The text is in the theme's text colour with a halo, so it reads on any track colour, light or dark. Where tracks cross or double back, no time sits on another, or on a track's name or a fix's own label: one that would goes to starboard, or, with no room there either, is left out; the earlier time keeps its place.
  • All. Labels and symbols can be at every fix, legacy's All; arrows can't.
  • The time asked for, not the nearest fix. Legacy Debrief marked the first fix at or after each multiple, so on a track with sparse fixes it might say 0931 for "every 10 min". Debrief draws where the track was at 0930 itself, along the geodesic between the fixes either side, exactly as it places each track's square at current time, so the label always says the time you asked for. It draws nothing inside a gap in the data, though: no position is made up where nothing was recorded.
  • Off and default. Each chooser has Off; arrows also have A few (default), what the map drew before. A track never set keeps the old picture.
  • From legacy plots. A .dpf file's display rules (30 min labels for every track, say) come in as the tracks' intervals. Where a plot has none, the fixes legacy Debrief showed with labels or symbols say how often, when they fall regularly; anything that doesn't fit is listed in the import notes.

docs.title: Thinned to fit, and said
docs.text: Zoom out and labels set every 10 minutes would pile on top of one another. The map raises the interval to the next round one that leaves them apart, 20 min, 30 min, 1 h, never 50 min, so the labels you see are still on round times; where a track is slow or doubles back, any still too close to the one before is left out. A quiet note above the key says so, naming the tracks when only some were thinned: Labels every 1 h or more, arrows every 30 min or more at this zoom; zoom in for more. It draws only what is in view, again after each pan or zoom, and never more than 100 labels on one track. Symbols and arrows are painted as one picture rather than thousands of separate marks, so panning stays smooth: with fifty tracks of two thousand fixes, each labelled every minute, a pan now holds the page for under a tenth of a second where it held it for over a second.

docs.title: Several tracks, set apart
docs.text:
The intervals are held by each track, so tracks set together can later differ. Set BLUE ONE's labels to every 30 min, then select both again: Labels says Mixed (unchanged), and leaving it so changes neither. Other… takes an interval typed as you'd say it, 90 s, 1h30, 2 hours, and says what it read, or what's missing:

On a phone the form keeps its three rows, a heading each and nothing else, and never scrolls sideways, down to 210 pixels:

docs.title: One fix, always
docs.text: Sometimes one time matters more than the rest: the moment of a turn, a weapon firing, a contact gained. The product owner asked for a single fix to be able to show its time label, or its symbol, whatever the track's intervals. Fixes… lists a track's fixes; choose one and press Time label or Symbol (in VS Code, Always show its time label in the fix's menu; right-clicking or pressing and holding the fix on the map opens it too). Each is one step. A fix forced on is never thinned away, since you asked for it, and drawn once where an interval falls on it as well. There is only on: a fix cannot hide a label its track's interval puts there.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: Frequencies: labels, symbols and arrows… is on the outline's menu for tracks, and in the Command Palette: three short lists, one after another, each starting at what the selected tracks have now; type an interval and it's offered at the top, and Back returns to the list before. A track's tooltip in the outline ends with its intervals, Labels every 10 min · Symbols off · Arrows every 5 min.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/set_track_frequencies takes the track ids and any of label_interval, symbol_interval and arrow_interval: a duration such as {"value": 10, "unit": "min"}, text such as "10 min" or "1h30", "off", or null for the default. One step, named as the form's is. debrief/mark_fix takes show_label and show_symbol. Python and TypeScript read typed intervals and name them alike, held to shared test vectors.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select BLUE ONE, Ctrl-click RED ONE, and choose Frequencies… under Track:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Legacy's 48 h and 72 h choices aren't offered: the intervals run from 1 s to 24 h, as asked.
  • A legacy plot's fixes shown at no regular interval aren't read in one by one; the import lists them.
  • Labels avoiding the narrative box beside a track at current time, or symbols and arrows: labels keep clear of one another, the tracks' names, fixes' own labels and the tracks' ends.

docs.title: Collation: one plot from many sources
docs.text:
An exercise rarely arrives in one file. The serial comes in from the range, a ship's own navigation log a day later, a colleague's corrected track the week after. Collation is putting them together: seeing which items have data for which platforms and when, choosing which supplies each period, and taking new data as it arrives without losing the work already done on the plot. Debrief now does all of that, from the catalogue, and keeps a record of every choice.

The pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser, and from VS Code's own test. The tracks and the navigation log are made up, as the sample exercise is.

docs.title: A source is a catalogue item
docs.text: The product owner settled what a "source" is: a catalogue item. A serial, a navigation log, a colleague's plot file: each is an item in the catalogue, and Debrief keeps, in each item's STAC metadata, when it came in, its revision, and the periods each of its tracks has data for. So the catalogue knows its coverage from its items alone, without opening every plot.

docs.title: New data, marked
docs.text:
New data comes in only through Debrief's import: no folder is watched, nothing polled. Import a navigation log for BLUE ONE into the catalogue, and it is marked New data for the open plot, with a sparkle and the words, never colour alone. Its reason, New data for Serial 1: BLUE ONE, within its period, is its tooltip and what a screen reader says. Only files imported are marked, and only when they share a platform with the plot and have data within its period, in the folders the plot draws from: never a plot made from this one, nor one that is itself a collation of others. A colleague's copy of the plot is marked only once it adds data.

The log's track is called Blue One. Debrief proposes it as the plot's BLUE ONE, ignoring case and spaces, and leaves the analyst to confirm, refuse or link a track of another name by hand.

docs.title: Taking it, as one step
docs.text:
Take is one step, named for the item: New data from BLUE ONE navigation log. BLUE ONE gains the log's fixes where the plot had none, here its twenty minutes after the plot's track ended; WATCHER, a contact the plot had never seen, is added. Where the plot already has data, it stays the plot's, and the step's record says the log has data then too. The mark clears; the item is now drawn from. Undo takes all of it back.

The analyst's work on the plot comes through: annotations, the narrative, marks on fixes, colours. A track moved, rotated, sheared, stretched or smoothed carries the same correction onto the new fixes, worked out from each existing fix's offset from where its source puts it, their courses and speeds changed with it. A fix dragged on its own moves only the new fix at its time. A track plotted by dead reckoning carries its corrections to course and speed.

The Timeline lists each period of data as an entry, by the item supplying it (Until 12:20:00Z. BLUE ONE: 120 fixes), so the coverage of a plot can be read, searched and filtered with everything else.

docs.title: Which source, period by period
docs.text:
The log and the serial both have BLUE ONE from 09:20 to 10:20. Which is right? Per period, the analyst decides: Coverage cuts each platform's time, within the plot's own period, wherever the sources with data change, and offers a list for each period. Pick the log for that hour and press Set (or Enter; moving through the list changes nothing), and BLUE ONE is stitched: the serial's fixes before, the log's in the hour, the serial's after. One step, BLUE ONE 09:20:00Z to 10:20:00Z from BLUE ONE navigation log, whose record says what the period had and has. Clicking a source's bar in a period chooses it too.

Serial 2's BLUE ONE turns out to be a different ship. Not this platform is one step, BLUE ONE in Serial 2 is not BLUE ONE, and it is proposed no more.

docs.title: Revised since taken
docs.text:
A colleague corrects the navigation log. Any recorded change to an item is a new revision, so Serial 1, which took data from it, may need review. The playground says so in a note, VS Code in a notification with Show in Catalogues, and the plot is flagged in Catalogue and Coverage until the analyst presses Reviewed. Take again reads the periods the log supplies from its latest revision, carrying the analyst's edits again. Each period remembers the revision it was read at, so a plot that took one hour of the log before the correction and another after says so, and stays flagged until the older hour is read again. Taking a revision that changed nothing the plot took makes no step at all.

On a phone, Coverage keeps every source's line and bar and never scrolls sideways, down to 210 pixels and in a wider font:

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: Catalogues lists each item's tracks and marks items New data, May need review or drawn from, each with its icon and words. An item's menu has Take data into the open plot…, Not now and Reviewed; a track's has Same platform as a track in the open plot… and Not this platform, all from the keyboard with Shift+F10. Coverage is a view below Catalogues, the same component as the playground's.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/coverage gives a plot's platforms, their sources and periods, and the items marked as new data. debrief/take_new_data, debrief/set_source_preference and debrief/link_tracks each make one step; debrief/review_flags lists every plot that may need review.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Under Try, New data arrives for this plot imports a navigation log for the open plot's first track; A colleague revises an item this plot drew from corrects it once taken:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• The Tote's study measures (groups of measures, course and speed rates, Doppler, range rate, time) wait for multi-plot bulk analysis, as the product owner decided.
  • Folders aren't watched. New data comes only through Debrief's import, by decision.
  • Reviewed isn't a step. Clearing a review flag is view state, kept with the plot with who cleared it and when, not in its history, as the product owner decided.

docs.title: Traceable figures: every image knows where it came from
docs.text:
A figure in a post-exercise report is only as good as the analysis behind it. Months later, someone asks: which plot is this, and was it before or after the track was corrected? Debrief's exported images now answer that themselves. Each carries an ID naming its plot and the exact step of the plot's history it was exported at, in its metadata and, small, in its corner; and Find source of image… takes the image, or that ID typed in, back to the plot as it was then.

The pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser, and from VS Code's own test, on the sample exercise, which is made up.

docs.title: The map, as you see it
docs.text:
Export image… draws the map as the analyst sees it: tracks, labels, symbols and arrows at their intervals, annotations, the narrative box, current time's markers, the north arrow and the scale bar. It is written from the map as the map drew it, so labels are where the map placed them, kept clear of one another, not placed again by something else. The map's buttons, its key, handles and the selection's highlighting are left out: they are for working, not for a report.

Three sizes: as on screen, a 16:9 slide (1600 × 900) and A4 landscape (1754 × 1240, 150 dots an inch). For a slide or A4 the map is laid out at that size for a moment, so its labels are placed for it, then put back. The colours are the editor's, or light ones for print whatever the theme. PNG or SVG; no JPEG.

docs.title: An ID in every image
docs.text:
Every image carries an ID like DBF1-PTETVDX3-KG8RB9E5X7Y58R98-M6SC7N75-Z in its metadata: a PNG's own text chunk and its XMP, an SVG's metadata. It names three things: the plot (by its catalogue and item, hashed: never its title), the plot's revision at the moment of export (the content hash its history records for that step), and the export itself. Nothing else goes into the image.

Word and PowerPoint may keep a picture's metadata, but often will not: Word compresses a document's pictures when it saves, by default, and saving as PDF re-encodes them. So a short form of the ID, DBF-PTET-KG8R-B9EM-69, is drawn in a corner, haloed so it reads on any colours, in whichever corner it covers least of the plot, and big enough (1.4% of the image's width) to read when the picture sits at half a page's width. That footer is the main trace. It is on for every export: turned off for one, it is on again for the next. Fourteen letters and digits, with no I, L, O or U to confuse, and a check: a mistyped one is caught, not looked up. Two of them are the export's own, so two images of the same view have different footers, and typing one opens that export's own view and time.

Each export is recorded in the plot itself, in its export log: the ID, when, who, the area and time shown, the Tote's tracks, the size and the file's name. A plot in a read-only catalogue cannot be written, so its exports go into the analyst's own export log, beside their Debrief settings, which Find source of image… reads too: every export stays traceable. The log is view state, like the time window, so an export is never a step in the plot's history: it changes neither the plot's revision nor anything that drew data from it.

docs.title: Back to the source
docs.text:
The plot moves on: a track recoloured, a fix corrected. The figure in the report still shows the plot as it was. Find source of image… takes the image file (or a Word or PowerPoint file, read picture by picture) or the ID typed from its corner, finds the plot in the analyst's catalogues and opens it at the step the image was exported at, rebuilt from its history and checked, as undo is, at the area and time exported, its Tote worked out as it was then. It is shown read-only: the map says so, every change is refused and said, and Go to latest returns to the plot as it is now.

A plot that has since moved to another catalogue, or been sent to a colleague, is still found, by its revision, and said to be a copy. Where an ID matches more than one export, each is listed with when it was made and the area it showed, and the analyst chooses: Debrief never guesses. A report with several figures is read picture by picture, so each traces.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: Export image… is on the map's title bar (the camera), the Outline's menu and the Command Palette: a size, what it shows (the ID in a corner, light colours), and where to save it. Find source of image… is on the Catalogues' menu: choose a file, or type the ID.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/export_image, debrief/find_image_source and debrief/open_revision do the same for an agent. An agent's export is drawn by the map open in VS Code, exactly as the analyst's is: the tool service asks VS Code, which draws it (the map laid out at the image's size for a moment, under a picture of itself) and writes the file, only into the workspace or the folder set for exports, and never over a file without asking the analyst. With no map open, the agent is told so.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Export the map, change the plot (recolour a track), then choose the image you saved, or type its ID, under Find source of image:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• No map, no agent export. An agent's export needs the map open in VS Code; the playground has none for agents.
  • A PDF of a report loses the metadata. Its pictures are re-encoded; the footer is the trace there.
  • One view at a time. Several views exported together come with the storyboard.

docs.title: The first hour: walkthroughs, and a web demo to try them in
docs.text:
An analyst new to Debrief should be producing something useful within an hour of first opening it (OUT-05). Debrief now has four short walkthroughs that teach the common work on the sample exercise, each step ticking itself off as the analyst does it, in VS Code and in the browser alike; and a web demo, full screen, where anyone can try them without installing anything.

The pictures come from the playground's test, which plays every walkthrough start to finish in a browser, and from VS Code's own test, on the sample exercise, which is made up. The browser's were taken again on 24 Oct 2026 for its docked layout.

docs.title: Four walkthroughs
docs.text:
Walkthrough What it teaches Open and explore a serial Current time and the time window; selecting tracks in the Outline; comparing them in the Tote; reading the narrative in the Timeline Import and collate Importing a REP file; seeing which source has data when, in Coverage; taking new data; choosing which source supplies a period Tidy a track Removing GPS glitches; smoothing; marking and labelling a fix; shearing a leg, the drag analysts use most in TMA Annotate and export a figure Drawing an annotation; labelling tracks with their times; exporting an image that traces back to its plot; finding that plot from the image

Each takes about ten minutes and works on a fresh copy of the sample's serial 1, titled after it (Serial 1: Tidy a track), so the sample itself never changes. A walkthrough can always start again clean: its copy is replaced and its steps unticked. Tidy a track's copy comes with three GPS glitches in RED ONE, put in as a step of their own in its history so they are never mistaken for real data; Import and collate's comes with BLUE ONE's navigation log, a REP file waiting to be imported.

docs.title: Ticked by doing, not by clicking
docs.text:
In VS Code the first walkthrough, Open and explore a serial, opens by itself the first time Debrief starts after it is installed, and only then. In the browser the walkthroughs are open whenever the page loads, in the playground, the web demo and the demo below, and set apart from the other panels in the theme's link colour: an edge down their side, a tinted heading, and the step numbers in it, the next step's a filled disc. On a phone, where the panels are one column, fold them and they stay folded in that browser.

Every step says what to do, where it is, and how to do it from the keyboard, with a picture drawn from the sample. Its button only takes you there: it opens the copy, or brings the panel or the command to hand. The step ticks itself off when you have actually done it, however you did it: from the form, on the map, from the keyboard. Finding the jumps ticks nothing; removing them does. A preview of smoothing is not smoothing; moving or stretching a track is not shearing it. And only the walkthrough's own copy counts: the same change to another of your plots ticks nothing, and with another plot open a step's button opens the walkthrough's copy before it does anything.

docs.title: In VS Code: the Get Started page
docs.text:
In VS Code the walkthroughs are on the Get Started page, as any extension's are: Debrief: Walkthroughs in the Command Palette, or Start a walkthrough in Catalogues before any catalogue is added. Open a copy of serial 1 builds the sample into a catalogue of the walkthrough's own, Walkthrough: Tidy a track, never touching the analyst's catalogues; pressed again, it asks whether to start again with a fresh copy or carry on.

The words of every step live in one file, which VS Code's walkthroughs are written from and the browser's panel reads, so the two never say different things.

docs.title: The web demo
docs.text: The web demo is Debrief full screen in your browser: every panel, docked in tab groups around the map, the walkthroughs open in a group of their own on its right, and the three serials of the sample exercise. With the steps beside the map, a step's words stay in sight while you do it in the other panels and on the map. On a phone the walkthroughs are the first panel instead. The Python tools run in the page, under Pyodide, as in the blog's demos. You can open a file of your own there too, a REP file, a legacy plot or a Word narrative: it is read in your browser and nowhere else. The demo's test opens such files, filters and highlights them in the Timeline, and exports and traces an image, watching every request the page makes. None carries the files, nothing is sent at all, not even as the tab closes, and nothing derived from them is kept in any of the browser's stores, so they are gone when you close the tab. The page also carries a strict Content-Security-Policy. One thing it cannot vouch for: Python itself, Pyodide, comes from the jsDelivr CDN without an integrity check, a risk we have accepted.

docs.title: Is an hour enough?
docs.text: The SRD's target (NFR-09) is an hour to import a serial, compose a storyboard and export it. The storyboard comes in Phase 4, so for now the product owner will trial what exists: import a REP file and a legacy plot, tidy a track, annotate, and export a figure traced back to its plot, against a provisional 40 minutes, with analysts who know the domain but have never used Debrief. It is a formative trial, its pass rule written down before it starts: four in five finish without help, the median quiet run within 40 minutes, no one over an hour. The protocol is written; the trial itself is still to be run. Meanwhile the playground's test does the trial's four tasks as a speed run, as fast as the page answers: 32 actions in all.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Walkthroughs is open at the top of the demo's side column (in the web demo, on the right of the map); choose one and press its first button:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• The trial. The onboarding trial with analysts is pending; its results will be posted.
  • The storyboard. NFR-09's full hour, storyboard included, is trialled again when the storyboard arrives in Phase 4.

docs.title: Panels where you need them: a docked layout in the browser
docs.text:
The browser version of Debrief, the playground and the web demo, had grown thirteen panels in one column beside the map, and analysts scrolled up and down to find them. Now, on any screen 900 pixels wide or more, the panels sit in tab groups around the map, grouped by task, and you can drag them where you want them.

The pictures are taken by the playground's test on the sample exercise, which is made up; the first is the layout before the change, from its pull request.

docs.title: Before and after
docs.text:
Before, at a laptop's 1366 pixels: one long column of panels on the left, the walkthroughs in a column of their own on the right.

After, the same screen: Time, the Tote with Tools and History as tabs beside it, and the Outline with the Catalogue on the left; the map with the Timeline and Coverage in a strip under it; the walkthroughs alone on the right, so a step's words are never hidden behind another tab. Nothing scrolls the page, and the map is 791 by 556 pixels, more than half the width.

The same in the light theme. The tabs, borders and handles take their colours from the theme, like everything else in Debrief.

On a smaller laptop screen, 1280 by 720, the same layout, the map 740 by 519 pixels:

docs.title: Fewer panels, and a top bar
docs.text:
Four panels were things used now and then, so they moved to a slim bar along the top: the Plot list, Import…, Export and Try, each a menu that opens under its button. Import… is in the Catalogue panel too, where new files arrive. Every control is where it was inside them, by the same name.

That leaves nine panels, grouped by task:

Where Panels For Left Time; Tote, Tools and History; Outline and Catalogue When, what is where, what is in the plot, and doing and what was done Under the map Timeline and Coverage The narrative and the data, in time Right Walkthroughs Learning, a step's words always in sight

The Outline takes the rest of the column, so its list shows 7 of the sample's 11 rows on a 1366 by 768 laptop, with its track and annotation buttons in sight below it. While playing, the Tote is one tab away from Tools, and its lines still show on the map.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text:
Drag a tab onto another group to join it, or onto a group's edge to split it. Here History has its own group under the Outline, and Coverage sits beside the walkthroughs, while a tool's form is open beside the map:

Where the map's place is narrower, as on a 1024 pixel screen, a tool's form goes under the map rather than squeezing it:

Your layout is kept in your browser, its shape only, never anything from a plot. Reset layout, in the top bar, puts it back as it started. Lists keep their place as you go, the Timeline at the entry you were reading.

Nothing reloads as you do it. The map, a tool's form and its results each run in a frame, and a frame moved in a web page starts again, losing what it showed. So they never move: the map stays where it is and the layout is drawn around it, and Python, running in the background, never notices.

docs.title: Without a mouse
docs.text: The keyboard goes through the layout group by group: Tab reaches a group's tab, then what its panel holds, then the next group; ← and → move along a group's tabs, Enter bringing one to the front. Shift+F10 on a tab, or the ⋯ at the end of each group, opens a menu to move the panel to another group (Move to left: Outline, Catalogue), or to a group of its own, or to reset the layout. Screen readers hear each group named by where it is and what it holds.

docs.title: Tablets and phones
docs.text:
On a touch screen 900 pixels wide or more, as a tablet on its side, the layout is docked too, with bigger tabs and handles; the ⋯ at the end of each group moves its panel without dragging. Narrower, on a phone and in the blog's demos, the panels are one column as before, each folding away by its heading, with the top bar above.

Drawing on the map, the note on how to draw is now one line at the top, and once you place a point it gives way to the distances and bearings.

The layout is built with Dockview, a small open-source docking library, in the browser only: VS Code arranges its own views. More in the guides: the browser layout and its keyboard equivalents.

docs.title: Sensor bearings
docs.text:
Bearings are where TMA starts. Legacy Debrief drew a platform's sensor cuts as lines from its track, and let you say which side of a towed array a contact was on. Debrief now does the same: bearings come in from REP and DSF files, legacy plots and a Rider's narrative, are drawn from the track at their time (or from a towed array trailing behind it), only in the time window, and a towed array's ambiguous pairs are resolved one cut at a time or a period at once, each an undoable step.

The pictures come from the playground, which runs in a browser, and from VS Code's own test. The tracks and bearings are the sample exercise's, made up as the exercise is.

docs.title: Cuts in the window, from the track
docs.text:
The sample's BLUE ONE now carries two sensors: a bow sonar (teal) and a towed array (purple). Each shows in the Outline under its track, saying how many cuts it has and how many are still ambiguous. With a twenty-minute window, the map draws only that window's cuts, each from where BLUE ONE was when it was taken. The bow sonar's point at RED ONE. The towed array's come in pairs: the array can't tell left from right, so each cut is two bearings mirrored about BLUE ONE's course, the one to port solid and the one to starboard darker and dashed. The cut current time is at is wider, with a dot where it was taken from.

Point at a line and it says what it is: the sensor and time, both bearings and the side each is on.

docs.title: Keep a side
docs.text:
One cut: click it. A click only selects the cut, and its choices appear beside it: what it is, Keep 051.0° (port), Keep 129.0° (starboard) and More… for its menu. Choose the bearing you believe and the other goes, one step: Port bearing kept on Towed array cut at 09:09:30Z. In a hurry, Alt-click the line you believe. A click never keeps a side by itself, so selecting a cut, or double-clicking to zoom, can't change it by accident (the review panel caught that the first version kept a side on any click). Right-click (or press and hold on a touch screen) for the cut's menu: keep either bearing, make it ambiguous again, or select it.

A period: the usual case after a turn, when the true bearings held steady and their mirrors swung. A sensor's menu in the Outline (right-click, or Shift+F10), or, with the sensor selected, Port… and Starboard… under Sensor: choose the side, then which cuts, the one at current time, those in the time window, those you've selected, or all of them, each saying how many it holds.

Port is kept for each cut by the side of the course BLUE ONE logged at that cut's time, as legacy Debrief told it. One step for all nineteen, named so the History says what was done: Port kept: 19 Towed array cuts 09:20:00Z–09:38:00Z. Its record holds the side, the sensor and the period asked for. Undo takes it back; Both again… (Make ambiguous again) is a step of its own, for when you change your mind later.

docs.title: Port and starboard, as legacy told them
docs.text: Which side is port depends on the course, and at a turn "the course" is a choice. Legacy Debrief took the course logged at the first fix at or after the cut's time. Our first version took the direction of the line between the fixes either side, and the review panel found legacy's own legs_20.rep where the two disagree: a cut taken in the minute the ship turned. TURNER above logs 000 heading north, then 090 at the 09:10 fix, having turned. Its cut at 09:09:30 is told against 090, as legacy told it: 051° is to port. Against the line between the fixes, still running north, it would have been starboard, and keeping port would have kept the wrong bearing. The case is now in the vectors both languages are held to.

docs.title: The array is behind the ship
docs.text:
A towed array trails hundreds of metres astern, and through a turn it's still on the leg the ship has left. Legacy Debrief drew its cuts from there, and now Debrief does too. Towed array offset… on the sensor's menu in the Outline: type the distance in your units, and how it follows: worm in the hole (legacy's default, back along the ship's own track) or plain (straight astern). One step, undone like any other: Towed array: 600 m astern, worm in the hole. A legacy plot's array offset comes in with the plot.

The cuts are drawn, and their sides told, from the array. Where the track before a cut is shorter than the array, it is run on astern of the first fix, as legacy did.

docs.title: Where the bearings come from
docs.text:
The product owner asked for every source legacy Debrief read, ported with its tests and its quirks:

  • REP ;SENSOR:, ;SENSOR2: and ;SENSOR3: lines: a bearing and range; a bearing and its ambiguous twin; a bearing with its accuracy, kept with the cut as written. NULL and NaN are no value, as legacy read them, and a line with no bearing gives no cut and is counted. A range of 0 on a ;SENSOR2: or ;SENSOR3: line is a dot where the cut was taken, as legacy drew it.
  • DSF files, REP files of sensor lines alone, read into the open plot: Read sensor data into this plot (DSF, REP)… on the Outline's menu, or Sensor data into the open plot under Import… in the playground. A sensor's track is the plot's track of its name, or the first starting with the same six letters, as legacy matched it; otherwise you're asked which track carries it, as legacy asked. A match by the first six letters only is offered first and asked to be confirmed, since a near name may be another ship.
  • Legacy plots (.dpf): each track's sensors and their contacts, with an array's offset, no longer listed as not imported. Older legacy Debrief wrote an ambiguous bearing of 0.000 on cuts that never had one; those come in as plain bearings, and cuts legacy resolved come in resolved.
  • A Rider's narrative (Word): a Rider entry's bearing, and its ambiguous twin, becomes a cut of the sensor Rider bearings on the platform's track, as legacy made it.

Frequency isn't imported: acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application, and the import says how many cuts gave one.

docs.title: Lines, not wedges
docs.text: We were asked to draw a bearing with its error as a wedge, where the data gives an error. We checked every format: ;SENSOR: and ;SENSOR2: carry none; ;SENSOR3: carries a "bearing accuracy" that legacy Debrief read and threw away, that legacy's samples leave NULL, and whose meaning no format or code states; legacy plots carry none. So, by the product owner's decision, bearings are lines, and ;SENSOR3:'s accuracy is kept with each cut as written, for when its meaning is agreed. A wedge waits for an error field agreed with the acoustic replay application's owners; the model can take one later without changing anything you see.

docs.title: Thousands of cuts, smoothly
docs.text: A towed array reporting every few seconds over a long deployment gives tens of thousands of cuts. Only those in the time window are drawn, painted as one picture rather than thousands of lines, each worked out once along the geodesic and cut into only as many pieces as the screen needs. The current cuts have a picture of their own, so playing time redraws one line per sensor. Measured: legacy Debrief's own large sample, 200,000 fixes with 611 cuts, draws in 46 ms and redraws in under 2; 10,000 cuts in the window redraw in about 13 ms, within a frame; moving current time takes a tenth of a millisecond however many there are.
