Working out which side 600 cuts keep, on that 200,000-fix track with a 500 m array, took 2.75 s; it now takes 0.21 s, reading only the fixes it needs. Saving the step still takes about 4 s on a plot that size, the cost of writing any change to it, which the History will take on next.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: The same, in VS Code's own way: sensors under their track in the Outline, Ambiguous bearings: keep port or starboard… and Cut at current time… on a sensor's menu, and quick picks for the side and the cuts.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/sensors lists a plot's sensors, and with cuts: true each cut in a period with its time, bearings, which was kept, the side and where it's drawn from: what a TMA solution will be rooted in. debrief/resolve_ambiguity keeps a side for cuts named, or for a sensor's cuts in a period, as one step. debrief/set_array_offset puts an array astern. debrief/import_sensor reads a file's sensor lines in, naming the track for any the plot hasn't.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Set a short window in Time, then click one of the towed array's lines and choose a bearing to keep, or select the Towed array in the Outline and use Port… under Sensor:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Wedges, until an error field is agreed.
  • Proposing the sides for you: a tool that reads ownship's turns and proposes each cut's side, for you to confirm, is a recorded future requirement.
  • A list of a sensor's cuts, coming with TMA, where a solution's period is chosen.
  • TMA itself, next: a solution rooted in the window's cuts, dragged with its bearing residuals live.

docs.title: TMA solutions
docs.text:
Bearings were the ground; this is what stands on it. Choose a period of a sensor's cuts, make a first guess at where the contact was and how it moved, and drag it on the map while its bearing residuals follow the drag, after legacy Debrief's Stacked Dots. Leave a wild bearing out of the RMS, split the solution into legs at a manoeuvre, and drag each leg on its own. Every one of those is a step you can undo, and a legacy plot's solutions come in as solutions.

The pictures come from the playground, which runs in a browser. The tracks and bearings are the sample exercise's serial 2, made up as the exercise is: BLUE ONE zigzags astern of RED ONE to get its range.

docs.title: Choose the period
docs.text: A new Bearings view sits to the right of the map, above the walkthroughs, so a walkthrough's steps stay in sight while you work (in VS Code, in Debrief's side bar). Select a sensor, or its track, and it lists the sensor's cuts: time, sensor and bearing, both bearings for a towed array's unresolved pairs. The list is virtualised: only the rows in sight are in the page, so a sensor with thousands of cuts scrolls as easily as one with ten. It's a listbox for the keyboard: Up and Down move, Shift with them extends the period, Home and End, Enter moves current time to the cut so the map picks it out. Until you choose, the period follows the time window.

docs.title: A first guess
docs.text:
Make solution… opens the first guess: where the contact was, along the first cut's bearing, and the course and speed it kept. Debrief fills in its own guess, 10,000 yards out (in your units: 4.94 nmi), a course across the bearing, 8 knots, and says beneath each field what it has read as you type. Here the analyst does as legacy's tutorial teaches: pins the start on the first bearing, 1.73 nmi out, and guesses the rest, 320°, 5 kn.

Or Two clicks on the map instead: the first and last cuts' lines are drawn, and you click on each where you think the contact was. Each click is taken onto its line; the course and speed follow from the two points and the cuts' times.

Either way it's one step, named so the History reads it: Contact 1 solution made: 60 Bow sonar cuts 12:24:00Z–13:08:30Z. The solution is an ordinary track plotted by dead reckoning, with a fix at each cut's time, tagged TMA in the Outline. That's the important design choice: every drag you already know (move, rotate, shear, stretch) works on it unchanged.

docs.title: Residuals, live
docs.text:
With the solution selected, the view becomes legacy's Bearing Residuals, its Stacked Dots, laid out as legacy laid it out: time runs up the left, the latest at the top, and beside each other the Bearing pane (every cut of the sensor, the solution's bearings as a line where it is) and the Error pane (each residual), with a Course/Speed pane to turn on for ownship's course and the solution's course and speed. The Error pane is pink until every error is within your cut-off (3° unless you set another), then green, and says so in words too.

Then do what legacy's tutorial says: drag the solution's end on the map (a shear: course and speed change together, the start held) and watch the errors. They move with the drag, every frame, marked (while dragging), and the Error axis fits them every frame too, so as they shrink they still fill the pane. Drag until they flatten about zero and the pane turns green. Let go and the step is saved, and Python's residuals replace the browser's.

For the fine tuning, drag a box round the leg's errors to zoom in; the zoom stays while you drag, and a double-click undoes it. Hold scale keeps the Error axis still if you'd rather; it widens rather than hide an error. Click a dot and its cut is selected, on the map and in the Outline, and current time goes to it.

The residuals are worked out in the browser with the same geodesic and the same rules as Python, held to the same test cases in both languages. A whole frame of 2,000 cuts (the residuals, the list and all three panes) takes 7 to 11 ms in Chromium, 600 about 4 ms.

Every cut of the period counts, from where it was taken, a towed array's from the array astern, except cuts you've hidden on the map, as legacy's Only plot visible data left them out: they come back as soon as you show them. A towed array's cut you haven't resolved is measured by whichever of its two bearings is nearer the solution, and the view says so, so you know the RMS assumed a side. Its other bearing is drawn too, faint and not counted, so you can see which side the plot favours. Next ambiguous (Alt+Down) takes you to the next one to resolve, right there in the view.

docs.title: Wild bearings and legs
docs.text:
A bearing you don't trust: choose it and press Space (or untick it) and it's left out of the RMS, one step, its dot a dotted ring. Undo counts it again.

A manoeuvre: choose the cut where the contact turned and Split into legs at 12:53:30Z. The solution stays one track, in two legs. On the map, choose This leg and click the leg you want: only that leg moves. As in legacy, each leg is independent: a leg you've already fitted never moves when you drag its neighbour; only the stretches joining it to the legs either side are worked out again. Merging two solutions moves nothing either.

docs.title: From legacy plots
docs.text: A legacy plot's TMA track now comes in as a solution: absolute legs as they were saved, relative legs (an offset from the host's sensor) turned into positions at import, along the geodesic where legacy used a flat earth, and the notes say how far any fix moved from where legacy drew it (a few hundredths of a mile on legacy's samples). It's rooted in its sensor's cuts, so its residuals are there at once.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: debrief/tma_create makes a solution from a sensor's cuts and a period (or named cuts), a contact, and a first guess or none for Debrief's defaults, and answers its residuals. debrief/tma_residuals reads them. debrief/tma_exclude_cut leaves cuts out of the RMS or counts them again, and debrief/tma_split_leg splits a solution into legs. Each change is one step, recorded with what was asked.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Open Serial 2, select Bow sonar under BLUE ONE in the Outline, go to Bearings right of the map, choose a period of cuts and Make solution…; then drag the solution's end on the map until the Error pane turns green.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Generated solutions: SATC, or a solution fitted to the bearings, stay out of scope.
  • Residuals while ownship is dragged: they're worked out again when the drag is saved, not while it goes.
  • Several sensors in one list: agents can root a solution in several sensors' cuts; the view lists one at a time.

docs.title: A walkthrough for bearings and TMA
docs.text:
Sensor bearings and TMA solutions had no walkthrough: the only taste of TMA was Tidy a track's shear. Now there is a fifth, Bearings and TMA, after Annotate and export a figure. Seven steps, about twelve minutes, on a fresh copy of serial 1, the same in VS Code's Get Started page and in the browser. It fits a solution the way legacy Debrief's TMA tutorial teaches, one leg at a time, and ends near what the bearings allow.

The pictures come from the playground, which runs in a browser. The tracks and bearings are the sample exercise's serial 1, made up as the exercise is.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Open a copy of serial 1 and its bearings. Bearings lists BLUE ONE's towed array. Each cut is two lines on the map, mirrored about the array's heading, until you keep one.
  2. Keep a side of an ambiguous bearing. The button chooses the cut at 09:46Z. The Bow sonar isn't ambiguous and reads 235.3° then, so keep 236.3° (starboard). The other ambiguous cuts are measured by whichever side is nearer the solution, and Bearings says so.
  3. Make a first guess. The button chooses the towed array's 102 cuts from 09:46Z to 12:00Z and opens the first guess: 4.94 nmi out along the first bearing, across it, 8 knots. Its RMS is 56°, far off, as a first guess should be.
  4. Put the start at RED ONE's range. Bearings never tell you range. An analyst tries one, fits, and tries another; the walkthrough gives it, 3.27 nmi. Move the whole solution 1.67 nmi along the first bearing, towards BLUE ONE. The RMS goes up, to 63°, because the course and speed are still the guess's.
  5. Shear the first leg to fit. Box the errors up to 10:32Z in the Error pane, then drag the solution's end, its start held: about 246° at 3.8 knots. Those 40 errors stand on the zero line, an RMS of 1.7°. After 10:32Z they run away: RED ONE turned.
  6. Leave out a wild bearing. Among the errors running away, one sits 40° left of its neighbours: the cut at 11:12Z. Space leaves it out.
  7. Split at the turn and fit the second leg. Split at 10:38Z, choose This leg, pin the second leg's start on its own first bearing and shear its end: about 200° at 5.2 knots. The RMS comes down to 1.8°.

Each button does that step's choosing for you, and you do the step, from the mouse or the keyboard; each step says which keys. Each step ticks only when you've done it: a side kept, a solution made, moved, sheared, a cut left out, a leg dragged after the split.

docs.title: Why the cue stays red
docs.text: Bearings shades its Error pane green when every error is within the cut-off, 3° unless you set another. The sample's sonar is good to about 1.5°, so over a hundred cuts a few always land beyond 3°. RED ONE's true track leaves 8 of the 101 beyond, the largest 4.4°. The walkthrough ends at 9 beyond, the largest 4.8°, and the last step says what to aim for instead: an RMS under about 2° and only a handful beyond.

docs.title: What we had to bend
docs.text: The sample had no wild bearing, so the copy has one cut turned 40° off, its two bearings turned opposite ways so they still mirror about the array's heading, and History says so. The range in step 4 is given, not found. A test plays the steps on the sample and fails if it stops giving the numbers the steps quote; another plays them in the browser through the forms and gets the same.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Open the web demo, choose Bearings and TMA in Walkthroughs, and press its first button.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Three guides keep Debrief consistent as it grows one pull request at a time.

Guide North Star (draft) Owner All guides An analyst who has learned one part of Debrief can predict the rest. Style guide: language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Ian Mayo Style guide: theme and UI Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Ian Mayo Interaction models Predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28). Ian Mayo Tool-author guide A scientist's first tool should take an afternoon. Ian Mayo

The North Stars are drafts for the team to refine during Phase 0. Owners are provisional until the team is staffed.

docs.title: How the guides grow
docs.text:
• A skeleton first. Each guide's version 0 names every top-level section, including empty ones marked with the phase that will fill them. New material goes into a known place. Material that fits nowhere is flagged at review as either new territory or out of scope.
  • With the feature. A guide is extended in the same pull request as the feature that needs it. The pull-request template asks.
  • Every entry cites what it serves. An entry cites the principle or requirement behind it (for example PRN-08 or CAP-24). An entry that cannot cite one is a warning sign.
  • Read end to end at every phase exit. Each owner reads their guide whole at the end of each phase, and resolves contradictions while they are few.

Automated checks for terminology and theme-token use arrive in Phase 1 (DEV-10).

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms Debrief uses in its interface, tools and documentation. The language section of the style guide says when to use them.

Adapted from DOMAIN_GLOSSARY.md in debrief/debrief-future, itself adapted from legacy Debrief's glossary, and corrected to the SRD. The changes are listed at the end.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Plot. The unit of analysis: one exercise serial or deployment period, its tracks, annotations, sensor observations and narrative, with the history of every change made to it. Stored as GeoJSON in a STAC catalogue (SUB-05).

Plot file. The one file that holds a plot: its content, its island and its whole history. Send it to a colleague and the history goes with it, undo included; they add it to a catalogue with Add a plot file…. Other GeoJSON tools can read it (SUB-07, SUB-19).

Catalogue. A folder of plots, sources and supporting files, described in STAC. Each catalogue holds data of one protection level (SEC-02).

Source. A file imported into Debrief, such as a REP file or a legacy plot. Debrief never changes a source; a revision arrives as a new source (SUB-10). A catalogue keeps its sources, but they don't travel with a plot file: the plot's first step holds what was imported, and its history names each source.

In collation, a source is a catalogue item: an imported file, kept as a plot of its own, or any other plot in a catalogue, from which a plot takes data (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026).

Supporting file. Video, imagery, acoustic files and other content that is not geographic data, kept beside a plot (SUB-06).

History (in guides, provenance). The record of every operation that produced a plot: imports, tool runs, edits and deletions, with who or what made them (SUB-18 to SUB-24). Kept in the plot file, all of it, always.

Step. One change in a plot's history: what made it, who, when, and what it changed. A step is in the plot, undone (can be redone) or replaced by a later change (kept on record) (SUB-19, SUB-21).

Checksum (in guides). A short fingerprint of some data that changes if the data does. Each step of a plot's history carries one covering the step and the step before, and the current step records the checksum of the plot's content, so a history altered outside Debrief is noticed. The island is outside every checksum (SUB-19).

Time window. The period of the plot being looked at, one for the whole plot. Sensor data is shown only within it (CAP-28, CAP-29). Saved with the plot, but not part of its history: changing it is never undone.

Saved window. The time window as saved in the plot. A tool that moves current time outside it shows a wider or moved window instead, without saving it; the time controller says so, with Keep to save the window shown and Revert to show the saved window again (CAP-28).

Context tracks. Each track's whole line outside the time window, drawn thin and quieter so the whole picture stays in view. A plot draws them visible (at least 3:1 against the map), faint or hidden (CAP-29).

Island (in guides). View state saved inside the plot file, so it travels with the plot, but outside its history: never recorded, never undone. The time window is the first, and the Tote's choice of tracks another. Everything else in a plot, a track's colour and what is hidden included, is part of its history (SUB-22).

Feature. Anything in a plot: a track, an annotation, a sensor, a sensor's cut, a narrative entry, or a set of sensor observations. Used where a statement covers them all, as in "Plot features" in the outline; otherwise name the kind.

Fix. A single timestamped position of a platform, with course, speed and depth where known. Depth is positive down.

Track. The movement of one platform over time: its fixes in order.

Annotation. A line, area, circle, ellipse, label, marker, note or period of interest drawn on or attached to a plot, or chart furniture such as the north arrow (CAP-03). An annotation with only a time, such as a note or a period, has no position (CAP-04). How it looks (colour, line, fill, label) is part of the plot: changing it is a step in its history. Write annotation, not shape, in the interface.

Circle, ellipse (annotations). Every position at one range from a centre; or an ellipse about a centre, its longer axis along a true bearing. Ranges are measured along geodesics. Kept in the plot file with their exact centre and size, and a polygon approximating them so other GeoJSON tools see the area (CAP-03).

Handle. A small square or circle on an annotation or a track selected on the map, dragged (or moved with the arrow keys) to change it: a corner, the point between two corners, a centre, a radius, an ellipse's axis end or side; a track's move and rotate handles, its pivot, and the diamonds at its ends, to shear or stretch it. Letting go is one step.

Pivot. The position a track is rotated about. Each fix keeps its range from the pivot; its bearing from the pivot turns. Unless the analyst chooses, the fix nearest current time (CAP-01).

Shear (tracks). Holding one end of a track, or of its fixes in the time window, and dragging the other: every fix moves in proportion to its time from the held end, so a straight leg at a steady speed stays one, with a new course and speed. The drag analysts use most with TMA legs. One step (CAP-01, CAP-21).

Stretch (tracks). Holding one end and dragging the other along the track: every fix keeps its bearing from the held end and its range from it is scaled, so speeds change and courses do not. One step (CAP-01, CAP-21).

Course made good, speed made good. The course and speed of a period of a track taken from its first fix to its last: what a shear or a stretch reports and is given.

Split, merge (tracks). Splitting a track at a time makes two tracks, the fixes before it and the fixes from it on; merging joins tracks into one in time order, and is refused where they overlap in time. Each is one step (CAP-01).

Jump. A fix the platform could not have reached in time from the last good fix before it: faster than a threshold speed, unless the analyst says three times the track's median speed, at least 10 kn. Jumps are found and shown first; those the analyst confirms are removed as one step (CAP-01).

Smoothing. Moving each fix of a track, or of a period of it, to the average position of itself and the same number of fixes either side, the first and last fixes staying where they are. Previewed first; applied as one step (CAP-01).

Marked fix. A fix with a colour, a label or a comment of its own, as legacy plots carry, or one that always shows its time label or symbol whatever its track's intervals (force on only). Found by its time, so the mark stays with its fix whatever else changes. Each change is one step (CAP-01, CAP-32, EXT-14).

Label, symbol and arrow intervals. How often a track is labelled with the time, marked with a small dot in its colour and given a direction arrow: each from every second to every 24 hours, or off (labels and symbols also at every fix, legacy All), held by the track (not its fixes) and set for several tracks at once as one step. Drawn on whole multiples of the interval of UTC (every 10 min is 0900, 0910, 0920), as legacy Debrief's symbol, label and arrow frequencies were, and thinned when zoomed out (CAP-32).

Moving a fix (a single fix). Putting one fix of a track somewhere else, alone: its time, its recorded course and speed, and every other fix stay. The speeds its new position implies, to reach it and to go on from it, are said. One step (CAP-01).

OTG, DR (over the ground, dead reckoning). How legacy Debrief plotted a track: OTG, each fix where it was logged; DR, from a start, each fix placed from the one before by the course and speed recorded there. Debrief asks which as each track is imported, unless the analyst said to use one choice for future imports (their setting, which they can clear); the mode is kept on the track, and changing it is one step (CAP-01). On a DR track an edit changes where it starts, or its courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again; its positions, courses and speeds as logged are kept unchanged beside it (see Track operations).

Fix list. A track's fixes in time order, each with its time, position, course, speed and any mark, for choosing one fix to colour, label or comment on.

Chart furniture. What a chart carries besides its data: the scale bar, always drawn, and the north arrow, which a plot shows or not.

Timeline. The view listing a plot's narrative entries, time-only annotations (notes and periods of interest) and fix comments in one time order, on one Zulu time axis. Choosing an entry moves current time to it; it follows current time while playing, until the analyst scrolls it (CAP-05, CAP-20). The SRD calls it the temporal view. See Timeline and narrative.

Collation. Putting a plot together from the catalogue items with data for it: seeing which item covers which periods, choosing which supplies each period of a platform, taking new data, and reviewing a plot when an item it drew from is revised. Done in the catalogue browser, Catalogues and Coverage (CAP-08 to CAP-12). See Collation.

Catalogue item (in collation, item). One entry of a catalogue: a plot, with its sources and files. Every import makes one, so an imported file and the analyst's working plot are both items.

Coverage. The periods a track has data for, from its first fix to its last, broken at gaps; for a plot, every source of data for each of its tracks, with those periods, side by side (CAP-08). Shown in Coverage and listed in the Timeline.

Platform (across items). The vessel or aircraft a track is of. Tracks in different items whose names match, ignoring case and spaces, are proposed as one platform; the analyst confirms, refuses, or links others by hand.

Source preference. Which catalogue item supplies each period of a track where more than one has data then: the analyst's choice, per period, one step each. The track is stitched from the chosen periods (CAP-09).

New data. A file imported into the catalogue after the plot, within the folders it draws from, sharing a platform with it and with data within its period, not yet taken or set aside (a colleague's copy of the plot, only once it adds data; never a plot made from it or from other items): marked with a sparkle and the words New data (CAP-10). Taking it is one step (CAP-11); Not now sets it aside until it is revised.

Revision (of a catalogue item). Its content after any recorded change, of data or details; known by the content's checksum, so undo brings a revision back. A plot with a period it took from an item at an earlier revision may need review until the analyst marks it Reviewed (CAP-12).

Folder tree (a plot draws from). The catalogue a plot is in, and the catalogues of the items it has taken data from: where its new data is looked for (CAP-10).

Image ID (in the SRD, GUID). What an image exported from Debrief carries to trace it to its plot: the plot, the exact revision exported and the export itself (SUB-25; decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). In full, DBF1-PTETVDX3-KG8RB9E5X7Y58R98-M6SC7N75-Z, in the image's metadata; its short form, DBF-PTET-KG8R-B9EM-69, in the image's footer and what an analyst types into Find source of image…: 4 symbols of the plot, 7 of the revision and 2 of the export, so two exports of one view have different footers. Digits and capital letters without I, L, O or U, with a check symbol, so a mistyped one is caught.

Footer (of an exported image). The image's short ID, haloed, 1.4% of the image's width high, in the corner it covers least of; on for every export, turned off for one with Image ID in a corner. The main trace, since an office program may drop an image's metadata.

Export log. The record, in a plot's island, of each image exported from it: its ID, the revision, when, who, the area and the time shown, the Tote's tracks, the format, size and colours, the file's name and whether it had a footer; its newest 500. Never a step: exporting changes neither the plot's revision nor anything that drew from it. A read-only catalogue's exports go into the analyst's own export log instead, exports.json beside their Debrief configuration (its newest 2,000), which Find source of image… reads too.

Shown read-only (an earlier revision). A plot as it was at an earlier step, rebuilt from its history, shown so it cannot be changed: what Find source of image… opens. Go to latest shows the plot as it is now.

Named set. A saved selection of features, reusable as a selection or as a tool's input (TL-11).

Narrative. The log of events from each platform, imported from REP files, legacy plots and Word or PDF documents, and combined on one Zulu time axis (CAP-19, CAP-20). A plot's narrative is all its narrative entries; it is read in the Timeline.

Narrative entry. One entry of a narrative: its time, its source, its type, its text and, perhaps, the track it belongs to. A feature of its own, with no position; adding, changing or deleting one is one step. Not a note, which is the analyst's own annotation.

Source (of a narrative entry). Who wrote it: the platform, person or document whose log it is, such as BLUE ONE. Not author or track: an entry may belong to a track, but its source is who logged it.

Entry type. What kind of narrative entry it is, in its source's own words, such as GenComment, CSD or Sonar. Free text: each source has its own.

Follow time. The Timeline keeping the entry current time is at in sight as current time moves. It stops when the analyst scrolls the list or moves through it with the keyboard; Follow time starts it again.

Dialect (of a narrative document). One of the layouts legacy Debrief read narrative in from Word and PDF: a narrative log (an entry a paragraph, its date, platform and type comma-separated and usually hidden), a Rider's narrative (a table), ASW data (positions of one platform: a track, not narrative) and dated narrative lines. Debrief tells which from the document itself (CAP-19). See Word and PDF documents.

FCS (fire-control solution). A narrative entry giving a contact's bearing, range, course, speed and classification. Kept as narrative; not yet made a TMA solution's position.

Highlighted phrases. Words or phrases the analyst names in the Timeline's menu (⋯), marked wherever they are in an entry's text. Like the filter, text size, wrapping and the columns shown, the analyst's own: kept in their view, never in the plot.

Serial. A period of an exercise, typically 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours.

docs.title: Sensors and TMA
docs.text:
Sensor. A device on a platform that observes others: sonar, radar or visual. In a plot, a sensor is carried by its platform's track, its host, and shows in the Outline under it, saying how many cuts it has and how many are ambiguous (CAP-22).

Cut (sensor cut, contact). One observation by a sensor: a bearing at a time, and perhaps an ambiguous bearing, a range, a label and a comment. Drawn on the map as a line from where its sensor was at its time (its host's position, or its towed array's astern), only in the time window; a cut of range 0 is a point. The current cut is each sensor's last cut at or before current time, drawn wider.

Sensor observations. Measurements from a sensor held as one opaque set (CON-02), for observation kinds Debrief does not yet draw cut by cut.

Bearing. The direction from one position to another, measured clockwise from true north. A relative bearing is measured from the platform's own heading; the Tote takes the primary's course as its heading, and writes relative bearings red to port and green to starboard: R045.0°, G120.0°. Debrief displays true bearings as three figures: 045.0°T.

Ambiguous bearing. A towed-array bearing that could be on either side of the array: two candidate bearings mirrored about the array's axis, drawn as two lines, the starboard one darker and dashed. The analyst resolves each to one side, a cut at a time (a click on it offers the choices; Alt-click keeps the line clicked) or for a period at once, as one step; Make ambiguous again brings both back (CAP-22). Port and starboard are told from the course logged at the first fix at or after the cut's time, where the sensor is, as legacy Debrief told them.

Array offset (towed array offset). How far astern of its ship a towed array is, set per sensor: its cuts are drawn, and their sides told, from the array. Worm in the hole, legacy Debrief's default: the array follows back along the ship's own track, so it lags through a turn. Plain: straight astern along the ship's course.

Bearing error. The uncertainty of a bearing. Debrief draws bearings as lines; none of the formats it reads gives an error it could draw (;SENSOR3:'s bearing accuracy has no agreed meaning), so wedges wait for a field agreed with the acoustic replay application's owners (product owner, 24 Oct 2026; CAP-22).

TMA (target motion analysis). Estimating a target's course and speed from bearings, typically bearing-only from passive sonar (CAP-21).

Solution (TMA solution). A track of a contact (Contact 1) plotted by dead reckoning, rooted in a period of a sensor's cuts by their ids, with a fix at each cut's time. It is dragged, split and merged as any track, and tagged TMA in the Outline. Made from a first guess: by form (a range along the first cut's bearing, a course and a speed; Debrief's defaults 10,000 yd, across the bearing, 8 kn) or by two clicks on the map, on the first and last cuts' lines.

Residual. A measured bearing less the bearing from where the cut was taken to the solution at the same time, from −180° to 180°. Small, unpatterned residuals suggest a good solution. An unresolved ambiguous cut is measured by the bearing nearer the solution, and said so; its other bearing is drawn faint, never counted.

RMS (root mean square error). Of a solution's residuals, over its cuts counted: those with a residual, shown on the map (a hidden cut is left out until shown again), and not left out by the analyst (a wild bearing, say), each left out or counted again as one step.

Bearings view. Where a sensor's cuts are listed and a solution's residuals shown, as legacy Debrief's Bearing Residuals view (its Stacked Dots) shows them: time up the left, the latest at the top, and side by side the Bearing, Error and Course/Speed panes, the analyst choosing which show; then the RMS and the solution's cuts. Live while the solution is dragged.

Error (in the Bearings view; a cut's residual). The Error pane plots each residual against time. Its axis fits the errors every frame of a drag, as legacy's did, so they fill the pane; Hold scale keeps the axis as it is, widening it if an error falls outside.

Cut-off (error cut-off). The analyst's limit for a fitted solution's errors, 3° unless they set another (in VS Code's Settings, debrief.tma.errorCutOff, or under ⋯ in the Bearings view; 0.01° to 180°). The Error pane is green while every error counted is within it and pink otherwise, as legacy shaded it, and says so in words: Every error within 3.0°, 2 of 60 beyond 3.0°, the largest 4.4°. An unresolved pair's other bearing is never counted (legacy's shading counted it).

Leg. A period of steady conditions. An ownship leg has steady course and speed; a bearing leg has a steady bearing rate. Changes of ownship leg give the geometry TMA needs. A solution's legs are periods of it, split at a time and joined: each is dragged on its own (This leg, the leg clicked), the other legs staying where they are and the joins either side solved again.

SATC (semi-automatic track construction). Generating a TMA solution automatically from bearings. Lower priority than manual TMA (CAP-21).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Angle on the bow (AOB). A track's aspect as another sees it: the bearing from the track to the observer less the track's course, red to port and green to starboard: R030.0° means the observer sees its port side. 000.0° is bows on. In the Tote, the secondary's angle on the bow as the primary sees it.

Bearing rate. How fast a bearing changes, in degrees per minute, to the analyst's angle decimals: positive drawing right (clockwise), negative drawing left. Steady (zero) with both on a steady course and speed means a constant bearing, as on a collision course.

Tote. The table of relative geometry between one primary and several secondary tracks at current time: range, bearing and the other measures of a measure group (CAP-06). Which tracks it compares is saved in the plot's island, so it travels with the plot but is never a step in its history. See Tote.

Primary, secondary (the Tote). The primary is the track the others are measured from, usually ownship; each secondary is measured from it. A track is never both.

Measure group. A named, reusable set of measures for a mode of analysis, defined by a study's lead analyst. The Tote is a view onto one (CAP-07). Every group extends core: range, bearing, relative bearing, angle on the bow and bearing rate from the primary, and each track's course, speed and depth.

Measure. One quantity the Tote shows: between the primary and a secondary (range, bearing, relative bearing, angle on the bow, bearing rate) or of one track (course, speed, depth). Worked out in Python at current time, where the map places each track.

Close range (the Tote). A range under 1 nmi. Where the analyst's lengths are in nautical miles, the Tote writes it in whole yards, 60 yd, as analysts call close ranges; from 1 nmi, in nautical miles.

Reversal (course). Recorded courses at two fixes that are opposite, within half a degree. There is no shorter way round between them, so the Tote does not interpolate: it takes the course of the fix nearer in time.

CPA (closest point of approach). The time and range at which two platforms are nearest.

Current time. The instant, within a time range, that every view follows. Shared state, with selection and viewport (SUB-26).

Display window. The earlier name for the time window, when each layer was to have its own. There is now one time window for the whole plot (CAP-28, decision 12 Oct 2026).

Storyboard. A sequence of map views, each with a time and narrative comments, exported as offline HTML, a PowerPoint quad chart or video (CAP-13, CAP-14).

Tool. An analysis operation written in Python: Debrief builds its form and offers it when it applies (section 6 of the SRD).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Time. Stored in UTC to the millisecond (SUB-01) and shown in Zulu time unless the analyst chooses a display zone.

Position. Latitude, positive north, and longitude, positive east, on WGS84. Debrief measures range and bearing along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, whatever the map's projection (SUB-03). Legacy Debrief used a flat-earth model, so its figures can differ by about 0.4% in range.

Units. Every stored quantity carries its unit. Analysts choose display units: knots, nautical miles, yards, metres, kilometres, degrees (SUB-02, SUB-04).

Direction Degrees Radians North 0° 0 East 90° π/2 South 180° π West 270° 3π/2

docs.title: Changes from the earlier glossary
docs.text: Earlier glossary Now Why Times have microsecond precision Millisecond precision; finer legacy times are truncated on import and the truncation recorded SUB-01, EXT-14 Contacts carry frequency Frequency is not imported; acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application CAP-22, EXT-03 Speeds include feet per second Knots, metres per second, kilometres per hour Schema unit enums Track segments: core, TMA (absolute, relative), planning, infill A TMA solution is a track by dead reckoning tagged with its contact and rooted in its cuts, its legs periods of it; a legacy relative leg becomes positions at import, an infill the join between legs. Planning segments are not yet in the v4 data model CAP-21 Depth in every location Positions are latitude and longitude; a track may carry a depth series, positive down Schema 0.0.4 World Location, World Speed, World Distance, World Vector Position, quantities with units Implementation names, not domain terms Plot is a collection of tracks Plot is the unit of analysis, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection in a STAC catalogue SUB-05

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
The sample data is a small exercise for demonstrations, walkthroughs and blog posts (DEP-08). It replaces the 1995 single-serial sample. Real, open AIS traffic gives the background picture; on top of it sits an invented exercise: a blue ownship, a red submarine, the ownship's sonar bearings and a scripted narrative, over three serials.

Everything except the AIS is fiction. Use only this data in blog posts and interactive examples (DEV-05, DEV-06).

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
uv run python -m debrief_sample build sample

This creates a catalogue in the folder sample, with one plot per serial. The same seed, built with the same versions of Debrief's libraries, always gives the same files, byte for byte; --seed gives a different exercise over the same AIS traffic.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
The exercise lies in open water east of the entrance to Chesapeake Bay, on 15 Jun 2023. The area was chosen because open AIS covers it, not for any naval use. It is on the continental shelf, mostly 10 to 35 m deep, so RED ONE's depths are notional.

Serial Time Story 1 08:00Z to 12:00Z BLUE ONE gains RED ONE, classifies it and follows it south-west, losing and regaining it. 2 12:00Z to 17:00Z RED ONE heads west for the shipping lane; BLUE ONE zigzags astern of it to resolve range. 3 17:00Z to 23:00Z BLUE ONE sprints and drifts; RED ONE evades, and is not regained after the first sprint.

Each plot holds:

  • Background traffic. 8 to 10 AIS tracks: merchant ships under way and at anchor, a tug, yachts and pleasure craft. Each is named by its type and a number, such as "Cargo 03", never by its real name.
  • BLUE ONE and RED ONE. One fix a minute. RED ONE's tracks carry depth. Both were written as REP files and imported, so they are sources like any analyst's.
  • Sonar bearings. Two sensors on BLUE ONE, each shown in the Outline under it and drawn as cuts in the time window (CAP-22; sensors and bearings):
    • its Bow sonar (teal), on RED ONE every 30 seconds, with a 1.5° error. It holds RED ONE only within 4.5 nmi, outside its baffles astern and while not sprinting, and within those limits contact comes and goes, so each serial has gaps: 177 to 349 cuts a serial;
    • its Towed array (purple), every minute, with a 2° error, out to 7 nmi: every cut ambiguous, its bearing and the mirror of it about BLUE ONE's course, in random order, as an array tells them. It is deaf within 15° of endfire (ahead and astern), and while BLUE ONE turns faster than 10° a minute or sprints; contact is gained and lost at random. 132 to 166 cuts a serial, left for the analyst to resolve: after a turn, the true bearing is the one that stayed put.
  • Narrative. About 35 entries per serial, in Zulu time, from BLUE ONE, RED ONE and exercise control (EXCON): intentions, alterations of course, first contact and its classification, contacts lost and regained, bearing reports with their drift, and closest approaches. Each entry has a kind (Course, Sonar, CPA, Log, Intention, Weather). The log is kept as a supporting file, and each entry is also a narrative entry in the plot, BLUE ONE's and RED ONE's belonging to their tracks, read in the Timeline (CAP-20).
  • The exercise area, as a shape, and two named sets: Exercise and Background traffic.

docs.title: Its history, as a worked example
docs.text:
Every plot records how it was made (SUB-18). Its history names each source with its content hash (SUB-11), and each tool with its version (SUB-24). The steps that use randomness record their seed and how each random generator is derived from it (SUB-20), and the synthesis records a digest of the serial's script, so a replay can tell whether it runs the same script.

flowchart LR
    B["debrief-sample<br/>seed 1995"] --> BR[blue-one.rep]
    B --> RR[red-one.rep]
    BR --> I1["REP import"]
    RR --> I2["REP import"]
    A[AIS extract] --> I3["AIS import"]
    I1 --> S["Sonar bearings<br/>seed 1995"]
    I2 --> S
    S --> P[bearings payload]
    N[narrative.txt] --> I4["Narrative import"]
    B --> AR["Exercise area"]
    B --> NS["Named sets"]
    I1 & I2 & I3 & P & I4 & AR & NS --> Plot[(Plot)]

To see the history of a serial, open its plot.geojson and read provenance. Each source sits in the plot's sources folder, read-only; checking the sources reports nothing when none has changed.

docs.title: The AIS data
docs.text: The background traffic comes from the US national AIS archive, published by NOAA's Office for Coastal Management on MarineCadastre.gov from the US Coast Guard's receiver network. It is a US Government work, in the public domain in the United States. One day was reduced to a small area, the serial windows and 16 vessels, thinned to one fix a minute, with military, law-enforcement, pilot and search-and-rescue vessels left out. Every identifier was removed. The reduction and the licence are described beside the extract, in python/debrief-sample/data/README.md.

docs.title: For walkthroughs
docs.text: Debrief's walkthroughs (CAP-25) never change the sample: each works on a copy of serial 1, titled after it, made by debrief_sample.walkthrough. VS Code builds a fresh sample for each walkthrough into a catalogue of its own, python -m debrief_sample walkthrough FOLDER TOUR; the playground copies the sample as the site shipped it. Tidy a track's copy has three GPS glitches in RED ONE, as a step of their own; Import and collate's comes with BLUE ONE's navigation log, a REP file of fiction like the rest; Bearings and TMA's has one of the towed array's cuts turned 40° off, a wild bearing, as a step of its own, since the sample's bearings have none. That walkthrough makes its TMA solution live, so the sample itself holds none. The walkthroughs' pictures are drawn from serial 1 by python -m debrief_sample media vscode/media/walkthroughs. See Walkthroughs.

docs.title: Not yet in it
docs.text:
• Ambiguous bearings from a towed array (CAP-22): the sonar is a bow sonar, so its bearings are not ambiguous.
  • A narrative as an analyst would import it, from Word or PDF (CAP-19): the log is plain text, and it is a supporting file rather than a source, because the builder wrote it.
  • Labels on fixes: REP labels are not yet imported.

docs.title: Interaction models
docs.text:
North Star: predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28).

Worked patterns applied the same way across hosts, tools and agents (DEV-08). Each model is one short page: the requirements it cites, a Mermaid sequence diagram, and a pointer to its reference implementation. Where an interaction is already a requirement, the model cites it rather than restating it.

Model Written in Status Selection and tool offering Phase 1 Requirements gathered Tool invocation and forms Phase 1 Requirements gathered Unavailable capabilities Phase 1 Requirements gathered Undo Phase 2 Written Conflicts Phase 2 Written Long-running operations Phase 2 Requirements gathered Check overrides Phase 2 Requirements gathered Time controller Phase 3 Written Annotations Phase 3 Written (forms; drawing and editing on the map) Track operations Phase 3 Written (part A: move, rotate, split, merge; part B1: shear, stretch; part B2: jumps, smoothing, marked fixes; part B3: single fixes, dead reckoning) Labels, symbols and arrows Phase 3 Written (intervals per track, aligned to the clock as legacy Debrief; thinning; a fix's own label or symbol) Tote Phase 3 Written (part A: primary and secondaries, the core measures, latency) Timeline and narrative Phase 3 Written (part A: narrative entries, REP and .dpf import, the Timeline following current time, filter, search, editing, scale) Sensors and bearings Phase 4 Written (sensors on their tracks and their cuts from REP, DSF, .dpf and Rider's narrative; cuts drawn in the window from the track; ambiguity resolved per cut or per period, one step each; the performance budget) TMA solutions Phase 4 Written (a solution made from a period of a sensor's cuts, by form or by two clicks, one step; a track by dead reckoning tagged with its contact and rooted in its cuts; residuals after legacy's Stacked Dots, live while dragging, an ambiguous cut's other bearing faint; hidden cuts and cuts left out not counted; legs split at a time, each dragged on its own, the others staying put; legacy .dpf solutions) Collation Phase 3 Written (coverage, platforms across items, source preference per period, new data, taking it, review flags) Exported images Phase 3 Written (the map as an image with an ID naming the plot and the revision, the footer, the export log; finding an image's source, read-only) Walkthroughs Phase 3 Written (five walkthroughs on fresh copies of the sample, Bearings and TMA the fifth, each step ticked by doing it; the same words in VS Code's Get Started page and the playground; the web demo) Browser layout Phase 3 Written (the playground's and the web demo's panels docked in tab groups around the map, from 900 px; the top bar; remembered per browser; the side column narrower) Keyboard equivalents Phase 3 Partly written (annotations, tracks, the Tote, the Timeline, collation, exported images, the browser's layout, sensor bearings, TMA)

Analysts review the Phase 1 models before they are built.

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text: How an analyst adds a line, area, circle, ellipse, label, marker or note to a plot, changes how it looks and when it is shown, deletes it, and finds notes by time. Part A: everything through forms. Part B: drawing annotations on the map, and changing them there by dragging handles or with the keyboard.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-03 Annotations (shapes, labels, chart furniture) are ordinary GeoJSON features, with provenance, export and tool support. CAP-04 An annotation with only a time has no geometry. CAP-05 A temporal view shows narrative entries and time-only annotations. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; undo is replay to a point. SUB-22 Content, how features are styled included, is recorded and undoable. SUB-04 Positions, ranges, bearings and times are read and shown in the analyst's notation and units. CAP-28 An annotation with a time or a period is drawn only while it falls in the time window. EXT-14, EXT-15 Legacy plots' annotations come in as far as the data model allows; what doesn't is listed. NFR-13 Every map action, drawing an annotation included, has a keyboard or form-based equivalent. SUB-26, SUB-28 Drawing changes neither current time, the window nor the selection; a change made elsewhere is never overwritten.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Seven kinds, one form. Add annotation… (the + on the Outline view's title bar, or on the Timeline's; Add… under Annotation, below the outline, in the playground) opens the annotation form beside the map. Its Kind is one of:

    Kind Is Positions Line a line through two or more positions, drawn along geodesics one per line Area a closed area with three or more corners one per line Circle every position at one range from a centre the centre, and a radius with its unit Ellipse an ellipse about a centre the centre; semi-major and semi-minor axes with their unit; the longer axis's orientation in degrees true Label text at a position one Marker a marked position one Note text at a time, with no position none: it needs a time

    A new annotation starts as a circle in the middle of the map, with nothing else filled in. The word shape is not used in the interface: shapes are kinds of annotation (style guide, language).

  2. Positions in the analyst's notation. A position may be typed as Debrief writes it (50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W), in degrees, minutes and seconds, in decimal degrees, without the symbols (50 20.12 N 4 7.21 W), with the hemisphere first (N50 20.12 W4 7.21), or as two signed decimals, latitude first (50.335, -4.120). Under each, the form says what it understood (Means 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W) or what is wrong with it. The same reading runs in Python and TypeScript, held to shared test vectors (schemas/vectors/positions.json), and agents may send positions as text too.

  3. Sizes in their units. A radius or semi-axes is a number and a unit: nautical miles, yards, metres or kilometres. The unit is kept with the value (SUB-02), so a circle of 2 nmi stays 2 nmi when the analyst's display unit is yards. A radius or semi-axis is at most 10,000 km: beyond about half the world, a circle drawn along geodesics folds back on itself. Orientation is degrees true, clockwise from north; 405 is read as 045.

  4. Time. No time (always shown), At a time or Over a period. Times are typed as for a tool's time fields (09:30Z, 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, 150930Z JUN 23), with what was understood said beneath; a new annotation's time starts at current time. With a time or a period, it is drawn only while that falls in the time window (CAP-28). A note always has a time.

  5. Style. Colour (the annotation amber, a track colour by name, or any colour as #rrggbb, its swatch beside the list); line solid, dashed or dotted, and its width in pixels; for areas, circles and ellipses a fill colour and how opaque it is; the label's size in pixels and where it goes (above, below, left, right, centre, or not shown). An area's, a circle's or an ellipse's label is hidden while the shape is too small on screen to carry it: under 70 pixels across where Debrief placed the label, or under 24 where the analyst (or a legacy plot) chose its place. Anything left at its default is drawn as Debrief draws annotations: amber, dashed, an area faintly tinted, so nothing a tool draws is mistaken for a track. An annotation drawn solid still has no direction ticks or end dots, and is still labelled. Style is content: changing it is a step (decision, 12 Oct 2026).

  6. Checked as typed, saved as one step. Each field says what is wrong beside it once the analyst has tried to save; nothing is sent until every field is right. Add (or Save changes) sends the description to the tool service, which checks it again, makes the annotation and records it as one step, named in the History view: Circle 'Exclusion zone' added, Style of Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed, Time of …, … renamed …, Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed (anything else, or several at once). Saving changes that change nothing records nothing: a field left as it was shown keeps its exact value, even where the form shows it rounded (a position to a thousandth of a minute, a time to the second). A field emptied is cleared: text, time and style go back to none. Ctrl+Z undoes it like any step.

  7. Changing one. Its properties form opens from the outline's context menu (Change annotation…), from Change… in the playground, or by double-clicking it on the map. It shows everything the annotation is, in the same fields; its kind stays as it is. A change made elsewhere since the plot was opened is never overwritten: Debrief shows the latest and says nothing was changed (SUB-28).

  8. Deleting. Delete on its form, Delete annotation on the outline's context menu (several at once, as one step), or Delete in the playground. Named sets keep their other members; a set left empty goes too. Undo brings everything back.

  9. Chart furniture. The scale bar is always drawn, in the analyst's distance unit. The north arrow is chart furniture the plot carries: North arrow on the Outline view's ... menu (checked when shown), or the North arrow button in the playground, adds or removes it as a step. The map is Web Mercator, north up everywhere, so the arrow points up. Grids, legends and other furniture are not done.

  10. The Timeline (CAP-05). Time-only annotations, notes and periods of interest, are listed in the Timeline with the plot's narrative entries and fix comments, in one time order: a note shows its name as its source and Note as its type, a period Period and when it ends. Choosing one moves current time to it, or to its start; outside the window shown the window widens or moves, shown but never saved (CAP-28). Since schema 0.0.19 the sample's log and a legacy plot's narrative are narrative entries, not notes; a note is the analyst's own annotation. See Timeline and narrative.

  11. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Adding, changing, restyling, deleting an annotation Yes, one each Yes Drawing on the map: placing points, cancelling No: the step is Add on the form that follows No Letting go of a handle, or a run of arrow keys on one Yes, one each Yes Showing or removing the north arrow Yes Yes Hiding an annotation on the map Yes (as for any feature) Yes Choosing a Timeline entry (current time), opening a form No No

  12. Drawing on the map. The map has a toolbar, Draw an annotation, below the zoom buttons: Line, Area, Circle, Ellipse, Label, Marker and Cancel. Choosing a kind starts drawing it: the button shows pressed, the map gets a focus outline and a cross for a pointer, and a note at the top of the map says what to do next and what has been drawn so far. Choosing the pressed kind again, Cancel (which leaves the keyboard on that kind) or Escape stops and keeps nothing; Backspace removes the last point placed.

    Kind Draw it by The map says Line clicking each position; double-click or Enter finishes positions placed, the leg to the pointer, range and bearing from the start, length Area clicking each corner; double-click or Enter finishes corners placed, the leg, range and bearing from the start, the area Circle clicking the centre, then the radius; or dragging from the centre radius, its bearing, the area Ellipse clicking the centre, the end of the longer axis (which sets the orientation), then the side (the width); or dragging from the centre to the axis end semi-major, semi-minor, orientation, the area Label, marker one click the position

    Ranges and bearings are along geodesics and in the analyst's units and notation (4.25 nmi 045.0°T); an area is in the square of the length unit (12.30 nmi²). A double-click places one point, not two. A line needs two different positions and an area three; finishing too soon says so and keeps drawing. A circle's radius and an ellipse's axes are kept in the analyst's length unit, to the decimals the map showed, so what is saved is what was read; an ellipse's side can never make the shorter axis the longer. While drawing, a click on a track places a point there; Ctrl or Cmd click still selects. Drawing never changes current time, the window or the selection.

  13. Finishing opens the form. A finished drawing opens the annotation form (Add annotation), with its kind, positions and size filled in, at the name. The analyst names it, gives it a time or a style if they want, and Add saves it as one step (Area 'Patrol box' added); Cancel (or closing the form) keeps nothing, and the dashed drawing leaves the map. Until then nothing is in the plot. Why the form, rather than adding at once with a made-up name: adding at once and then naming it would be two steps for one annotation, and Undo would take away only the name; a made-up name ("Area 1") would end up in plots. With the form, each finished annotation is one undoable step with the analyst's own name, and Cancel leaves no trace in the history.

  14. Changing it on the map. An annotation selected on its own, and drawn on the map now, shows handles in the theme's focus colour, and the note at the top says how to use them (on a map narrower than 480 pixels the note gives way to the map; each handle's own name says it):

    Kind Handles Line, area one at each position or corner; a smaller, dashed one between each pair (an area's closing side too); a filled one in the middle that moves it all Circle its centre (moves it); its radius Ellipse its centre (moves it); the end of its longer axis (length and orientation); its side (width) Label, marker its position

    Dragging a handle changes the annotation as the pointer moves, saying what it now measures; letting go saves the change as one step, named for what was done: Circle 'Keep clear' moved, Circle 'Keep clear' resized, Area 'Patrol box' reshaped (a corner moved, added or removed, or an ellipse's axes), Area 'Patrol box' moved (all of it). Escape during a drag puts it back, and nothing is recorded. Dragging a between-handle adds a corner (or position) there. Moving a whole line or area moves every corner by the same change of latitude and longitude, as a parallel rule would on a chart. Sizes keep their own units: a circle of 4 km stays in km.

  15. The keyboard. Every drawing and every change can be made without a pointer:

    • Drawing: Tab to the toolbar and press Enter on a kind; the keyboard goes to the map, which shows a cross in its middle. The arrow keys pan the map under the cross (as they always do), Space places a point at the cross, Enter finishes, Backspace removes the last point, Escape cancels.
    • Changing: Tab to a handle (each is named for a screen reader: Area 'Patrol box': corner 2 of 4; drag it, or use the arrow keys; Delete removes it). The arrow keys move it 5 pixels, 25 with Shift; a run of presses is saved as one step once they stop (under a second), on Enter, or when the keyboard moves on; Escape first puts it back. Presses made while that step is still being saved are not lost: the map says so, and they are made as the next step once it is. Arrow keys on a between-handle add a corner there. Delete or Backspace on a corner removes it, unless that would leave an area fewer than three corners or a line fewer than two, which the map says.
    • Exactly: the properties form (item 7) changes any position or size by typing it, as before.

  16. Shared state and conflicts. Drawing and editing change neither current time, the time window nor the selection; tracks stay selectable with Ctrl or Cmd click. If the plot changes elsewhere during a drag (a colleague, an agent), the map shows the latest at once, drops the drag and says The plot was changed elsewhere, so your change was not made. Debrief is showing the latest; try again if you still want to. A change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused the same way (SUB-28). A change the service refuses for any other reason is said in a notification, and the map shows the annotation as it is.

  17. For agents. The same steps through the tool service: debrief/add_annotation (annotation: the description the form sends, positions as numbers or text), debrief/edit_annotation (feature, and annotation with only what changes, so {"appearance": {...}} restyles; a member given as null is cleared, and a time given replaces a period, or a period a time; the north arrow has nothing to change), debrief/delete_annotations (features) and debrief/set_north_arrow (shown), each with base as for any change. In VS Code the commands debrief.addAnnotation, debrief.editAnnotation, debrief.deleteAnnotation, debrief.toggleNorthArrow and debrief.goToTime take the same arguments instead of opening the form.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Map
    participant Form as Annotation form
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    Analyst->>Map: Area; click each corner; double-click
    Map->>Map: sketch, with range, bearing and area as it goes
    Map->>Host: annotation_drawn (corners, name empty)
    Host->>Form: show_annotation_form (the drawing)
    Analyst->>Form: name it; Add
    Form->>Host: save_annotation
    Host->>Service: debrief/add_annotation (one step)
    Host->>Map: show_plot (it is selected: handles)
    Analyst->>Map: drag a corner, let go
    Map->>Host: edit_annotation (feature_id, the whole description, changed)
    Host->>Service: debrief/edit_annotation (base)
    alt changed elsewhere since base
        Service-->>Host: CONFLICT
        Host->>Map: show_plot (the latest); nothing was changed
    else
        Service-->>Host: one step: "Area 'Patrol box' reshaped"
        Host->>Map: show_plot
    end
sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Form as Annotation form
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Plot as Plot file
    Analyst->>Form: kind, name, centre, radius, style, time
    Form->>Form: read positions and times; say what they mean or what is wrong
    Analyst->>Form: Add
    Form->>Host: save_annotation (the description)
    Host->>Service: debrief/add_annotation (description, base)
    alt changed elsewhere since base
        Service-->>Host: CONFLICT
        Host->>Analyst: nothing was changed; showing the latest
    else
        Service->>Service: check it; make the feature (a circle: its polygon along geodesics)
        Service->>Plot: one step: "Circle 'Exclusion zone' added"
        Service-->>Host: new base, the feature's id
        Host->>Host: reload: map, outline, Timeline, History
    end

docs.title: How circles and ellipses are kept
docs.text: GeoJSON has no curves. A circle or an ellipse is kept as a polygon of 72 sides approximating it, built along geodesics, as its geometry, so that any other GeoJSON tool draws the area it covers and a plot's extent includes it, plus its own properties: shape (circle or ellipse), centre, and radius, or semi_major, semi_minor and orientation, each with its unit. Debrief draws and edits it from those, along geodesics and smooth at any zoom, never from the polygon; every change makes the polygon again, and a rule checked on reading refuses a polygon that no longer matches its centre and size. A point with a radius would have been smaller, but other tools would see only a point, and a plot's extent would leave the circle out.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Schema (0.0.12): AnnotationProperties (shape, centre, radius, semi_major, semi_minor, orientation, furniture, appearance), AnnotationAppearance and AnnotationSpec in schemas/linkml/features.yaml; the rules in debrief_schemas.documents (_annotation_problems); fixtures plot/valid/annotations-every-shape.json and the circle-*, ellipse-*, line-*, chart-furniture-* and annotation-* invalid ones.
  • Kernel: debrief_kernel.geodesy.circle_ring and ellipse_ring; debrief_kernel.formatting.parse_position and its TypeScript twin parsePosition (ts/kernel/src/positions.ts).
  • Making and naming changes: debrief_stac.annotations (build, spec_of, describe_change); Catalogue.add_annotation, edit_annotation, delete_annotations, set_north_arrow; the service methods in debrief_tools.service.
  • Drawing and editing on the map: what each click, drag and key makes, the readouts and the handles in vscode/webview/drawing.ts (free of Leaflet, unit-tested); the toolbar, sketch, handles, dragging and nudging in vscode/webview/mapedit.ts; rangeBearing, travel and geodesicArea in vscode/webview/geodesic.ts; the messages annotation_drawn and edit_annotation with annotation (schema 0.0.13); the host side in vscode/src/panels/map.ts (receive) and the command debrief.addDrawnAnnotation; the step names in debrief_stac.annotations.describe_change.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Docked, 900 pixels wide and 480 high and more (decisions, product owner, 23 Oct 2026). The panels sit in tab groups around the map, and the analyst drags a tab to rearrange them. Each group shows one panel at a time; its tabs name the others. The default is task-grouped (second round, 23 Oct 2026; the left column's groups, 24 Oct 2026):

    ┌──────────── top bar: Plot ▾ · Import… · Export ▾ · Try ▾ · Reset layout ────────────┐
│ Time                │                                       │ Walkthroughs         │
│ Tote|Tools|History  │                 map                   │ (alone: a step's     │
│ Outline | Catalogue │                                       │  words never hidden) │
│                     ├───────────────────────────────────────┤                      │
│                     │ Timeline | Coverage (22%)             │                      │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

    The side columns take about a fifth of the width each. The map is 791 × 556 pixels at 1366 × 768 (58% of the width) and 740 × 519 at 1280 × 720; the Timeline and Coverage take 22% of the centre's height. Tools and History are tabs beside the Tote, the Tote in front, so the Outline and Catalogue take the rest of the column (product owner, 24 Oct 2026): the Outline shows 7 of the sample's 11 rows at 1366 × 768, 4 at 1280 × 720 and all of them at 1920 × 1080, where under the earlier default it showed about 2 at 768 pixels high. While playing, the Tote is one tab away from Tools, and its lines still show on the map. Time is as tall as it needs, and the Tote's group as tall as the sample needs from 1280 × 720, with no scroll inside either. The Outline's track and annotation buttons stay in sight below its list, which scrolls on its own. No tab strip overflows at 1024, 1280, 1366 or 1920 pixels. Nothing scrolls the page; each panel scrolls on its own.

  2. The top bar holds what is used now and then, so the columns hold only panels (decision, product owner, 23 Oct 2026): the Plot list; Import…, Export ▾ and Try ▾, each a menu that opens under its button; and Reset layout. A menu closes on Escape (the keyboard back on its button), on Tab out of it, on a click elsewhere (into the map too), on its button again, and when the window is resized or, narrow, the page scrolls. The Catalogue panel has an Import… button too, opening the same menu; a file chosen to import closes it (accepted as built, product owner, 23 Oct 2026).

  3. Panels. Time, Tote, Outline, Catalogue, Timeline, Coverage, Tools, History and Walkthroughs, listed once in vscode/play/panels.mjs. Every panel stays: none can be closed. The map has no tab and takes no panel as a tab; a panel can be dropped beside it, splitting its place.

  4. Rearranging. Drag a tab onto another group's tabs or its middle to join it; onto a group's edge, or the dock's, to split. Without a pointer, and by touch, each tab has a menu (Shift+F10, the menu key, or a right-click), and each group a ⋯ button that opens the menu of the panel in front: Move to left: Outline, Catalogue for each other group (named by where it is and what it holds), Move to a group of its own, and Reset layout. When a column empties, the map takes its room.

  5. A tool's form never squeezes the map (panel review, 23 Oct 2026). Beside the map, a tool's form, its results or a list such as the fixes takes a third of the map's place, 260 to 380 pixels; where the map's place is narrower than 640 pixels (from 900 to about 1280 pixels wide with the default columns), it goes under the map instead, as on a narrow screen. The map stays at least 380 × 160 pixels.

  6. Remembered in this browser (decision, product owner, 23 Oct 2026). The playground and the web demo keep the layout in the browser's local storage, under debrief.play.layout, with a version (2 since the second round): its shape only, the panels by id and name, the groups and their sizes, never anything from a plot or a file. They share the one key, so the web demo and the playground open as the analyst last left either (accepted as built, product owner, 23 Oct 2026). A layout is used only if it would come out whole: this version's, exactly this page's panels, each in one group once, the map alone in its own, sizes a screen could have (more than 0 and less than 20,000 pixels), nothing floating and every panel rendered always. Any other, unreadable, outdated, incomplete or absurd, gives the default and is forgotten; one that fails to build all the same is forgotten too, and the default built, so the page always comes up. Reset layout gives the default and remembers it. Two windows of the playground open at once each remember the layout as they last changed it: the last change wins, the other's is overwritten. A blog's demo (?panels=…) always starts from the default made from the panels it lists, the same every time, and remembers nothing.

  7. The frames never reload. The map, a tool's form, its results and the annotation form are frames, and moving a frame in a page reloads it. So none is ever moved: the map and the form beside it stay where they are and are laid over the map's place in the layout; dragging, tab switching, splitting, Reset and going narrow and back move only panels without frames. Every panel stays in the page while hidden, so what it shows and its controls are as they were. Python, in its worker, is untouched. Tested: a marker in the map's and the form's frames, and the plot's history from Python, survive all of it.

  8. Scroll and the keyboard are kept (panel review, 23 Oct 2026). A panel moved in the page loses its scroll, so going narrow and back, and Reset, keep each list's place (the Timeline's entry at its top, the Outline's scroll) and each docked panel's scroll, given back as each list gets its size, however long the layout takes to place it, even where the browser had already pulled a list back as the window widened (24 Oct 2026). Going narrow, the keyboard on a panel's tab goes to its heading's fold button; going docked, from the fold button to the tab; on anything inside a panel, it stays there. A menu of the top bar open as the layout changes closes, the keyboard back on its button.

  9. Narrower than 900 pixels, or lower than 480, the panels are the one side column as before, each folding by its heading (decision, 14 Oct 2026), the walkthroughs first; below 600 pixels the page scrolls, the map first. Docking needs the room (engineering decision, 23 Oct 2026). Fold buttons show only here: docked, tabs replace them, and which panels were folded is kept for the narrow layout. The top bar is the same at every width, wrapping onto two lines on a phone.

  10. By touch, from 900 pixels, docked too (product owner, 23 Oct 2026): on a touch screen (pointer: coarse) tab strips are 32 pixels high, tabs and each group's ⋯ at least 32 pixels, a sash's grip 24 pixels wide, and menu items 32 pixels high; a panel is moved from the ⋯ menu, or dragged.

  11. Theme. Tabs, sashes, groups and drop places are drawn from the theme's variables, light and dark (style guide, Theme); the Walkthroughs tab carries the guidance accent, as the panel does.

  12. The drawing note is one line (product owner, 23 Oct 2026). Drawing on the map, how to draw is one line at the top of the map, the whole of it in its tooltip; once a point is placed the readout takes its place, how to draw still said to screen readers; with the keyboard on the map, a line of keys under it. It never covers more than the top tenth of the map. The note is the map's own, so VS Code shows it the same way.

sequenceDiagram
    actor A as Analyst
    participant P as Page (host.ts)
    participant D as Layout (dock.ts, Dockview)
    participant S as Browser storage
    A->>P: Opens the playground, 1366 px wide
    P->>S: Remembered layout?
    S-->>P: None, or another version's
    P->>D: The default, task-grouped
    D-->>P: The map's place
    P->>P: Lays the map over it (never moved)
    A->>D: Drags History's tab below the Outline
    D->>S: The layout's shape, versioned
    A->>P: Narrows the window below 900 px
    P->>D: Panels back to the side column
    P->>P: The map in the page's flow, not moved
    A->>P: Widens it again
    P->>S: Remembered layout
    P->>D: As the analyst left it

docs.text:
Action Keys Move through the layout Tab: each group's tab in front, then what its panel holds, then the next group's tab; the left column top down, the map (and the form beside it), what is under it, then the right; before the first group and after the last, the top bar. Inside the map's frame, its own order. Move along a group's tabs ← →, Home, End; Enter or Space brings the tab's panel to the front Move a panel to another group, or a group of its own Shift+F10 or the menu key on its tab, then ↑ ↓ and Enter; or Tab to the group's ⋯ and Enter Reset the layout Reset layout in the top bar, or in a tab's menu Open Import, Export or Try Tab to its button in the top bar, Enter; Escape closes it, back to its button

For screen readers each group's tab strip is a tab list named by where it is and what it holds (Panels, left: Outline, Catalogue), and each panel a tab panel named by its tab, holding the panel; the groups are not regions of their own (the panels' contents are drawn outside them), and the map is named Map. A panel moved from its menu takes the keyboard with it, to its tab, which a screen reader reads out.
