docs.title: Collation
docs.text: How an analyst puts a plot together from the catalogue items that have data for it: which items cover which periods, which item supplies each period of a platform, new data arriving, taking it, and products flagged when an item they drew from is revised.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-05 The temporal view shows data coverage per source, with narrative entries and time-only annotations. CAP-08 Collation is done in the catalogue browser: managing the catalogue, viewing coverage, importing, converting. It is not a separate component. CAP-09 The choice of which source to prefer is the analyst's, made in the browser with coverage visible. CAP-10 New data for the current plot is marked in the browser with an icon or halo, limited to the folder tree the plot draws from. CAP-11 The analyst chooses when to take new data; taking it merges into the plot, preserving annotations and reconstruction. CAP-12 When upstream data is revised, the analyst is told, and the browser highlights downstream products that may need review. SUB-10, SUB-11 Sources are never changed; provenance names each, with its content hash. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step, undone by replay. SUB-22 View state in the island is neither undoable nor recorded. NFR-01 Interactive updates within 500 ms on busy plots. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. A source is a catalogue item (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). Every file Debrief imports becomes an item of its own: a REP file, a legacy plot, a Word or PDF narrative, a colleague's plot file. Any item can supply data to a plot, and a plot is itself an item, so the plot an analyst collates into can later be a source for another. Collation never changes an item it reads from (SUB-10).
  2. Coverage. Each item's tracks and the periods each has data for: from a track's first fix to its last, broken at each gap. A gap is a time between two fixes more than ten times the track's median time between fixes (the upper of the middle two, as the map's labels and smoothing judge one) and more than five minutes, so a busy track's pause for breath is not a gap; with fewer than three steps between fixes there is no median, and no gap. A single fix is a period of an instant. Debrief works coverage out at every change to an item and keeps it in the item's STAC metadata (debrief:coverage), so a catalogue's coverage is read from its items alone, never their plots. Python and TypeScript work spans out alike, held to schemas/vectors/collation.json.
  3. One platform across items. Tracks whose names match, ignoring case and runs of spaces (BLUE ONE, Blue One, blue one; not BLUE-ONE), are proposed as one platform. The analyst confirms (Same platform), refuses (Not this platform, after which it is proposed no more), or links a track of another name by hand. Each is one recorded step on the plot's track (platform_links, platform_unlinks), named Blue One in Nav log confirmed as BLUE ONE, BLUE ONE in Serial 2 is not BLUE ONE, MERCHANT in Nav log linked to BLUE. A link to an item that supplies a period of the track cannot be undone by unlinking: choose another source for that period first, or undo the step that took it.
  4. Source preference, per period (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). For each of the plot's tracks, Coverage lists every source with data for its platform (the plot's own data, items linked, items proposed) and cuts the track's time where the sources with data change, within the plot's own period (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): a track of the same name far outside it is still proposed, but offers no period to choose. Where two or more have data for a period, the analyst picks which supplies it on the period's list and presses Set (or Enter on the list), or clicks that source's bar in the period; moving through the list makes no step. The track is stitched from the chosen periods. The choice is one recorded step, BLUE ONE 09:20:00Z to 10:20:00Z from Nav log, whose record says what the period had and has (Was Serial 1: 61 fixes, Now Nav log: 361 fixes) and names the item and the revision taken (drawn_from). The track keeps which item supplies which period (supplies, in time order, each from its first fix to its last, with the revision it was read at), so Coverage shows it and the next choice starts from it. Periods of one item read at two revisions are two periods, each naming its own. The plot's own data, as it was first recorded, is a source like any other: choosing it again puts back what was imported. A period with data no fix of the plot's track comes from yet shows as Not taken; choosing a source for it takes that period. The seconds between the last fix one source supplies and the first the next supplies are no period to choose: the track has no gap there.
  5. New data arrives only through Debrief's import (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): no folder is watched and nothing is polled. An item is marked as new data for the open plot when it came into the catalogue after the plot did (STAC's created; for an item saved before items kept it, its first step's time), within the folder tree the plot draws from (its own catalogue, and those of items it has taken data from), shares a platform with the plot (linked or proposed) and has data within its period; and the plot has neither taken it nor set it aside at this revision (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). Only an item that came in by importing files is new data: its history starts with a record naming the files (debrief:imported). An item made from this plot's data, a product of other items and an item made by hand never are. A colleague's copy of this plot (their histories share their first step, debrief:origin) is new data only once it has steps since they parted that add data: an import, data taken from an item, a track or a narrative entry added. The mark is a sparkle and the words New data, never colour alone; its reason (New data for Serial 1: BLUE ONE, within its period) is its tooltip and is read by screen readers. Items outside the folder tree are never marked.

  6. Taking new data is the analyst's choice (CAP-11): Take in Coverage or on the item in the catalogue (Take data into the open plot… on the item's menu in VS Code). It is one recorded step, named for the item (New data from Nav log), and its record says what it did (BLUE ONE 120 fixes, WATCHER added) and names the item at the revision taken. For each track of the item:

    • matched (linked, or proposed by name, which taking confirms) to one of the plot's tracks: the plot's track gains the item's fixes where it has no data of its own; where another item supplies a period, that period stays as the analyst chose, and the record says the item also has data then (choose which in Coverage); where this item already supplies a period (taken before), that period is read again from the item's latest revision;
    • unmatched: added as a new track of the plot, supplied by the item;
    • nothing new at all: refused, saying why, with Not now to set the item aside;
    • the item's data as the plot has it already (taken before, or a revision that changed nothing the plot took, such as a colour): no step, so no new revision of the plot and no product flagged for nothing; the plot is marked as reviewed against that revision instead, and the analyst is told.

    The record counts only fixes added or changed. Collation's steps are a tool's (kind: tool, debrief-stac.collation), never mistaken for a file's import. The mark clears once taken. Not now sets an item aside for the plot: view state in its island, never a step, until the item is revised. Undo takes a whole take back. 7. The analyst's work survives (CAP-11). Annotations and narrative are untouched. Marks stay with their fixes, found by time; a mark whose fix a new source replaces moves to the nearest fix without one, and the record says so. A track's colour, frequencies, hiding and plotting mode are its own and are kept. Edits are carried to new fixes: each existing fix's offset from where its source puts it is worked out (for the plot's own data, the track as the plot first recorded it; for an item's, the item at the revision each period was read at), and a new fix is moved by the offsets of the fixes either side of it in time, in proportion to its time between them, or as the nearest beyond the first or last. Its recorded course and speed go through the same change, as a shear or a stretch carries a fix's own: a rotation turns the course, a stretch scales the speed, a shear changes both, so a new fix's course and speed agree with where it and the next are. A move is carried exactly; a shear, being proportional to time, exactly within the period it covered; a rotation, a stretch and smoothing, closely. A fix dragged on its own moves only the new fix at its very time, never those about it. On a track plotted by dead reckoning the edits change courses and speeds (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026), so a new fix's course gains the change in course of the fixes either side and its speed their change in proportion, its course, speed and position as logged are kept beside it, and the positions after it are worked out again by dead reckoning; an item with no courses and speeds cannot supply a DR track, and says so. Replay never reads an item again: each step records its output, so undo, redo and a colleague's copy of the plot need none of the items (SUB-19). 8. Revisions. Any recorded change to an item, of its data or its details, is a new revision (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): its revision is its plot's content hash (debrief:revision), which changes with every step and comes back with undo. Changing only an item's view (its time window, its Tote) is no revision. A product is any plot whose tracks take data from an item (each period naming the item and the revision it was read at, kept in its STAC metadata as debrief:drawn_from): a plot that took data, a copy saved from one, a colleague's plot file added with its history. When a period was read at a revision of the item other than its revision now, the product may need review; once none of its data comes from the item any more, it is not flagged for it. Then: VS Code says so once, in a notification naming the plot and the item, with Show in Catalogues; the playground says so in a note. The product is flagged in the catalogue (a warning symbol and May need review, with the reason as its tooltip) and in Coverage, with Reviewed to clear the flag. Clearing is view state in the product's island, never a step (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026); the island keeps who cleared it and when (by, at), a light audit trail, as it does for Not now. The flag comes back at the item's next revision. VS Code says a revision once in each session, so after a restart it says outstanding ones once more. Taking the item again (Take again under Revised since taken) reads the periods it supplies from its latest revision. Items a product names that are not in the analyst's catalogues are passed over.

docs.title: What is a step, and what isn't
docs.text: Where Undoable In the history Taking new data The plot's tracks (supplies, platform_links), new tracks Yes Yes, naming the item and its revision Choosing which item supplies a period The track's supplies and fixes Yes Yes, naming the item, the period and its revision Confirming, refusing or linking a platform The track's platform_links or platform_unlinks Yes Yes Setting new data aside (Not now) The plot's island (collation.dismissed, with who and when) No No Clearing a review flag (Reviewed) The product's island (collation.reviewed, with who and when) No No Taking an item whose data the plot has already The plot's island (collation.reviewed) No No Coverage, revisions, what an item drew from The item's STAC metadata, worked out at each change

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text:
• Catalogues lists each item's tracks under it, with the periods each has data for (08:00:00Z – 12:00:00Z · 241 fixes), and, with a plot open, how each is known to it (proposed as BLUE ONE, linked to BLUE ONE). Items are marked open, New data, May need review or drawn from, each with its icon and words, the reason in the tooltip and read by screen readers. An item's menu (right-click, Shift+F10) has Take data into the open plot…, Not now: set this new data aside and Reviewed: clear the review flag; a track's has Same platform as a track in the open plot… and Not this platform. Show coverage is on the view's title bar.
  • Coverage, a view below Catalogues (folded until used), is the same component as the playground's: May need review, New data with Take and Not now, Revised since taken with Take again, then each of the plot's tracks with a line and a bar for each source, the periods it supplies filled, the rest outlined, and a list for each period with a choice. Platforms with a choice to make are open; the rest are folded, so a study of fifty items stays readable.
  • Agents and keyboard macros: Debrief: Take data into the open plot… and Debrief: Reviewed: clear the review flag in the Command Palette; debrief.collate takes what Coverage would send.

docs.title: In the playground
docs.text: Catalogue lists the items in the folder tree the plot draws from, each with its marks, its tracks (folded under N tracks) and Open, Take, Not now and Reviewed; plots elsewhere in the catalogue that may need review are listed after them. Coverage is the same component as VS Code's. Under Try, New data arrives for this plot imports a navigation log for the open plot's first track (fiction, like the sample: every 10 s over part of its period and on after it ends, 120 m from where the plot has it, under its name in other letters, and a contact the plot has never seen), as an analyst's import would; A colleague revises an item this plot drew from corrects that log by 0.1 nmi, as one step in it.

docs.text:
Where Key or gesture Does Coverage Tab Reaches Reviewed, each Take and Not now, each platform's heading, each Same platform, Not this platform and Unlink, and each period's list A platform's heading Enter, Space Opens or folds it A period's list ↑ ↓ (or Alt+↓ to open it) Picks an item for that period: no step yet A period's list, or its Set Enter; click, tap The item picked supplies that period: one step A source's bar Click, tap Chooses that source for the period clicked, where it has data: one step (the list is the keyboard's way) An item or track in Catalogues Shift+F10, menu key; press and hold on a touch screen Its menu: take, set aside, clear a flag; same platform, not this platform The playground's Catalogue Tab, Enter Each item's buttons; Enter or Space on N tracks lists them

Coverage has no menu of its own, so nothing needs pressing and holding: every choice is a button or a list. Every button, list and bar is at least 24 pixels tall on a touch screen or a phone's width, and focus stays where it was when Coverage is drawn again after a step. A refused choice puts its list back to the source supplying the period. A platform with more than 40 periods to choose lists the first 40 and says how many more: their bars choose them.

docs.title: Performance (NFR-01)
docs.text:
Coverage reads each item's STAC metadata, a few kilobytes, never its plot; only the open plot is read whole, which opening it does anyway. Measured on the development container on 16 Oct 2026, with fifty items of four tracks of 2,000 fixes each (400,000 fixes; test_coverage_of_a_study_of_fifty_items_stays_responsive):

What Measured Coverage of a plot, the first time (its plot file read, every item read) 150 to 230 ms Coverage again (items unchanged since, read from memory by their file's version) 35 to 45 ms Fifty gappy sources of one platform, a hundred spans each (5,000 spans, 9,800 periods; test_coverage_of_gappy_sources_stays_responsive) 250 to 370 ms the first time, 15 to 30 ms after Review flags for the whole catalogue 5 to 230 ms (items read, or from memory) Coverage of serial 1 of the sample (six items, with the navigation log) in the playground, Pyodide, asking to answer median 70 to 90 ms, slowest 160 to 330 ms, over 20 asks in each of three runs Working out a plot's coverage for its metadata at a save, fifty tracks of 2,000 fixes 90 ms the first save in a process, under 2 ms after (spans kept by each track's times' hash)

A platform's periods are cut by a sweep along the time, each source's spans opening and closing at their bounds, so the work grows with the number of spans rather than spans times bounds (Python and TypeScript alike); its rows are kept while its sources, its supplies and its fixes are unchanged. The Timeline finds a track's pieces in one pass over its fixes.

Budget: coverage within 500 ms the first time a plot of a 50-item study is opened and within 100 ms after; review flags within 500 ms. Taking new data and choosing a period read the items involved in full, and their histories where a revision must be replayed: they are steps, within NFR-01's 5 s failure line, not drags. Keeping each item's coverage in its metadata costs each save of a plot the spans of its changed tracks only, a few milliseconds beside the save itself.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: What happens when a plot changes on disk while an analyst has it open.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-28 Debrief detects the change and never silently overwrites it. SUB-29 Offer to save as a new plot; offer to merge non-overlapping changes by replaying deltas; never merge overlapping changes automatically; never lock files. SUB-14, SUB-35 Refuse newer-schema files; warn before writing a newer-schema file into a shared catalogue. NFR-11 Saves are atomic; a failed save leaves the original intact and says so. SUB-19 The plot's whole history is in its plot file, protected by checksums.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Plots are never locked (SUB-29). Instead every change says which version of the plot it was made against (its base), and is refused if the plot has moved on.

  1. Noticed while open. Debrief checks each second whether the open plot's file has changed on disk: another window, another analyst on a shared folder, an agent. The plot file holds the plot's whole history, so Debrief compares the history's current step, how many steps it holds, and the checksum of the content the current step recorded. If the plot has moved on, the map, outline and History view show the latest, and a notification says "Serial 1 was changed elsewhere. Debrief is showing the latest." (SUB-28). Nothing the analyst had done is lost: their changes were already saved as steps. If only the plot's time window changed (its island), Debrief shows the new window and says so, without reading the plot again.
  2. Met by a tool run. If the plot changed between the analyst opening it and running a tool, the tool's result is not saved. Debrief asks, in a dialog:
  3. where the two changes touch different features: Combine the changes (the tool's result is applied on top of the other change) or Save mine as a new plot;
  4. where they touch the same features (including a named set that refers to a feature the other change deleted): only Save mine as a new plot. Overlapping changes are never combined automatically.
  5. Cancel saves nothing and shows the latest; the analyst can run the tool again.
  6. Saved as a new plot. The new plot, Serial 1 (your changes), has the history the analyst was working from (every step up to it, unchanged, checksums and all), the same sources and files, and then their change. The original keeps the other change. Debrief offers to open it.
  7. Met by undo. Undo is refused if the plot changed since it was shown; Debrief shows the latest and says nothing was undone.

  8. Newer schema. A plot written by a newer Debrief is refused, with the version it needs, and never partly loaded (SUB-14). Before saving a change, an undo or an import would write a newer schema into a catalogue other analysts share, Debrief says so and asks: Save anyway updates the catalogue's declared version; closing the dialog saves nothing (SUB-35). Until schema 1.0 a catalogue must match exactly to open at all (SUB-13), so the question first appears after 1.0.

  9. Changed outside Debrief. A plot whose history fails its checksums (a step altered, removed or moved by hand) is shown as its file holds it, but Debrief changes nothing in it and says so: "This plot's history has been changed outside Debrief: step 2 of its history is not as Debrief recorded it. Debrief shows the plot as its file holds it, but will not change it. Ask whoever sent it for a fresh copy." A plot whose content no longer matches its intact history (edited in another program, say) is rebuilt from its history, the file as found is kept beside it, and Debrief says so. A change to the time window alone is never treated as either.

Each save rewrites the whole plot file, content and history together, through a new file that replaces the old one only once it is complete, and takes a lock for the milliseconds it lasts, so two processes saving at once can't interleave; a reader never waits (NFR-11). If a process dies part-way, the plot file is the one from before that save, whole; opening the plot says a save was interrupted.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant History as Plot history
    Note over History: someone else adds step 5
    Analyst->>Host: Run closest approach
    Host->>Service: tools/call (base: step 4)
    Service->>History: commit (base step 4)
    History-->>Service: Conflict (mergeable: different features)
    Service-->>Host: isError, _meta debrief/conflict
    Host->>Analyst: Combine the changes / Save mine as a new plot / Cancel
    Analyst->>Host: Combine the changes
    Host->>Service: tools/call (base: step 4, on_conflict: merge)
    Service->>History: commit step 6 after step 5
    Host->>Host: reload plot and History view

docs.title: Exported images
docs.text: How an analyst exports the map as an image for a report or a slide, and how anyone holding that image, in a Word report or a PowerPoint deck months later, finds the plot it came from, as it was then.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-25 Images exported from Debrief carry an embedded GUID in their metadata linking back to their source. EXT-05 Report images: out, with embedded GUID metadata. OUT-04 Traceable figures in Word and PowerPoint: any exported image traces back to its source plot by GUID. OUT-01 Report figures produced without leaving Debrief. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; earlier states are reached by replay. SUB-22 View state in the island is neither undoable nor recorded. SUB-30 One map component in every host. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. What is exported is what the analyst sees (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): the map drawn as it is drawn on screen, never redrawn another way. Tracks and their parts in the time window, context tracks, labels, symbols and arrows at their intervals, annotations and their labels, the narrative box beside its track, current time's markers, the Tote's lines, the north arrow and the scale bar, land and the graticule. Labels are where the map placed them, kept clear of one another, because the image is written from the map as laid out. Not in it: the map's controls and key, its notes, the drawing toolbar, handles, fixes ringed to check, and the selection's outline and the dimming of everything else, which are for working, not for a report.
  2. Three sizes, two colours. As on screen (the map's own size, twice over for sharpness), Slide, 1600 × 900 (16:9, laid out at 1200 × 675 and scaled by 4/3 so its text reads at a slide's size) and A4 landscape (1754 × 1240, A4 at 150 dots an inch, laid out at 877 × 620 and doubled). For a size other than the screen's the map is laid out at that size for a moment, the same area fitted, so labels are placed and thinned for it (the narrative box on the side its marker has room at that size), then put back exactly as it was. A picture of the map as it was covers it meanwhile, so the analyst sees no jump and no flash of colour; anything sent to the map meanwhile (a selection made, say) is shown once it is put back, never undone by it. As on screen colours, or Light, for print: VS Code's Light Modern, whatever the editor's theme; data colours are the same in both.
  3. PNG or SVG; no JPEG (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). An SVG keeps every line and label as a vector, its text as text, with its letter-spacing and tabular figures; each image clips to an id of its own, so two pasted into one document do not share one. A PNG is that SVG drawn onto a canvas. The map draws no reference tiles; were one ever shown it would be left out, and said (expert panel, 16 Oct 2026).

  4. Each image carries an ID (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026) naming the plot, the exact revision exported (the plot's content hash, so the step on screen) and the export itself, so a figure traces to exactly what was on screen even after the plot is changed:

    Written Where In full DBF1-PTETVDX3-KG8RB9E5X7Y58R98-M6SC7N75-Z The image's metadata: a PNG's iTXt chunk debrief:figure and its XMP (dc:identifier), before the image data; an SVG's metadata element, as XMP Short DBF-PTET-KG8R-B9EM-69 The footer, and what an analyst types

    In Crockford's base 32: digits and capital letters without I, L, O or U, so it reads aloud and types without confusion. In full: DBF1; the plot key, 8 symbols, the first 40 bits of the SHA-256 of the catalogue's own id and the item's id (as collation names items, never a title or a folder's name, so it means the same on every analyst's machine); the revision, 16 symbols, the first 80 bits of the plot's content hash; the export, 8 random symbols, so two exports of one view are two images; and a check symbol, Luhn mod 32 over the rest. The short form, DBF-PPPP-RRRR-RRRE-EC, keeps 4 symbols of the plot key, 7 of the revision and 2 of the export, with a check symbol of its own: enough to find the plot and the step among a catalogue's plots, and to tell one export of a revision from another (one in 1,024 shares the export's two symbols with another of the same revision; then both are listed to choose from). Any one symbol mistyped is caught, never looked up. Typed, case, spaces and dashes do not matter, and O is read as 0, I and L as 1. Nothing else goes into the image: not the plot's title, its catalogue's name nor who exported it. Python and TypeScript hold the format to schemas/vectors/figure-ids.json. 5. The footer (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): the short form, 1.4% of the image's width high (22 pixels on a slide, 25 on A4; never under 14; product owner, 16 Oct 2026, down from 2% so it does not dominate a slide), so it still reads when Word shows the image at half a page's width, in the theme's quieter text colour and haloed in the background's, so it reads on any theme and over any track. It goes in the corner, of the four, where it covers least of the plot (the fewest points of its tracks, annotations and labels), beside, never over, the scale bar or the north arrow; bottom left where nothing is in the way. On by default, and on again for every export: turned off for one export with Image ID in a corner, it is not remembered off (expert panel, 16 Oct 2026); the size and colours are remembered. It is the main trace once an office program drops an image's metadata (see Office programs below). 6. Each export is logged in the plot's island (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): its ID, the revision, when, who, the area exported (its viewport), current time and the time window, the format, size and colours, the file's name (not its folder) and whether it had the footer (PlotView.exports). With it, the Tote's tracks shown (tote). View state: never a step, so an export changes neither the plot's revision nor any product that drew from it, and undo never takes one back. The newest 500 are kept, the oldest dropped first; an image whose entry is gone still traces by its ID, only its view and time are not restored (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). Who exported and the file's name stay in it. An entry's time must be within its window, whoever sends it. 7. The analyst's own export log (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): where the plot's log cannot be written (its catalogue is read-only), the export goes into exports.json beside the analyst's Debrief configuration, naming the catalogue and the plot; Find source of image… reads it as it reads the plots', so every export stays traceable. The newest 2,000 are kept. The analyst is told which log has it. 8. Find source of image. Pick an image (Debrief reads its metadata: a PNG, an SVG, or each picture in a Word, PowerPoint or LibreOffice file) or type the ID from its footer. Debrief finds the plot in the analyst's catalogues, at the step whose revision the ID names, and opens it read-only as it was then: rebuilt by replay from its history and checked against the step that recorded it, as undo is, so it is exactly what was on screen. The view and the time come from the export log where it has the image; the map says The plot at step 3 of 7, as when image DBF-PTET-KG8R-B9EM-69 was exported. Read-only. with Go to latest. Nothing can be changed there: every change is refused, and said, until the analyst goes to the latest. The History shows the step as shown read-only. The Tote is worked out on the plot as it was then, with the tracks it showed when the image was exported, so the view traced matches the figure, its lines included (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). 9. Several match. A footer's short form, or an ID typed from an old image, can name more than one export of a revision; each is listed with when it was exported and the area it showed, for the analyst to choose. Debrief never picks one, first or last (expert panel, 16 Oct 2026). Each picture in a Word or PowerPoint file is read on its own, so a report with several figures traces each; a picture that cannot be read (encrypted, damaged, compressed in a way Debrief cannot read) is skipped and said why, and the others are still read. 10. Copies. A plot moved to another catalogue, or sent to a colleague, has another plot key but the same revisions: where no plot of the image's key has its revision, any plot that does is found, and said to be a copy, with the same content then. Several found are listed to choose from. 11. A plot whose history is damaged (shown as its file holds it, never changed) is still exported, its ID naming its content's hash, and traced (expert panel, 16 Oct 2026). 12. An earlier revision exports as itself: exported while shown read-only, an image's ID names that revision, so its short form is the same.

docs.title: What is a step, and what isn't
docs.text: Where Undoable In the history Exporting an image The plot's island (exports: the export log), or the analyst's own export log No No Showing an earlier revision Nowhere: the plot file is not changed The image's ID The image (metadata, footer) and the export log

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text:
• Debrief: Export image… (the camera on the map's title bar, the Outline's menu, the Command Palette) asks three things, each from the keyboard: the size (a list), what it shows (Image ID in a corner and Light colours, for print, ticked or not), and where to save it, as PNG or SVG by the name given (the plot's title and the image's short ID). The size and colours are remembered for next time; the footer is on each time. A notification names the file and its ID, with Copy ID and Show in folder.
  • Debrief: Find source of image… (Catalogues' title bar menu, the Command Palette): Choose an image file… or Type the ID from the image's corner…, the ID checked as it is typed. The plot opens read-only, at the view and time exported; Go to latest is on the map, its title bar and the History's.
  • Agents and keyboard macros pass the choices and the file: debrief.exportImage with {format, preset, theme, footer, file, overwrite}, debrief.findImageSource with {file} or {id}, and choose (counting from 0) where several match; without it the analyst is asked. A file given this way is written only inside the workspace's folders or the folder set in Debrief: Export folder (debrief.exportFolder), resolved through any link, and over a file there only with overwrite and the analyst's yes to Replace (expert panel, 16 Oct 2026). The tool service writes no image file: the extension does.
  • While an earlier revision is shown read-only, the extension refuses every tool service request aimed at that plot that is not on an allow-list of methods that leave a plot alone (schemas/vectors/service-methods.json, held to Python's list), and opens it without finishing an interrupted change, which would write to it.

docs.title: In the playground
docs.text: The Export image panel: Format, Size, Colours and Image ID in a corner (ticked again after each export), then Export image…, which hands the file to the browser to save. There is no save dialog to rename it in, so the panel says plainly that the file's name has the plot's title in it (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026). Below it, Find source of image: choose a file, or type the ID from its corner and press Find (or Enter). The plot is opened as it was, read-only, with Go to latest on the map; any plot found is also listed with Open as exported, with when it was exported and the area it showed; where several match, none is opened until the reader chooses.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text:
debrief/export_image with {store, item, file, preset?, theme?, footer?, overwrite?, agent} exports the plot as the analyst would (decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): the tool service asks the map open in VS Code to draw it, through the same path as Export image…, and the extension writes the file, within the folders above, asking the analyst before replacing one. Refused, and said, if no map is open (no VS Code polling the service) or the map shows another plot. Drawing lays the analyst's map out at the image's size for a moment, under a picture of it. An earlier revision shown read-only exports as itself. debrief/find_image_source reads a file or a typed ID, listing every export it names, and skipped for pictures it could not read; debrief/open_revision gives the plot as it was at a revision; debrief/figure_id gives a fresh ID. A host gives debrief/export_image the image it drew (image): the ID is put into its metadata, the export logged, and the image given back to write.

Only debrief/export_image may send a request up to 48 MB (an image); every other method keeps the 10 MB limit.

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text:
Where Key or gesture Does VS Code Export image…: ↑ ↓ Enter on the size, Space to tick, Enter; the save dialog Exports the map VS Code Find source of image…: ↑ ↓ Enter; the open dialog, or type the ID and Enter Opens the plot as it was, read-only The map, an earlier revision Tab to Go to latest, Enter; tap The plot as it is now The playground's Export image panel Tab through its lists, the tick box and Export image…; Enter in the ID box finds it As VS Code

docs.title: Office programs (informative)
docs.text:
Tried on 16 Oct 2026, with a PNG exported from the sample. python-docx, python-pptx and LibreOffice were the only office programs tried: Word and PowerPoint themselves were not available, so nothing here says what they do.

Into Then The ID in the picture's metadata A .docx by python-docx Kept: the picture is stored byte for byte A .pptx by python-pptx Kept: stored byte for byte The .docx and .pptx Saved again by LibreOffice 7 as .docx, .pptx and .odt Kept The .docx Saved as PDF by LibreOffice Gone: the picture is re-encoded

Word compresses a document's pictures to 220 pixels an inch on save by default, and its Compress pictures and saving as PDF re-encode a picture: any of them may drop the metadata. So the footer is the main trace, typed into Find source of image…; the metadata is a convenience where it survives. Find source of image… reads a Word, PowerPoint or LibreOffice file picture by picture, so a whole report can be checked at once.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Measured in the playground's test on 16 Oct 2026 (headless Chromium, the sample's serial 1), from Export image… to the file handed to the browser, Python under Pyodide minting, stamping and logging: a slide's PNG in 670 to 720 ms, A4 landscape in light colours in about 670 ms, a PNG as on screen in about 620 ms, an SVG as on screen in about 340 ms (after the expert panel's review, which added the picture laid over the map while it is resized: 90 to 270 ms more than before). The map is laid out at the image's size and put back within a few frames; the analyst sees Preparing the image… over a picture of the map. Finding a plot by an image reads the item ids of each catalogue and only the plots whose key matches. Each item lists the revisions its plot has had (debrief:revisions, written with each step), so a copy, found by its revision alone, or an ID that matches nothing, reads only the items, never a plot without the revision; an item from before items kept the list is read whole.

docs.title: Keyboard equivalents
docs.text:
How every map action can be done without a mouse.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 3. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement NFR-13 The interface is operable by keyboard; every map action (dragging a track, drawing an annotation, measuring) has a keyboard or form-based equivalent; themes, including high contrast, are honoured.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Written so far for annotations and for moving, rotating, shearing and stretching tracks; the rest of the map follows in Phase 3.

Map action Without a pointer Draw a line, area, circle, ellipse, label or marker Tab to the map's Draw an annotation toolbar, Enter on a kind; the arrow keys pan the map under the cross in its middle, Space places a point there, Enter finishes, Backspace removes the last, Escape cancels. Or Add annotation… and type the positions (annotations, items 1 to 6). Drag a corner, centre, radius, axis or label Tab to its handle; the arrow keys move it 5 pixels (25 with Shift); the run of presses is one step when they stop, on Enter, or when the keyboard moves on (presses made while it is saved follow as the next step); Escape puts it back. Or type the change on its properties form. Add a corner between two Arrow keys on the handle between them. Remove a corner Delete or Backspace on its handle. Cut at current time… on the same menu says the bearings and sides of the cut the map emphasises and opens its menu (keep either bearing, ambiguous again, select it): move current time to reach any cut. The Command Palette has both. In the playground, a sensor row's menu, and, with a sensor or a cut selected, Port…, Starboard… and Both again… under Sensor below the Outline. The choices beside a clicked cut are buttons: Tab between them, Enter to choose, Escape back to the map. Set a towed array's offset astern Towed array offset… on a sensor's menu in the Outline, or the Command Palette: type the distance (0 for at the ship), then choose worm in the hole or plain; one step. In the playground, a sensor row's menu. Find source of image…: a list, then the open dialog or the ID typed and Enter. On the map, Tab to Go to latest and Enter. docs.title: Labels, symbols and arrows
docs.text: How an analyst chooses how often a track is labelled with the time, marked with a symbol and given a direction arrow; where the map draws them, and how it keeps them legible at any zoom.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-32 Select one or more tracks and set how often their fixes are labelled, marked with a symbol and given a direction arrow, each from 1 second to 24 hours; one change applies to every selected track; the intervals are held per track. SUB-22 Presentation content, like colour: each change is one recorded, undoable step. SUB-01 Times are UTC; the analyst's time zone is for display only. SUB-03 Positions between fixes are along the geodesic. EXT-14 A legacy plot file's content comes in, and what does not is listed. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Three intervals, held by the track. Each track has label_interval, symbol_interval and arrow_interval on its own properties: one value for the track, never one per fix (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). Each is a duration, a whole number of seconds from 1 s to 24 h; or off; for labels and symbols, all, at every recorded fix, legacy Debrief's All (product owner, 15 Oct 2026; arrows have no All); or left out, Debrief's default. The defaults are what the map drew before: no time labels, no symbols, and a few arrows along the track's part in the time window (up to five, at the middle of legs). Arrows set off draw none. Schema 0.0.20.
  2. One step for all the tracks chosen. Select the tracks (Ctrl-click in the outline or on the map), then Frequencies: labels, symbols and arrows… (the outline's menu, the Command Palette) or Frequencies… under Track in the playground. One change is one step for every track chosen, named for what it set: Labels every 10 min, arrows every 5 min on BLUE ONE and RED ONE; Symbols off on 3 tracks. Undo takes it back for all of them. The intervals stay per track, so tracks set together may later differ.
  3. The form. A heading, the tracks it is for, and a chooser each for Labels, Symbols and Arrows, nothing else (the product owner rejects cluttered forms). Each shows what the tracks have now. Where they differ it shows Mixed (unchanged), and a chooser left so changes nothing for any of them. The choices are Off (and, for arrows, A few (default); for labels and symbols, All (every fix)), then every 1 s, 5 s, 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 5 min, 10 min, 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h, legacy Debrief's choices, and Other…, a box to type an interval in: 90 s, 1h30, 2 hours, 1 day, or all (not for arrows). Beneath it the form says what it read (Means every 1 h 30 min) or what is wrong (Say the unit, such as 30 s, 10 min or 1 h 30 min.; An interval is from 1 s to 24 h.), and sends nothing until it is right. In VS Code the same choices come as three short lists, one after the other, each starting at what the tracks have now; typing an interval offers it at the top. Only what changed is sent: a chooser showing what every track already has changes nothing, and with nothing changed there is no step.
  4. On whole multiples of the interval, as legacy Debrief. Items fall at each whole multiple of the interval of UTC: every 10 min is 0900, 0910, 0920, wherever the track starts (legacy LightweightTrackWrapper.setFixes rounds the track's start up to a multiple of the frequency). UTC has no daylight saving, so every 24 h is midnight Zulu every day. A track too short to hold a multiple gets one, at its start, as legacy Debrief labels it. Only within the time window and the track's span: outside the window a track is context (thin, faint or hidden as the plot says) and carries none, as it carries no arrows or dots.
  5. Where the track was then. Between fixes, the position is along the geodesic in proportion to time, exactly as the square at current time is placed (pointAt in geodesic.ts, the same code as positionAt, held to schemas/vectors/track-positions.json). Legacy Debrief instead marked the first fix at or after each multiple, so with sparse fixes its labels said the fix's own time (0931); Debrief labels the time asked for, on the line. Nothing is drawn inside a gap in the data (fixes more than ten times the track's median time between fixes apart, as smoothing treats a gap): no position is made up where nothing was recorded.
  6. What is drawn.
    • A label is the time, HHmm, legacy Debrief's default fix label; HHmm.ss where the interval is not whole minutes (or, at every fix, where the fix's time is not); and ddHHmm on the first label of each day that is drawn, so the day is never in doubt. It is in the analyst's time zone, Zulu by default, with no zone letter, as on a chart. It sits to port of the track's course, as legacy Debrief places a fix's label, at the end of a short leader in the track's colour, the text in the theme's text colour with a halo, so it is legible on any track colour and any theme. Labels never overlap: all tracks' labels are placed together, earliest first, each to port, or to starboard where port is taken (by another label, a track's name, a fix's own label or a track's end marker), or left out where both are; a fix's label always shown is placed first and never left out. They sit above arrows and markers, below the tracks' names.
    • A symbol is a small dot in the track's colour, with a thin halo in the map's colour.
    • An arrow is the map's chevron, centred on the line and pointing along the course there (the leg leaving a fix, at a fix; the last course it made, where the track stood still). None is drawn within 12 px of a track's first or last fix in the window, where an arrow on the end marker would read as a second arrowhead. A track with an arrow interval set (or off) draws none of the default few.
    • At every fix (all), each fix's time, until fixes would be closer on screen than the spacing; then the smallest preset at least the fixes' median time apart, thinned as any interval is.
  7. Thinned to fit, and said. Zoomed out, items set close together would pile up. The map raises the interval to the smallest clock-friendly multiple of it that leaves them far enough apart on screen (labels 44 px, arrows 28 px, symbols 10 px, on the track's average speed across the screen), so thinned labels still fall on round times: 10 min becomes 20 min, 30 min or 1 h, never 50 min. Where the track is slower than its average, or doubles back, any item closer than that to the one before is left out. No track draws more than 100 labels, 150 arrows or 400 symbols, and only what is in view, or near it, is drawn, again after each pan or zoom. A quiet note above the key says what was thinned, naming the tracks where only some were: Labels every 1 h, arrows every 30 min at this zoom; zoom in for more; Labels every 20 min on RED ONE at this zoom; zoom in for more. It also says some labels left out where more than a quarter of a track's gave way to others.
    • Cheap to pan. Symbols and arrows are painted on one canvas, not drawn as thousands of elements; labels already drawn are kept from one pan to the next; each track is projected once, and positions are worked out once a time (along the straight line on the map's plane on legs under 2 km, where it is the geodesic to well under a millimetre; along the geodesic on longer ones). Budget, measured in the playground with 50 tracks of 2,000 fixes each, labels every minute, symbols every second and arrows every 30 s: redrawing them after a pan takes 5 to 35 ms, and a pan blocks the page once, for 50 to 90 ms, where it blocked it 10 to 14 times for over a second in all before (headless Chromium, software rendering). The budget: after a pan, within 50 ms to redraw and 100 ms blocked; zooming into the densest view, at most 300 ms, once. Zoomed in, every item comes back.
  8. A fix's own label or symbol, always (force on only). A single fix can always show its time label, its symbol or both, whatever the track's intervals and at any zoom: show_label and show_symbol on the fix's mark (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). There is no per-fix off. A forced fix is drawn once where an interval falls on it too, and is never thinned away: it was asked for. Set from the fix's menu (right-click or press and hold the fix on the map; Fixes…): Always show its time label, Always show its symbol and their opposites in VS Code, Time label and Symbol buttons (pressed when on) in the playground's fix list; each change is one step (BLUE ONE fix at 09:31:00Z: time label always shown). The mark follows its fix through moves, splits, merges, smoothing and jump removal, as any mark does.
  9. Shown with the track's details. The outline says each track's intervals: in VS Code, the track's tooltip ends Labels every 10 min · Symbols off · Arrows every 5 min; in the playground, a track with any set has a quiet second line naming those set, and the whole line when pointed at. A fix's details (its tooltip on the map, the fix list) say time label always shown, symbol always shown. Agents read the intervals in the plot debrief/open returns, on each track's properties.
  10. Agents. debrief/set_track_frequencies with features (track ids) and any of label_interval, symbol_interval, arrow_interval: a duration ({value, unit}), seconds, text such as "10 min" or "1h30", "off", "all" (labels and symbols at every fix), or null for the default. One step; refused, saying why, for an interval outside 1 s to 24 h, arrows at every fix, or a feature that is not a track. debrief/mark_fix takes show_label and show_symbol (true, or false to stop).
sequenceDiagram
  actor Analyst
  participant Form as Frequencies form
  participant Host as Host (VS Code or playground)
  participant Python as debrief/set_track_frequencies
  participant Map
  Analyst->>Form: Labels every 10 min, Arrows every 5 min (2 tracks)
  Form->>Host: only what changed
  Host->>Python: features, label_interval, arrow_interval, base
  Python-->>Host: one step: "Labels every 10 min, arrows every 5 min on BLUE ONE and RED ONE"
  Host->>Map: the plot again
  Map->>Map: multiples of 10 min in the window and in view, thinned to fit
  Map-->>Analyst: labels to port, arrows on the line; a note if thinned
  1. Legacy plots. A .dpf file's display rules (CoreFormatter: Label, Symbol or Arrow, every so many milliseconds, for one named track or every track) become those tracks' intervals; legacy All (an interval of 0) becomes all for labels and symbols. Legacy Debrief writes no frequency on a track itself, so where no rule says, the fixes it showed with their label, symbol or arrow give the interval, where they fall exactly as legacy Debrief would have shown them at a preset, or at every fix. Everything else is listed in the import notes: an inactive rule, an interval outside 1 s to 24 h, arrows at every fix, a rule naming no imported track, a symbology match (legacy did not apply it either), a rule not on regular intervals (applied on whole multiples here), and arrows shown at no interval (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). Labels and symbols shown at no interval are kept as those fixes always showing theirs, and the notes say how many (product owner, 16 Oct 2026).

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text: The form is a form: Tab between choosers, arrow keys within one, Enter applies, Escape cancels. In VS Code the lists are VS Code's own, one after another, with Back to the list before (product owner, 16 Oct 2026). A fix's menu opens by right-click, press and hold on a touch screen, or the fix list from Fixes… (keyboard equivalents).

docs.text:

docs.title: Selection and tool offering
docs.text:
How an analyst selects features, in the map, outline or catalogue, and how Debrief offers the tools that apply to that selection.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-26, SUB-27 Selection is shared state that views, extensions and tools can all read and set. TL-06 Each tool declares the feature types it applies to. TL-08 The tools offered are those that apply to every selected item. TL-09 A tool declaring an unknown type is not offered, and Debrief says why. TL-11 Named sets are reusable as a selection. NFR-13 Selection is possible by keyboard.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
One selection, everywhere. The analyst selects features in the map or the outline, and every view shows the same selection (SUB-26).

Gesture Map Outline Select one feature Click it Click it Add or remove one Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Select a range — Shift click Select all — Select all on the Outline's toolbar, or Ctrl+A in the tree: every row listed Select a row's children — Select children on the Outline's toolbar Clear Escape, or click empty sea Clear selection on the Outline's toolbar Zoom to the selection Selected button, top left —

Ctrl or Cmd adds in both places, as everywhere in VS Code. Shift selects a range in the outline, and does nothing on the map, which has no order to make a range of.

  • Showing selection.
  • On the map. Each selected feature gets a dotted outline in the theme's text colour. That colour is never a force colour, so selecting tracks never makes them look blue or red. Everything else is dimmed.
  • In the outline. Selected features are marked selected. The last one selected elsewhere is revealed and highlighted.
  • In the tools view. The selection is counted.

  • The Outline's toolbar (product owner, 28 Oct 2026). Compact icon buttons at the top of the Outline act on its selection; each has a tooltip saying what it will do, or why it cannot. In VS Code they are in the Outline view's title bar; in the playground, a row above the tree.

    Button Icon (VS Code codicon) What it does Hidden on map eye when everything selected is shown; eye-closed when all of it is hidden; color-mode when some of each (the playground's is a half-closed eye) All shown: hides them all. All hidden: shows them all. Mixed: shows them all, the usual convention for a mixed toggle (aria-pressed="mixed"). One step, named with a count (3 tracks and 12 cuts hidden on the map), through the same hide and show operations as the Tools' Hide cuts and Show cuts. Tracks, TMA solutions, sensors, cuts, annotations and sensor observations can be hidden; a leg or a position cannot, and is left out, the tooltip saying so. Narrative entries are not in the Outline: they are read in the Timeline. Colour symbol-color The selected that have a colour (tracks and solutions, sensors, cuts, annotations; not chart furniture) take one colour: the palette, or a custom #rrggbb. One step. Disabled, saying why, when nothing selected has a colour. In VS Code a QuickPick; in the playground a small popover of swatches (arrow keys among them) and a custom colour. Select all check-all Every row listed: the rows of the branches open, as Ctrl+A in the tree. A sensor's cuts are not selected unless it is open. Select children type-hierarchy-sub The selection replaced by the direct children of what is selected: a track's sensors, a sensor's cuts (all of them, though VS Code pages a sensor of more than 500), a solution's legs, a leg's positions. Their branches open, the first child brought into sight. Disabled when the selection has none. Clear selection clear-all Nothing selected.

    VS Code's title bar shows one of three hide commands (debrief.selectionHide, debrief.selectionShow, debrief.selectionShowAll) by the context key debrief.selectionVisibility (visible, hidden, mixed or none); debrief.selectionColourable, debrief.selectionHasChildren and debrief.selectionNotEmpty enable the others. Its tooltips are the commands' titles, which cannot change, so the reasons are said when a command is run instead. The native tree cannot be told to select many rows, so rows selected by the toolbar are marked selected in their description, as before, and the first is revealed.

    In the playground the toolbar is role="toolbar", one tab stop with a roving tabindex: ← and → move along it (wrapping), Home and End to its ends, Enter or Space presses. A button that cannot act stays reachable (aria-disabled), its reason its description. Icons are drawn in the text colour, so they follow light, dark and high-contrast themes; under forced colours they take the system's colours, a pressed toggle the system's Highlight.

  • The selection's count, said. The Outline no longer has a hint line under its heading ("1 feature selected · Ctrl-click to add, Shift-click for a range", product owner, 28 Oct 2026): the gestures are taught by the walkthroughs (Open and explore a serial, Select tracks in the Outline). A screen reader still hears the count when it changes (3 tracks and 12 cuts selected), from a polite live region.

  • Offering tools. Whenever the selection changes, the tools view asks the tool service which tools apply to every selected item, within each tool's count limits (TL-08). The rule lives in Python, so agents get the same answer (TL-14).
  • Explaining tools not on offer. Tools that don't apply are listed under Other tools, each saying what it needs ("select 2 tracks"), rather than being hidden (CON-10).
  • Unknown data types. Tools that name a data type Debrief doesn't know appear under Not available, with the reason (TL-09).
  • Time-only annotations. These have no position, so they appear only in the outline (CAP-04).

    participant Map as Map (webview)
    participant Host as Extension host

    participant Service as Tool service (Python)

    Map->>Host: selection_changed [NELSON, BLUE]
    Host->>Outline: refresh (marks selected)
