docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Selection state: vscode/src/session.ts.
  • Map gestures: vscode/webview/map.ts.
  • Outline: vscode/src/views/outline.ts.
  • The Outline's toolbar: what each button does and says, vscode/webview/outlinetoolbar.ts; the playground's, vscode/play/outlinebar.ts; VS Code's title bar, package.json and debrief.selection* in vscode/src/extension.ts.
  • Tools view: vscode/src/views/tools.ts.
  • The offering rule: debrief_tools.registry.applies.

Not yet: keyboard selection in the map (NFR-13, Phase 3), named sets as selections (TL-11), and selection shared with other extensions and tools (SUB-27, Phase 2).

docs.title: Sensors and bearings
docs.text: How bearings from a platform's sensors come into a plot, how the map draws them, and how an analyst resolves a towed array's ambiguous bearings to one side. The ground TMA stands on (TMA solutions, CAP-21).

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-22 Import bearings and ambiguous (towed-array) bearings; the analyst resolves each ambiguous bearing to one side. Bearings are drawn as lines (product owner, 24 Oct 2026). Frequency is not imported. CAP-21 A TMA solution is rooted in a selected period of bearing data, its positions at the sensor's observation times in that period, with live bearing residuals while it is dragged. CAP-28, CAP-29 Sensor data is shown only within the plot's time window, which is the volume strategy for weeks of bearings. CAP-33 Later: a tool that proposes the side of ambiguous bearings from ownship's manoeuvres, for the analyst to confirm. Recorded, not built. SUB-22, SUB-24 Presentation is content: colour and hiding are steps. Every change is one recorded, undoable step with its parameters. EXT-01, EXT-14 REP files and legacy plot files are read as legacy Debrief read them, and what is not imported is listed. NFR-04, NFR-06 The drag budget (100 ms), and observation-heavy plots. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. A sensor belongs to its track. A sensor is a feature of its own (kind: sensor): its name, the track that carries it (host_track_id, its host), its colour, whether it is hidden, and how legacy Debrief drew it (legacy_symbology). A towed array has an array offset too: how far astern of the ship it is (array_offset, a length) and how it follows the ship (array_mode: worm_in_hole, legacy Debrief's default, or plain); below. Each of its observations is a cut, a feature too (kind: sensor_cut): its sensor, its time, its bearing, and where the file gives them, its ambiguous bearing, which of the two was kept (resolved), its range (0 is a point, below), the position it was taken from (origin), ;SENSOR3:'s bearing accuracy as written (bearing_accuracy, kept, not drawn), a label, a comment, a colour of its own, and whether it is hidden. Neither has a geometry: a cut is drawn from where its sensor was at its time (the host's position, or its array's astern of it), wherever the host is moved, split or merged; a cut with its own origin is drawn from there, and never moves with its host. A cut is its own feature, as a narrative entry is, so keeping a side of ten cuts is a step that stores ten small features, not a sensor of thousands. Schema 0.0.23.
  2. Four ways in. As legacy Debrief read them, with its tests ported:
    • REP and DSF files. ;SENSOR: (a bearing, a range), ;SENSOR2: (a bearing, its ambiguous twin, a frequency, a range) and ;SENSOR3: (a bearing, its accuracy, a frequency and its accuracy, a range) lines. A .dsf file is a REP file of sensor lines alone, read as legacy Debrief's ImportReplay read it: into a plot already open (Read sensor data into this plot (DSF, REP)…, the Outline's menu; Sensor data into the open plot under Import… in the playground), since it has no track of its own. A REP file imported as a plot brings its sensor lines in with its tracks.
    • Legacy plots (.dpf). Each track's sensors and their contacts: name, colour, visibility, every cut's time, bearing, ambiguous bearing (and whether legacy kept one side), range, label, comment, colour, visibility and line style. No longer listed as not imported.
    • Rider's narrative (Word). A Rider entry's bearing (273), with its ambiguous twin (92/112), becomes a cut of the sensor Rider bearings on the entry's platform's track, as legacy Debrief made it a sensor cut; the entry stays in the narrative, its bearing in its text. An arc (096-112) and No B are not cuts, and the record says so.
    • Agents. debrief/import_sensor (below).
  3. Which track. A sensor line names its track. It is carried by the plot's track of that name, ignoring case, or else the first one whose name starts with the same six letters (legacy BabelFish). A track matched by its first six letters only is offered first and asked to be confirmed (NELSON_GB matches NELSON by its first six letters only: which track carries NELSON_GB's sensors?), since a near name may be another ship; debrief/preview_sensor says matched_by (name or prefix). Where none matches, the analyst is asked which track carries it, or Do not read these (legacy Debrief asked, Sensor track not found); an agent says it in hosts. A sensor named UNKNOWN takes the file's name. A sensor of the same name already on the same track takes the new cuts (legacy TrackWrapper.add), so reading two files of one array makes one sensor. A file read into the plot before (by its content, under any name) is said first, and read again only if the analyst says so.
  4. Read as legacy Debrief read them, quirks kept: a token starting with N (NULL, NaN) is no value, so a line whose bearing is NULL gives no cut and is counted in the notes; a ;SENSOR: range of 0 is no range, but a ;SENSOR2: or ;SENSOR3: range of 0 is a range of 0, drawn as a point where the cut was taken, as legacy Debrief drew it; a ;SENSOR2: or ;SENSOR3: line must have a label; a ;SENSOR3: line has no ambiguous bearing, and from a sensor named UNKNOWN that gives a frequency, a bearing of 0 is none. A bearing outside 0 to 360° is read modulo 360 (-153.5 is 206.5). Ranges are yards. A sensor's colour is its symbology's second letter, legacy's colour code. Times are UTC, to the millisecond.
  5. What is not imported, said in the step's record. Frequencies (every cut that gives one, and a .dpf sensor's base frequency): acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application (CAP-22, EXT-03). Line styles: cuts are drawn solid, or dashed for a towed array's starboard bearing. An array centre from measured data (a .dpf's other array modes): its cuts are drawn from the track's position, and the notes say so. Cuts outside their host's fixes are kept but not drawn, as legacy Debrief drew none. ;SENSOR3:'s bearing accuracy is kept, as written, on each cut (bearing_accuracy), and not drawn (below). A .dpf sensor's array offset (<Offset Value="-200"/>, astern) comes in with its mode (Worm in hole or Plain; none said is legacy's default, worm in the hole), and the notes say so: its array 200 m astern (worm in the hole): its cuts are drawn, and their port and starboard told, from the array.
  6. A legacy plot's ambiguous bearings, read right. Older legacy Debrief wrote AmbiguousBearing="0.000" with HasAmbiguousBearing="false" on cuts that were never ambiguous: a placeholder, read as no ambiguous bearing and counted in the notes (of the 20,665 cuts in legacy Debrief's sample plots, 16,945 are such). A non-zero twin with HasAmbiguousBearing="false" is a cut legacy resolved: it comes in resolved, keeping the bearing legacy kept, and Make ambiguous again brings the other back (318 cuts in the samples; 922 still ambiguous, 2,480 with no twin). A .dpf track of overlapping legs (segments whose times overlap, so imported as a track per leg) gives each leg its own sensor of its cuts, each in the leg it falls in (else the nearest), so every cut is drawn from the leg it was taken on.

docs.title: A towed array astern (decision, 24 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
A towed array is hundreds of metres behind the ship, and through a turn it is not where the ship was a moment ago along its heading: it is still on the ship's track before the turn. Legacy Debrief drew an array's cuts from the array, and so does Debrief v4 (product owner, 24 Oct 2026):

  • A fixed offset per sensor, in metres unless a unit is given (300 is 300 m, whatever the display's length unit, as arrays are measured; 300 yd is yards): Towed array offset… on a sensor's menu in the Outline (or the Command Palette; in the playground, the sensor row's menu), titled Array offset: Towed array on BLUE ONE, then how it follows the ship. Past 5 km it warns: longer than any towed array, likely a unit mistyped. 0 is at the ship. One step, undone like any other: Towed array: 300 yd astern, worm in the hole. Agents: debrief/set_array_offset.
  • Worm in the hole (legacy WormInHoleOffset, its default): the array is that distance back along the ship's own past track, fix by fix, so it lags through a turn. Each leg is the geodesic between fixes, as the map draws it. Where the track before the cut is shorter than the offset, the rest is run astern of the first fix along its logged course, as legacy did. The track's along-track distance is worked out once and bisected, so a track of 200,000 fixes, or one that sat still for hours, costs a geodesic or two a cut (600 cuts on a 200,000-fix track still for three-quarters of it: 26 s before, 0.18 s in Python, 23 ms in the map). Plain (like legacy's Plain, not the same): straight astern of the ship along the course logged at the next fix (as port and starboard are told), where legacy's getBacktraceTo took a course blended between the fixes either side by time. On a steady course they agree; through a turn they differ: with a 500 m array, at 2,000 random times, the array is up to 56 m from legacy's on Ambig_tracks.rep (more than 25 m at 208 of them), and up to 981 m on legs_20.rep, whose fixes log a turn of 90° or more at once.
  • Cuts are drawn from the array, and port and starboard told from it: the course is the one logged where the array is (below). A cut with its own origin is drawn from there.
  • Held to schemas/vectors/sensor-cuts.json in both languages: legacy WormInHoleOffset's own test track (a 400 m array round two turns), an L-shaped track with a 600 m worm, its plain counterpart, and a dense turning track across the antimeridian.

docs.title: Port and starboard: the logged course (decision, 24 Oct 2026)
docs.text: Which side a bearing is on is told against the course logged at the first fix at or after the cut's time, as legacy isBearingToPort took it (getNearestTo, a fix at or after the time); where the track logs no course, the direction of travel between its fixes there. With an array offset, the course is the array's (logged where the array is, at the time the ship was there), a deliberate departure from legacy (product owner, 24 Oct 2026): legacy's isBearingToPort always took the ship's course at the cut's time. An array's ambiguous bearings are mirrored about the axis the array is actually lying on, which, through a turn, is the course the ship had where the array now is, not the ship's heading. It changes the side of few cuts: on legacy's Ambig_tracks.rep, 41 of its 721 cuts with a 500 m array, 183 with 2 km. So at a turn, a cut taken between the last fix on the old heading and the first on the new is told against the new heading, as legacy told it. legacy legs_20.rep's case is in the vectors: a track running north between fixes, its next fix logging 090, a bearing of 045 is port, as legacy said, where the line between the fixes would call it starboard.

docs.title: On the map
docs.text:
1. Lines from the host, in the time window. Every cut in the time window is drawn: from its host's position at its time, along the geodesic between fixes, exactly as the square at current time is placed (pointAt), or from its array's position astern of it (above), or from its own position where the file gave one (wherever its host is); along the geodesic at its bearing, to its range, or else past the edge of the view (twice the view's larger side, at most five degrees of arc, legacy Debrief's length). None is drawn outside its host's span, unless it has its own position. A cut of range 0 is a dot where it was taken. Each is in its sensor's colour, or its own. A cut outside the window is not drawn at all: the window is the volume strategy (CAP-29). A hidden sensor, a hidden host, or a hidden cut is not drawn.
  2. Two bearings until one is kept. An ambiguous cut is two lines, both in its sensor's colour: the one to port of the logged course solid, the one to starboard darker and dashed, so the sides are told apart without colour (legacy Debrief drew starboard darker). Which side a bearing is on is legacy relBearing's: the bearing less the host's course there, within ±180°, port when below zero. A resolved cut is its kept line alone, solid.
  3. The current cut. For each sensor, the cut current time is at (the last at or before it, in the window) is drawn wider, haloed in the map's colour, with a dot where it is drawn from. The key says what each kind of line is, once the plot has cuts.
  4. Pointing at a cut says its sensor and time, its bearings and the side each is on, which was kept, its range, label and comment, and, for an ambiguous one, Click for its choices; Alt-click this line to keep it. The side is the one worked out when the line was drawn, so pointing reads no fixes (it took 44 ms a frame on ALPHA.rep before).
  5. A click selects (decision, 24 Oct 2026). A plain click on a cut's line, or a tap, selects the cut and shows its choices beside it: what it is (its label too), Keep 045.0° (port), Keep 135.0° (starboard), or Make ambiguous again once resolved, and More… for its menu. Tab moves between them, Enter chooses, Escape closes and returns to the map. A plain click never changes a cut: a click meant to select, or the first of a double-click to zoom, kept a side by accident before (panel finding H2). Alt-click one of an ambiguous cut's two lines to keep that one at once, one step. Ctrl-click adds a cut to the selection, or takes it out. The second click of a double-click does nothing. Selected cuts are haloed as a selected track is, and with a selection elsewhere the rest are dimmed; selecting its sensor or its host selects all its cuts' lines.
  6. Exported images draw the cuts as the map shows them, the current ones wider (SUB-25).

docs.title: Resolving ambiguity
docs.text:
1. One cut. Click a cut's line and choose Keep 045.0° (port) beside it, or Alt-click the line to keep: one step, named Port bearing kept on Towed array cut at 09:21:00Z. Right-click it, or press and hold it on a touch screen, for its menu: Keep 045.0° (port), Keep 135.0° (starboard), Make ambiguous again once resolved, Keep a side for more cuts… and Select this cut. In the playground the menu is a short dialog of the same choices. From the keyboard, Cut at current time… on a sensor's menu in the Outline opens the menu of the cut the map emphasises, its bearings, sides and label said, so every cut can be read and kept without a pointer by moving current time to it.
  2. A run, boxed in Bearings (product owner, 28 Oct 2026). The usual way, before any solution: select the sensor in the Outline, turn on Course/Speed in Bearings to see ownship's legs (BLUE ONE's course and speed in its colour) beside the bearings, then Select bearings and drag a box over the run of dots that is the contact. Each unresolved cut boxed keeps the side whose dot was boxed, one step for them all (Kept 27 Towed array cuts to starboard, 09:46:00Z–10:13:00Z); a cut boxed on both sides is left, and said. A box toggles (product owner, 28 Oct 2026): box a resolved run again, its kept dots, and it is made ambiguous again in one step, both faint dots back (Made 27 Towed array cuts ambiguous again, …), so a side kept wrongly is undone where it was seen; a box over both, one step saying how many of each (Kept 14 cuts to starboard and made 13 ambiguous again). A cut never ambiguous is untouched. The zoom stays, to box the next run. From the keyboard, the same step: the run selected in the Outline, Keep port, Keep starboard or Make ambiguous again in the Tools (TMA solutions).
  3. A period. Cuts selected in the Outline (a sensor expanded to its cuts, a run Shift-clicked): Keep port, Keep starboard or Make ambiguous again in the Tools, one step for them all (product owner, 27 Oct 2026). Or Ambiguous bearings: keep port or starboard… on a sensor's menu in the Outline (or the Command Palette): Keep port bearing, Keep starboard bearing or Make ambiguous again, then which cuts: The cut at the current time, Cuts in the time window, Selected cuts or All cuts, each saying how many cuts it holds and how many have two bearings. In the playground, the same on a sensor row's menu, and, while a sensor or a cut is selected, Port…, Starboard… and Both again… under Sensor, below the Outline (shown only then, so the list keeps its rows). Port and starboard are offered for every cut, as legacy Debrief offered them: for each cut, the bearing on that side of the course logged where its sensor was at that cut's time is kept (above). A hidden cut, or a hidden sensor's, is left out of the window and all, and the notes say so (2 hidden cuts left as they are: show them to resolve them.); selected, it is resolved.
  4. One step, with what was asked. Every resolution is one recorded step, however many cuts: Port kept: 132 Towed array cuts 08:46:00Z–12:00:00Z; Ambiguous again: 3 Towed array cuts 09:00:00Z–09:02:00Z; cuts named of both sides, Mixed-side kept: 2 Towed array cuts … (a name too long for the History leaves out its period, said in its next note). Its record holds what was asked: the side, the sensors and the period, or how many cuts were named. Cuts with no ambiguous bearing, cuts already so, and cuts where the side cannot be told (outside the host's span, or where it never moved) are left as they are, and the step's notes say how many. A resolution that would change nothing changes nothing, and says why.
  5. Undo, and back to ambiguous. Undo takes a resolution back like any step. Make ambiguous again is its own step, for a cut or a period, when the analyst changes their mind after other work.
  6. What a cut keeps. A resolved cut records which bearing was kept (bearing or ambiguous_bearing), not the side. A side depends on the logged course at the cut's time; moving the host, or setting an array offset, later does not swap a resolved cut's bearing.

docs.title: In the Outline and the Timeline
docs.text:
1. The Outline. Each sensor is a row under its host track, with how many cuts it has, and how many are ambiguous and resolved: Towed array: 132 cuts · 40 ambiguous · 92 resolved. Its menu: keeping a side (above), Change colour…, Hide on map and Show on map, each one step (Colour of Bow sonar set to green). Cuts are not rows: a sensor may have thousands.
  2. Not in the Timeline (decision, 24 Oct 2026). The Timeline lists narrative entries, notes and periods to read in time order. Cuts would bury them: the sample's serial has 393 cuts against 46 narrative entries, a towed array gives one every 30 to 60 seconds, and a legacy DSF file gives every cut a label. The current cut is emphasised on the map instead, and the narrative already says when a contact was gained or lost. The cuts are in the Outline (product owner, 27 Oct 2026, superseding 24 Oct's cut list in the Bearings view): a sensor expands to its cuts, each its time, bearing (both, ≈, for an ambiguous pair not yet resolved, or the side kept), range and whether hidden; a run of them selected (Shift-click, Shift with the arrows) is kept to a side, hidden, shown, deleted or made a TMA solution of from the Tools, one step each (TMA solutions).

docs.title: Tracks edited
docs.text:
1. Splitting and merging. Splitting a track gives its sensors' later cuts to the new second track, as a sensor of the same name, and the step's note says so (Towed array: its 10 cuts from the split on are a sensor of BLUE ONE (2)'s). That sensor has a new id (sensor-blue-one-2-towed-array), so a TMA solution rooted in the later cuts follows them by their cut ids, not the sensor's. Cuts the split would move keep where they were drawn from and the course their side was told by, pinned (their own origin and course, marked origin_derived, so TMA can tell a derived origin from a recorded one), and the notes say how many: those between the first part's last fix and the second's first (outside both parts' spans), a towed array's whose worm reached back past the split, and those whose logged course was at a fix now in the other part. A pinned cut is drawn, and resolved, as before. Merging tracks moves their sensors to the merged track, and sensors of one name there are one again with every cut, as legacy Debrief joined them, so a track split and merged has its sensors as they were; the joined cuts keep the colour of the sensor they came from, and the sensor kept takes the other's legacy symbology if it had none. Two sensors of one name whose array offsets or modes differ are other arrays, as drawn: they are kept apart, each with its own cuts, and the notes say why (Towed array: kept as two sensors, as their arrays differ (at the ship; 300 m astern, worm in the hole), so each keeps its own cuts, drawn as before.). Moving, rotating, shearing or stretching a track moves the origin of every cut drawn from it; a cut with its own origin stays where it was recorded.
  2. New data taken in (collation): a supplied item's sensors come with its tracks, carried by the plot's track each was matched to or added as (joined by name to a sensor already there), with only their cuts in the periods the item supplies, and the note says so: Towed array: 6 cuts taken with NELSON. Cuts left out because another item supplies that period are counted, not dropped silently: Towed array: 7 cuts 05:30:00Z to 06:00:00Z not taken: another item supplies NELSON then. A revision of an item that adds only cuts is new data too (4 new cuts), and choosing a period from another item in Coverage brings that item's cuts in the period with its fixes.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
1. debrief/sensors (reading): the plot's sensors, each with its host, colour, whether it is hidden, how many cuts, ambiguous and resolved, and its first and last cut's time; with cuts: true, each cut in period (at most 20,000 in all) with its time, bearings, which was kept, the side its first bearing is on, its range, label, comment and where it is drawn from: what a TMA solution is rooted in.
  2. debrief/resolve_ambiguity (changing): keep (port, starboard, bearing, ambiguous_bearing, or ambiguous for both again) and either cut_ids, or sensor_ids and perhaps a period (hidden cuts left out). With keep bearing or ambiguous_bearing, other_cut_ids names cuts kept on their other bearing in the same step, as a box in Bearings asks (product owner, 28 Oct 2026): a cut named in both was boxed on both sides and is left, said in the step's notes; hidden cuts are left; clear_cut_ids names resolved cuts made ambiguous again in the same step (a box over their kept bearings). One step. debrief/set_array_offset (changing): sensor_ids, offset ({value, unit}, or null for at the ship) and mode. One step. debrief/sensors gives a sensor's array_offset_m and array_mode, and each cut's origin from the array.
  3. debrief/preview_sensor says what a file's sensor lines hold, and which track would carry each, changing nothing; debrief/import_sensor reads them in, one step, with hosts naming the track for a track name the plot has not, and again to read a file read before. Both are in schemas/vectors/service-methods.json, so an earlier revision shown read-only refuses the changing ones.
sequenceDiagram
  actor Analyst
  participant Map
  participant Host as Host (VS Code or playground)
  participant Python as debrief/resolve_ambiguity
  Analyst->>Map: click a cut's line
  Map-->>Analyst: the cut selected; beside it, Keep 045.0° (port), Keep 135.0° (starboard)
  Analyst->>Map: Keep 135.0° (starboard), or Alt-click the starboard line
  Map->>Host: resolve_asked {feature_id, keep: ambiguous_bearing}
  Host->>Python: keep, cut_ids, base
  Python-->>Host: one step: "Starboard bearing kept on Towed array cut at 09:21:00Z"
  Host->>Map: the plot again
  Map-->>Analyst: the kept line alone
  Analyst->>Host: Towed array's menu: Keep port bearing, Cuts in the time window
  Host->>Python: keep: port, sensor_ids, period (the window)
  Python->>Python: each cut's side from the course logged where its array was
  Python-->>Host: one step: "Port kept: 132 Towed array cuts 08:46:00Z–12:00:00Z"

docs.title: Bearing error: drawn as lines (decision, 24 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
The SRD asked for a bearing error, where a file supplies one, drawn as a wedge. Of the formats legacy Debrief read:

  • ;SENSOR: and ;SENSOR2: carry no bearing error.
  • ;SENSOR3: carries a bearing accuracy in degrees (and a frequency accuracy). Legacy ImportSensor3 read both and threw them away, unused. Legacy Debrief's sample files give NULL for it, and no format or code says what it means: a standard deviation, a half-width, a 95% bound.
  • A .dpf plot's sensor contacts carry none.

So bearings are drawn as lines only, no wedges (product owner, 24 Oct 2026). ;SENSOR3:'s accuracy is kept on each cut as it was written (bearing_accuracy, as text, so 1.5 stays 1.5), not drawn and not interpreted, for the field to be agreed later. A wedge needs an error field agreed with the acoustic replay application's owners, its meaning included; the model can hold an optional error on a cut later without changing anything here.

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text: Everything on the map has a way without a pointer (keyboard equivalents): a sensor's menu in the Outline (Shift+F10 or the menu key; press and hold on a touch screen) keeps a side for the cut at current time, the window, the selected cuts or all, and Cut at current time… says the current cut's bearings and sides and opens its menu (a screen reader reads both, where the map's lines are a picture); Ambiguous bearings: keep port or starboard… is in the Command Palette; in the playground, Sensor's buttons under the Outline while a sensor or a cut is selected. A tap on a cut's line selects it and shows its choices, as a click does (a tap never keeps a side); pressed and held, its menu, as it is right-clicked. The choices beside a cut are a dialog: it has the keyboard first, so a screen reader reads the cut (its details are its description) before any choice and Enter keeps nothing by accident; Tab moves among the choices and stays among them, Enter chooses, and Escape goes back to the map. Towed array offset… is on the sensor's menu and in the Command Palette.

docs.title: Performance budget
docs.text:
Painting is on one canvas, as the map's symbols and arrows are: a sensor of thousands of cuts is one image to pan, not thousands of elements. Each cut's lines are worked out once, along the geodesic, and kept while the host and the cut are unchanged; a line is cut into only as many pieces as keep it within a quarter of a pixel of the geodesic on screen. The current cuts are on a canvas of their own over the rest, so moving current time repaints one line per sensor.

Measured in headless Chromium with software rendering (the playground's map page; medians, with the 95th percentile where it matters):

Plot First draw (once) Window moved, pan, zoom Current time moved Legacy ALPHA.rep (200,000 fixes) and ALPHA_CUTS.dsf (611 cuts) 46 ms 0.7 ms (1.5 ms) 0.1 ms The sample's serial 1 (393 cuts, 132 ambiguous) 0.9 ms 0.2 ms 10,611 cuts in the window, half ambiguous 330 ms 13 ms (22 ms) 0.1 ms 50,611 cuts in the window 1.4 s 81 ms (134 ms) 0.1 ms

Before the lines were cut to fit and the current cuts given their own canvas, 10,611 cuts took 119 ms (194 ms) for every step of current time.

The budget: moving current time (playing, dragging the slider, and a TMA drag, which moves no cut) under 1 ms for any number of cuts; moving the window, panning or zooming within a frame (16 ms) for up to 10,000 cuts in the window and within NFR-04's 100 ms for up to 50,000; the first draw within half a second for each 10,000 cuts. Past 50,000 cuts in the window, narrow the window: that is what it is for (CAP-29). The playground's test holds the sample to it on every run.

In Python, resolving cuts reads only the host's fixes it needs (a track's times and positions are parsed as asked for), and a worm walks back through a dense track's short legs on the local ellipsoid (to a part in 10⁷), taking the geodesic only of the leg that holds the array; both languages do it alike. Resolving 600 cuts of a 500 m worm on ALPHA.rep (200,000 fixes, one a second), resolve() alone: 2.75 s before (every fix parsed, every leg a geodesic, 43,000 of them), 2.16 s with fixes read as asked for, 0.21 s now.

Known debt: a step's cost on a large plot is the plot's. The whole step on ALPHA.rep still takes 4 to 6 s, of which about 4 s is writing any step to a plot of 200,000 fixes: composing, validating, hashing and writing the whole plot (changing a sensor's colour there takes 4 s too; reading ALPHA_CUTS.dsf in, 6 s). That is the History's (one content-addressed plot per step), not the sensors', and is for the History to fix, by writing only the features a step changed.

History growth. A step stores each cut it changes whole: about 330 bytes per cut per step. Resolving all 611 cuts of ALPHA_CUTS.dsf adds some 200 kB to the History; resolving a towed array's cuts a window at a time adds as much in all.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Bearing-error wedges, until a field is agreed (above).
  • The automatic ambiguity resolver (CAP-33): proposing each cut's side from ownship's manoeuvres (a true bearing steady across a turn is on the side whose relative bearing changed by the turn), for the analyst to confirm or change as one step. Recorded, not built.
  • Array offsets that vary, or an array centre from measured data (legacy's other modes): an array is a fixed distance astern.
  • Frequency, by decision (CAP-22).

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Model: SensorFeature, SensorCutFeature, AmbiguityResolution in schemas/linkml/features.yaml; the rules in debrief_schemas.documents (a cut's sensor in the plot, a sensor's host track, bearings from 0 to under 360°, a resolution only of an ambiguous cut); the geometry in debrief_kernel.sensors and vscode/webview/sensors.ts, held to schemas/vectors/sensor-cuts.json (legacy relBearing's own test cases, the default length, cuts across a turn, a turn logged at the next fix as legs_20.rep, a stationary host, the antimeridian, high latitude, a range of 0, worm-in-the-hole and plain arrays).
  • Python: debrief_io.rep (parse_sensor), debrief_io.sensor_import, debrief_io.dpf and debrief_io.dpf_import, debrief_io.narrative (Rider bearings); debrief_stac.sensors and Catalogue.add_sensors, Catalogue.resolve_ambiguity, Catalogue.set_array_offset; debrief_kernel.sensors.array_place (the worm); debrief/sensors, debrief/resolve_ambiguity, debrief/set_array_offset, debrief/preview_sensor and debrief/import_sensor in debrief_tools.service; the sample's sensors in debrief_sample.synth (TowedArrayModel).
  • Hosts: vscode/webview/sensormap.ts (the canvas, hit testing), vscode/webview/map.ts; the commands debrief.resolveAmbiguity, debrief.cutMenu, debrief.setArrayOffset and debrief.importSensor in vscode/src/extension.ts, vscode/src/sensorimport.ts, the Outline in vscode/src/views/outline.ts; the playground's in vscode/play/host.ts.
  • Tests: python/debrief-kernel/tests/test_sensors.py, python/debrief-io/tests/test_rep_sensors.py, python/debrief-io/tests/test_dpf_sensors.py, python/debrief-stac/tests/test_sensors.py, python/debrief-tools/tests/test_sensors_service.py, vscode/test/unit/sensors.test.ts, vscode/test/play/sensors.mjs, and a step of vscode/test/integration/suite.ts.

docs.title: Time controller
docs.text: How an analyst sets the plot's time window and current time, plays through them, and what is saved where.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-28 One time window for the whole plot, independent of its overall time range, saved in the plot file as view state. A tool's time outside it is shown, never saved, until the analyst keeps or reverts it. CAP-29 Tracks for a whole deployment at once, at least 3:1 against the map outside the window by default; sensor data only within the window. SUB-22 View state in the island is neither undoable nor recorded; two analysts changing it at once are told, not overwritten. SUB-26, SUB-27 Current time (an instant and a range) is shared state that views, extensions and tools read and set. SUB-28 A change made elsewhere is never silently overwritten. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, in any theme.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. One controller, every host. VS Code shows it as the Time view at the top of the Debrief sidebar, above the catalogues, outline, tools and history. The playground shows the same component at the top of its side column. The map only draws: it has no control of its own.

    The controller is compact, so the whole of it shows without scrolling at the height VS Code first gives the view (at 1440 × 900, with the other Debrief views open), note and all. From the top: the window's start and end, with its length, on one line; the window's slider; the note, when there is one, on one line; current time's slider, with the step beside it; and ‹, ▶, ›, the speed and current time on one line. Names that a caption would repeat are on hover and for screen readers instead. 2. The time window is a slider with two handles over the plot's whole period. Drag a handle to move that end; drag the band between them to move the whole window. Above it, the window's start and end, and how long it is. The window is never shorter than one second: the handles stop a second apart and never cross. A plot saved with a window of no length opens showing its first second, and that is saved only if the analyst moves it. 3. Current time is a slider over the window, never outside it. When the window moves past current time, current time moves with it. ‹ and › step back and forward; the step, about a hundredth of the window (1 s up to 1 day), shows beside the slider. Current time itself shows at the end of the buttons' line. 4. Play (▶, or Space) moves current time forward at the chosen speed and stops at the end of the window. Playing from the end starts again at the window's start. The speeds are multiples of real time:

    Speed Plays For 1× real time a close-quarters encounter, second by second 10× ten minutes a minute an approach 60× (the default) a minute a second a four-hour serial in four minutes 600× ten minutes a second a serial in under half a minute 3600× an hour a second a week's deployment in under three minutes

    Current time moves ten times a second while playing: smooth to follow, without flooding the views. A window shorter than one of those moves (the speed times a tenth of a second: 6 s at 60×) cannot be played: Play is off and says Window too short to play at 60×: widen it or slow down, on hover and to screen readers. It stays focusable, so the reason can be read.

  2. What the map shows. Within the window, tracks are drawn in full: solid lines 2.5 px wide, direction ticks, a hollow dot at the first fix in the window and a filled, labelled dot at the last. Outside it, each whole track stays in view as a context track, so a deployment of weeks still reads as one picture (CAP-29): a solid line 1.5 px wide, with no ticks, dots or labels, in the track's hue made quieter (moved toward the theme's text colour). Annotations with a time or a period are drawn only while it falls in the window; annotations without one always are. Sensor data will be drawn only within the window (CAP-29); bearings are not drawn yet.

    Context tracks are set for the plot and saved in its island like the window. In VS Code they are in the Time view's ... menu, on its title bar: Context tracks: Visible, Faint and Hidden, the plot's choice checked (the commands debrief.contextTracks.visible, .faint and .hidden, which run debrief.setContextTracks). When the analyst's setting draws faint as visible, the view's title says so. The playground has no title menu: its Context list is beside the window's length.

    Setting Draws them Visible (the default) At least 3:1 against the map's background on any theme, as drawn. Debrief works this out from the theme's editor background: opacity 0.6, and each colour's lightness moved away from the background only as far as it needs. Faint Fainter (opacity 0.35), for a busy plot. No 3:1 promise. Hidden Not at all: only the window shows.

    An analyst who needs the contrast everywhere turns on the setting Debrief › Map: Minimum Context Contrast (debrief.map.minimumContextContrast): faint is then drawn visible on every plot they open, without changing the plot; hidden is still hidden. High-contrast themes draw context tracks in the track's own colour, opaque, 1 px wide. Selecting a feature dims the others, context tracks included, but never below opacity 0.3, and never on a high-contrast theme. 6. Moving shows; letting go saves. The map follows the window as it moves. The window is saved in the plot when the analyst lets go: the pointer is released, or the key is released. Holding an arrow key down saves once. Saving on every movement would rewrite the plot file many times a second and, on a shared folder, look to a colleague like a flood of changes. 7. What is saved where.

    Where Undoable In the history Time window, context tracks The plot file, in its island No No Current time Shared state, not saved No No Colour, hiding, data The plot, through its history Yes Yes

    The window travels with the plot: a colleague given the plot file opens it on the same window. Ctrl+Z never changes the window, and moving the window never conflicts with a change to the plot's content. 8. Shared state follows the window. The range of current time in shared state is the window as shown, so tools and other extensions see it, and it follows a drag at once. 9. A tool's time outside the saved window. Closest approach, say, moves current time to the moment it finds. If that is outside the saved window, Debrief shows it without saving anything:

    • the window shown widens by the least amount that takes the time in, but never to more than twice the saved window's length. Beyond that, the window moves instead: the saved length, centred on the time, kept within the plot's period;
    • the part of the window bar that differs from the saved window is hatched, and a note says Showing beyond saved window (or Showing a different period from the saved window, when it moved), with Keep and Revert at its right. The note is one line: in a narrow view its text is cut short, and shows whole on hover. It stays until the analyst chooses, and screen readers hear all of it (a polite live region);
    • the tool's message adds (outside your saved window). The history records the tool's run and its result, such as the closest approach's time, never a window.

    Keep saves the window shown, as letting go does, conflict checks included (SUB-28). Revert shows the saved window again, with current time moved to its nearest edge. Dragging a handle or the band, or moving a handle from the keyboard, saves the window as left, so it counts as Keep. Moving current time, stepping and playing inside the window shown neither save it nor clear the note. If the plot is closed or VS Code reloads, the window shown is lost and the saved one returns.

    A tool whose purpose is to set the window (none ships yet) can ask for its range to be saved (save_window on its state_change). Debrief saves it, through the same path, only when the analyst ran that tool by hand from its form on the plot still open; a run by an agent, a command, a chain or a replay is shown as above, never saved. 10. A colleague's window. If someone else changes the plot's window, Debrief notices (it watches the plot file as well as its history), shows the new window without reading the plot's content again, and says so. If the analyst lets go of a window after a colleague changed it, theirs is kept: Debrief shows it and says Someone else changed the time window, so yours was not saved. Nothing is merged or overwritten silently (SUB-28).

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
Focus Key Does A window handle ← → ↑ ↓ Moves that end by a step (a hundredth of the plot's period); saved when the key is released A window handle Page Up, Page Down Ten steps Window start Home, End To the plot's start; to a second before the window's end Window end Home, End To a second after the window's start; to the plot's end Current time ← → ↑ ↓ One step (a hundredth of the window) Current time Page Up, Page Down Ten steps Current time Home, End The window's start and end Any slider Space Play or pause Speed ↑ ↓ Choose a speed Keep, Revert Enter, Space Save the window shown; show the saved window again Context tracks (the playground's list) ↑ ↓ Visible, faint or hidden. In VS Code, the view's ... menu, or the commands in the Command Palette

Each slider has a name and says its time to screen readers (aria-valuetext). Colours come from the theme only.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Controller as Time controller
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Map
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Plot as Plot file
    Analyst->>Controller: drag a window handle
    loop as it moves
        Controller->>Host: time_changed (current time; range = window)
        Host->>Map: set_time: draw the window
    end
    Analyst->>Controller: let go
    Controller->>Host: window_changed (the window)
    Host->>Service: debrief/set_view (view, hash last read)
    alt changed elsewhere since it was read
        Service-->>Host: CONFLICT
        Host->>Service: debrief/open: read the view again
        Host->>Controller: show_time (their window)
        Host->>Analyst: yours was not saved; showing theirs
    else
        Service->>Plot: rewrite the island only, under the history's lock
        Service-->>Host: new view hash
    end

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• The component: vscode/webview/timecontrol.ts and timecontrol.css; its rules, free of the page, in vscode/webview/timelogic.ts (window limits, steps, speeds, Player, WindowGesture, windowForTime, placeToolTime, SavedWindow), tested in vscode/test/unit/timecontrol.test.ts and timewindow.test.ts.
  • Context tracks: vscode/webview/contrast.ts (contextStyle: colour, opacity and width per theme), tested against every palette colour on Dark+ and Light+ in vscode/test/unit/contrast.test.ts; drawn by applyContext in vscode/webview/map.ts.
  • VS Code: the Time view, vscode/src/panels/timeview.ts and vscode/webview/time.ts; saving and noticing the island in vscode/src/extension.ts (saveWindow, saveContext, saveView, applyToolState, refreshView, watch); the window in shared state in vscode/src/session.ts (windowChanged, onView); what the map draws in vscode/webview/map.ts (drawWindow). The commands debrief.setTimeWindow and debrief.setContextTracks set them for agents and keyboard macros; the Time view's title menu runs debrief.contextTracks.visible, .faint and .hidden, checked through the context key debrief.contextTracks.
  • The playground: vscode/play/host.ts (saveView, showToolTime) and set_view in vscode/play/play.py. It has no settings: the minimum-contrast setting is always off there.
  • Messages: show_time (with saved_window, context_tracks, minimum_context_contrast), window_changed, context_changed and set_context (WebviewMessage). VS Code's Time view no longer sends context_changed, since the choice moved to its title menu; the kind stays in the schema.
  • The service: debrief/set_view and debrief/open; Catalogue.write_view. The island's context_tracks and a result's save_window are in the schema (0.0.10).
  • The tests: the integration test's time window and context steps; the playground test's playTheTimeController and its closest approach steps, and vscodeTimeView, which loads VS Code's Time view page at the view's first size and checks that everything shows without scrolling, with the note and without.

Not yet: drawing sensor data (bearings arrive with Phase 4's D stream, and will be limited to the window); the window following current time while playing; a choice of step.

docs.title: Timeline and narrative
docs.text:
How an analyst reads a plot's narrative along with a replay: narrative entries from every platform, with time-only notes and periods, the comments on fixes and each track's data coverage, in one time-ordered list, the Timeline; how it follows current time without fighting the reader; how entries are chosen, filtered, searched, highlighted, added, changed and deleted; and how narrative is held and imported, from REP files, legacy plots, and Word and PDF documents.

The product owner decided on 15 Oct 2026 that narrative is read in the Timeline, not a view of its own: one list on one Zulu time axis, which data coverage joined with collation on 16 Oct 2026 (CAP-05, CAP-08; see Collation).

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-05 An optional temporal view shows narrative entries, time-only annotations and data coverage per source; choosing an entry moves current time to it. CAP-19 Narrative is imported from Word and PDF in the legacy parsers' dialects, ported to Python with their tests. EXT-04 Narrative documents: Word and PDF, several dialects. CON-09, CON-10 The playground runs the same Python in the browser; a capability it lacks is explained, never failed at the point of use. CAP-20 Narratives from several platforms are combined on a single Zulu time axis. EXT-14 A legacy .dpf plot's narrative is imported, as far as the data model allows. NFR-06 Usable with 12,000 narrative entries scaled by three to five: the stress bound. Typical narratives are a few hundred entries (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; undo replays to the step before. SUB-04 Times are written by the formatting service, in the analyst's settings.

docs.title: Narrative entries
docs.text:
1. An entry is a feature of its own. Kind narrative, with no geometry, as a time-only annotation has: its time (UTC, to the millisecond), its source (who wrote it: a platform, a person or a document, such as BLUE ONE; legacy Debrief's track name on an entry), its entry_type (the source's own kind of entry, free text: legacy logs use GenComment, Posn, CSD, FCS; the sample uses Course, Sonar, CPA, Log), its text (which may run to several lines) and the track it belongs to, track_id, where there is one. Schema 0.0.19.

    One feature an entry, not one feature holding a whole log: each entry added, changed or deleted is then one small step in the history, holding that entry alone. A log of 12,000 entries held as one feature would put all 12,000 into the history at every change. 2. The plot's narrative is every narrative entry in it. There is no narrative layer to create first: entries from a REP file, a legacy plot, the sample's script and the analyst's own typing are one narrative. A legacy plot's narrative layers are kept as named sets of their entries, with the layers' names, as its annotation layers are. 3. One Zulu time axis, one order. By time; at one time by source, ignoring case (and between sources differing only in case, capitals first); from one source at one time, in the plot's order, which is the order its log gave them. Two platforms' entries at one second therefore always come in the same order, whichever log was imported first, and a log's own order at one second is kept. Legacy Debrief sorted entries at one time by source, then type, then text, which put a log's own order at one second out of order, and dropped entries alike in all four; both are kept here. Python and TypeScript are held to the same cases, schemas/vectors/narrative-order.json. 4. Notes and narrative are kept apart. The sample's scripted log, and a legacy plot's narrative entries, were time-only note annotations before schema 0.0.19; they are narrative entries now. A note the analyst adds through the annotation form stays an annotation: the analyst's own remark, with a name, a style and perhaps a period, drawn by the annotation tools, hidden or shown like any annotation. Both are listed in the Timeline. 5. Belonging to a track. An entry imported or added belongs to the plot's track of its source's name, ignoring case and spacing, where there is exactly one; the form and agents may choose another, or none. A track deleted since leaves the link, which is then ignored.

docs.title: Importing narrative
docs.text:
1. REP files. ;NARRATIVE: lines (date, time, source, text) and ;NARRATIVE2: lines (date, time, source, type, text) are read as legacy Debrief's ImportNarrative and ImportNarrative2 read them: fields separated by spaces or tabs; the source, and a type, in quotes where they hold spaces; the text the rest of the line, tabs kept, trimmed; dates in the same 1950 to 2049 window as fixes. As in legacy Debrief, a ;NARRATIVE: line has no type: an unquoted source with a space, HMS TORBAY, reads as the source HMS and the text TORBAY…. Unlike legacy Debrief, text run on after a closing quote is kept for the next field rather than dropped with the quote. A line that cannot be read is listed with its number and why. A REP file of narrative alone makes a plot.
  2. Into the plot already open. Read narrative into this plot (REP, Word, PDF)… (on the Timeline's title bar in VS Code; A narrative into the open plot under Import your own in the playground; debrief/import_narrative for agents) reads a second platform's log into the open plot as one step: the file is kept in the plot's item as a source, read-only and hashed, the step's record names the importer, its version and that source (and for a document its dialect and the analyst's choices), and it lists what was not read (fix lines, which belong to an import as a plot of their own, and lines that could not be read, each with why). Undo takes the whole log out again. A Word or PDF document is read in legacy Debrief's dialects, the analyst asked first what legacy Debrief asked: see Word and PDF documents. Import plot file (REP, .dpf, Word, PDF)… makes a plot of a document's narrative alone, as of a REP file's.

Read in before. A file already read into the plot is known by its content hash, which the step that read it records for its source, whatever the file is called now (product owner, 15 Oct 2026); an entry already in the plot by its time (to the millisecond), source and text, compared as the importer matches a platform to a track: ignoring case and spacing, the source as written or as the name of the track it belongs to. Before anything else is asked, the analyst is told, and offered Skip entries already in the plot or Cancel:

  • in VS Code, a Quick Pick titled copy.docx is already in the plot, its line saying when and by whom it was read in, as which step, and how many of its entries are in the plot (Read in on 15 Oct 2026 09:30:00Z by Ian (step 4, Narrative read from red-one-log.docx). 5 of its 7 entries are in the plot.); the skip says how many entries are not, or Nothing new to read;
  • in the playground, the same line in red at the top of the reading form, whose action becomes Skip entries already in the plot; Cancel reads nothing;
  • for agents, debrief/preview_narrative says it (earlier: each step that read the file, with at, by, how and the source's name; already: how many of its entries are in the plot), and debrief/import_narrative refuses such a file, nothing read, with code -32003 and a message saying the same, until duplicates is "skip" (read only the entries not in the plot) or "add" (read them all again; the record says the plot has them twice).

The same applies when the file is new but some of its entries are already in the plot, from another file or by hand (3 of the 7 entries in blue-log.docx are already in the plot). Skipped entries are listed in the step's record as not read again; the source already kept is the step's source, not kept twice. A read since undone is not in the plot, so it is not said; a file of the same name with other content is still refused, to be renamed. 8. Legacy plots (.dpf). Narrative entries come in with their time, source, type and text; the entry type, which the Phase 2 import listed as not imported, is kept.

docs.title: The Timeline
docs.text:
1. One component, every host. VS Code shows the Timeline as a view in the Debrief sidebar; the playground shows the same component in its Timeline panel, which folds away like every side panel. It replaced a native tree, which could not search, filter, follow current time without taking the keyboard, or hold sixty thousand entries.

  2. A quiet table. Column headings once, Time, Source, Type, Entry; then a row an entry, with nothing labelled in the rows:

    Time Source Type Entry 15 Jun 2023 08:29:00Z ● BLUE ONE Sonar Bow sonar contact, bearing 277.0°T. Classifying. 08:30:00Z ● BLUE ONE Course Came to 215.0°T, 10.0 kn. 08:58:00Z EXCON Log Permission granted.
    • The time in the editor's monospaced font, written by the formatting service in the analyst's settings; a day's date heads its first entry.
    • The source, with its track's colour where it belongs to one; the type quieter; the text wrapping, with its line breaks.
    • A note shows its name as its source and Note as its type, a period Period and Until … before its text, a fix comment its track and Fix. One hidden on the map says so.
    • Data coverage (CAP-05, CAP-08; decision, product owner, 16 Oct 2026): each period a track has data for, from its first fix to its last and broken at gaps as collation breaks them, cut where the catalogue item supplying it changes. Its source is that item (the plot's own title for the data it was imported with), its type Data, its text the track and how many fixes, Until … before them: Until 12:00:00Z. BLUE ONE: 241 fixes. In the track's colour; hidden on the map, it says so. Choosing it moves current time to its start. Worked out in TypeScript from the plot alone, as Python works out coverage, held to the same vectors (schemas/vectors/collation.json).
    • Entries outside the time window are drawn fainter: still read, still chosen.
    • Where the list is narrow (VS Code's sidebar, the playground's side column, a phone), time, source and type are one line and the text goes under them, aligned with the source, so the time is a gutter down the left. The page never scrolls sideways.
    • Following current time. The entry current time is at (the last at or before it, among those listed) is marked by a bar in the theme's highlight and a quiet ground. As current time moves, while playing or stepping or from a tool, the list keeps that entry in sight: it scrolls only when the entry leaves the middle of the view (its top tenth to three quarters down), and then puts it a third of the way down, so what comes next is seen below it. It never moves the keyboard, and never animates, so a reader is not pulled about.

    The reader always wins. Scrolling the list (wheel, touch, scrollbar) or moving through it with the keyboard stops it following. Follow time then appears in the bar, with an arrow towards where current time is (↑ or ↓); it starts following again and brings the entry into sight. Choosing an entry also starts following again, since current time moves to it, and so does pressing Play (product owner, 15 Oct 2026): playing is asking to read along. Scrolling away while it plays stops it following again, as at any other time; pausing leaves it as it is.

    Following starts afresh, at current time, when another plot is opened; the same plot shown again after a change (an entry added, an undo) keeps the reader's place. The host says which plot it is (plot_id on show_timeline). 12. Choosing an entry (click, tap, Enter or Space) moves current time to it, or to the start of a period. Outside the window shown, the window widens or moves to take it in, shown but never saved, exactly as for a tool's time, with Keep and Revert on the time controller (CAP-28). Where several entries share a second, the one chosen is the one marked, not the last of them. 13. Filter and search. Filter opens checkboxes, with counts, for each kind (Narrative, Notes and periods, Fix comments, Data coverage), source and type; unticked ones are left out, and Filter (2) says how many are. Show all puts them back. The search box finds text in an entry's text, source or type, ignoring case, and marks it; Escape clears it. Under the list, 12 entries of 120 while anything is left out. The filter and the search are the reader's own (product owner, 15 Oct 2026), kept in the page (VS Code's webview state; the browser's storage in the playground, every read and write guarded), never in the plot: two analysts reading one narrative want different filters, and neither changes what the plot says. Following and current time work among the entries listed. Agents filter for themselves (debrief/narrative); debrief.timelineEntries answers for the whole plot, so its current is the entry current time is at among all of them, which is the row the reader sees marked unless their filter leaves it out. 14. Adding, changing and deleting an entry. + (or N with the list focused; Add narrative entry… in VS Code) opens a short form above the list: Time (starting at current time, in any of the analyst's notations: 09:30Z, 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, 150930Z JUN 23), Source and Type (each suggesting those the plot has), Track (following the source's name until chosen) and Entry. Edit and Delete appear on the row being worked with (the one chosen, or the keyboard's), so the list stays quiet; F2 or double-click changes, Delete deletes. Each is one step, named in the History view (Narrative entry by BLUE ONE at 08:40:00Z added, …: text changed, … moved to 08:41:00Z, … deleted), undone like any other: Undo in the History view, or Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on macOS) from the Timeline itself, as from the map, the Outline or the History view, except in the search box and the form's text boxes, where it undoes the typing (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes. Deleting from the keyboard keeps its place, on the entry after the one deleted. A form that cannot be saved says why and stays open; a change made elsewhere meanwhile is never overwritten (SUB-28). 15. On the map. The entry current time is at, where it belongs to a track, is shown beside that track's square: its source in bold and the start of its text, in a small box in the theme's colours, never in the way of the pointer, to the left where the right is short of room. It goes when ten minutes of plot time pass with no later entry for a track, so an entry long past does not linger. The map is never sent the narrative itself: a plot may hold sixty thousand entries.

    Narrative on the map, a box under the list, turns it off and on (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). It is the plot's choice, not the reader's: kept in the plot's island (PlotView.narrative_on_map, left out meaning on), like the Tote's Lines on the map, so it travels with the plot file; never a step, never undone (SUB-22). A colleague's change meanwhile is never overwritten (SUB-28). 16. The outline has one row, Narrative: 120 entries from 3 sources, which shows the Timeline; the entries are not listed there one by one (product owner, 15 Oct 2026: kept as it is).

docs.title: What is a step, and what isn't

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text:
In the Timeline Keys Touch Move through the list (stops following) Up, Down, Page Up, Page Down, Home, End swipe Move current time to the entry Enter or Space tap Change the entry F2 or E tap it, then Edit Delete the entry Delete tap it, then Delete Add an entry N or Insert + Search /; Escape clears; Down back to the list the box The reader's view (highlights, choosing, text, columns) Tab to ⋯, Enter; Escape closes ⋯ Close the form Escape; Ctrl+Enter saves Cancel Undo or redo the plot's last step Ctrl+Z; Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y (Cmd+Z, Cmd+Shift+Z on macOS), anywhere in the Timeline but a text box Undo in History

The list is a listbox for screen readers: each entry read with its full date and time, its source, type and text; the keyboard's place is its active option, the entry current time is at its current one (aria-current="time").

Ctrl+Z is decided in the Timeline's page as the key is pressed, against what has focus then: in a text box it is left to the text; elsewhere the page asks its host to undo (undo_asked, redo_asked in VS Code, which runs Undo as the map's Ctrl+Z does, and only when there is something to undo). A context key that a keybinding read would reach the page's host after focus had moved, so a Ctrl+Z straight after clicking into the search box could undo the plot.

docs.title: The reader's view: highlights, choosing, text and columns
docs.text:
1. One small menu, so the bar stays quiet. Legacy Debrief's Narrative viewer had extras the product owner kept (15 Oct 2026): phrases highlighted, an off switch for choosing an entry moves current time, the text's size and a wrap toggle, and which columns show. They are in a menu, ⋯ in the bar beside Filter, a box under the bar like the filter's, never a row of controls above the list:

    In the menu What it does Highlight words, phrases, separated by commas Each word or phrase is marked wherever it is in an entry's text, ignoring case: bold, underlined in the theme's highlight, so it is told from what the search found (shaded) without colour alone. The longest phrase at a place wins (contact lost whole, not contact); the search wins where the two meet. Twenty phrases at most. A row with one is read as …, highlighted by a screen reader. Choosing an entry moves current time On, as before. Off, choosing an entry (click, tap, Enter) puts the keyboard's place on it, showing its Edit and Delete, and leaves current time, and the list's following, as they were: for reading back through a log while a replay holds its place. Wrap long entries On, as before. Off, each entry is one line, cut with an ellipsis; the whole text is still read by a screen reader and shown in the form. Text 12px, A−, A+ The list's text from 11 to 18 px; the bar and the menu keep theirs. Columns: Time, Source, Type The columns shown; the entry's text always is. Narrow, with the time hidden, the text starts at the left edge.

    ⋯ is drawn like Filter (2) when anything differs from the Timeline's own view. Escape closes the menu, back to its button. Like the filter, the view is the reader's own (product owner, 15 Oct 2026): kept in the page (VS Code's webview state; the browser's storage in the playground, guarded), never in the plot, never sent to the host. The page never scrolls sideways at any of these settings, at 210, 280 or 390 px, in a wider font than this machine's (the tests' check).

docs.title: Scale (NFR-06)
docs.text:
Typical narratives are a few hundred entries; the product owner rarely sees more (15 Oct 2026). That case must be quick, and is:

Where What, at 2,000 entries Time Python, desktop One entry changed; undone about 20 ms; 10 to 20 ms Playground (Pyodide) A 2,000-line log read into an open plot and shown 0.8 s Playground An entry added through the form, saved, the plot opened again and the list shown; undone the same way 190 to 250 ms; 220 to 250 ms

The playground's round trip is mostly the plot opened again after the step (read from Python, the map and every panel redrawn), as for any step: 115 to 160 ms with 36 entries.

The stress bound stays the legacy sample's 12,000 entries scaled by three to five, measured with 60,000 synthetic entries:

Where What Time Python, desktop One step adding all 60,000; the plot file 20 MB, 35 MB with its history 1.4 to 2.5 s Python, desktop One entry changed; undone (12,000 entries: 0.11 s; 0.08 s) 0.7 to 1.0 s; 0.5 to 0.6 s Python, desktop Ordered; a query by source and text (debrief/narrative) 0.2 to 0.6 s; 0.3 s Timeline logic Ordered; filtered, rowed and laid out; searched 50 ms; 40 ms; 13 ms Playground (Pyodide) A 60,000-line log read into an open plot and shown 8 to 30 s Playground The list built; rows drawn 20 to 90 ms (0.4 s on a busy machine); 15 to 20 Playground Scrolling by the wheel: time between frames p50 and p95 16.7 ms (60 a second) Playground A search through all of them 30 to 60 ms

A change rewrites the whole plot file, history included, and checks it whole before it is written: that is the design (one file, history included, 13 Oct 2026), and at 60,000 entries it costs most of a second. The review of 15 Oct halved it with small changes (the plot's period read from its earliest and latest times only; a plain narrative entry checked by hand before its JSON is hashed; the file read and hashed once a change, not twice); anything more, such as checking or hashing only what changed, is not worth building for narratives of a few hundred entries.

Only the rows in sight are drawn (with 400 px above and below), each measured once drawn; the rest are estimated from their text's length and the column's width, and the row at the top of the view stays put when estimates become measurements. Two things made the Python side fast enough: JSON Schema checks each feature against its own kind's class (narrative entries by an exact hand-written check that is never more lenient than the schema, a test holds it to that), instead of trying every feature class in turn (37 s for 20,000 entries before, 1 s after); and a history keeps the plot it built while the file is unchanged.

docs.title: Word and PDF documents (CAP-19)
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief read narrative from Word (.doc, .docx) and PDF in four dialects, in Debrief.ReaderWriter.Word. They are ported to Python in debrief_io.word, with the cases of their tests on synthetic documents (DEV-05: none of legacy Debrief's documents or their text is copied), and checked against legacy Debrief's own expectations on its sample documents where a checkout of it is at hand (DEBRIEF_LEGACY): the same 13, 5, 18, 364, 350, 371 and 285 entries, the same 15 Rider entries and 28 ASW positions.

Dialect Known by Read as Narrative log (ImportNarrativeDocument, and ImportWord_LEGACY before it) anything not below; .doc, .docx and PDF An entry a paragraph, DTG,day,month,year,platform,type,text, the DTG HHMM or DDHHMM, the metadata usually hidden text. A short entry (DDHHMM text, HHMM text) takes the date and platform from the entry before, its type FCS if it starts with a track number, otherwise none (legacy N/A; the Timeline's filter lists entries with none as (no type)). Text alone continues the entry before, every line of it up to the next entry (product owner, 15 Oct 2026), so a PDF's long entry, a line a paragraph, is whole; past 2,000 lines, a runaway document, the rest is listed as not read. 12 Mar 20 marks a new day. START OF RECORDS and END OF RECORDS FOR bound the entries in a longer document. A line starting with a number is a short entry only if its time is in order: see below. Rider's narrative (ImportRiderNarrativeDocument) a first table whose first cell is DTG Start Its second row the start DTG (220000Z JUL 09, to the hour) and, fifth, the platform; from its fourth row an entry a row: time of day, bearing (273, 92/112, an arc 096-112, No B), beam, text. Every entry of type Rider, written [Brg:92/112, Beam:12/13] text as legacy Debrief wrote it. ASW data (ImportASWDataDocument) five TMPOS lines in its first hundred Positions of one platform: a track, not narrative. Imported as a plot of its own, the track named as the analyst says (legacy Debrief asked); refused, saying so, when read into an open plot. TIMPD gives the year. Dated narrative (ImportWordDummy) a line yyyy,MM,dd,HH:mm[:ss], Type, platform and text after the date. Legacy Debrief never offered it; read here rather than misread as a narrative log.

The corrections legacy Debrief made are made, and said in the step's record: a day that goes backwards with no new month or year (a mangled cut and paste) keeps the day before; an entry at 23xx whose hidden day is one after its DTG's (logged just after midnight about the evening before) takes the DTG's day; a six-figure short entry whose day is earlier than the last is in the next month. Two more, for a log with no metadata (a PDF), new here: a four-figure short entry more than twelve hours before the entry before it is past midnight, on the next day (legacy Debrief put it on the same day, almost a day back), said in the record; and a short entry at 23xx just after an entry past midnight (00xx) is a late entry on the evening before, as legacy Debrief corrected a full entry's day (it put a six-figure one a month on).

A number at the start of a line is not always a time (product owner, 15 Oct 2026). Legacy Debrief read any line starting with four or six figures as a short entry, so 2000 yds, closing. was an entry at 20:00. Here such a line, with no metadata, is an entry only when its time, after the day corrections above, is in order with the entries around it; otherwise it is text of the entry before, and the step's record lists it (1 line starting with a number was read as text of the entry before, not as an entry: its time would be out of order with the entries around it (line 12: "2000 yds, closing.")). Out of order is either:

  • behind: more than an hour before the entry before it (or a day marker after that entry). A late entry is written up within the hour; one dated by the late-entry rule is in order. A day rolling over is in order: a six-figure DTG gives the day, a day marker gives it, and a four-figure time more than twelve hours back is past midnight.
  • ahead: more than an hour after the entry after it, that being the earliest of the next three entries that are not themselves more than an hour before the entry before. The earliest, so that numbers in a row (2000 yds, 2100 yds) do not vouch for each other; a late entry after it, within the hour, does not count against it.

An entry with its metadata (DTG,day,month,year,platform,type,text) is never text, however out of order: its metadata says it is an entry. So that one entry out of order does not take the rest of the log with it, a line more than an hour behind is still an entry when the next entries, two at least, are all with it and all more than an hour before the entry before: it was the entry before that was out of order. The limits, said plainly: the last line of a log has nothing after it, so a number there is checked against the entry before only; a run of four or more numbers, each well ahead, vouch for each other and are entries, as legacy Debrief read them, and the log goes on from the entry after them; a genuine late entry written more than an hour late, followed by entries in order, is text. Legacy Debrief's sample logs have none of these: their counts are unchanged.

FCS entries are read as legacy Debrief read them (bearing, range in kiloyards, yards or metres, course, speed, classification, track number, the solution's source) and kept as narrative: TMA solution positions on the platform's track wait for TMA solutions in the data model (Phase 4, D stream), and the record says how many there were. A Rider entry's bearing, with its ambiguous twin, is also a cut of the sensor Rider bearings on the platform's track, as legacy Debrief made it (product owner, 24 Oct 2026; sensors and bearings); the entry keeps it in its text.

Where this differs from legacy Debrief, deliberately: times are UTC throughout (legacy Debrief read some in the machine's time zone); a day or time that does not exist is listed, not rolled on (legacy's 31 April was 1 May); a long type missing its comma keeps its whole first word (legacy cut its last letter); every line continuing an entry is joined to it (legacy joined six, dropped the seventh and went on joining; product owner, 15 Oct 2026); a bad line or Rider row is listed with its number and why, and reading goes on (legacy stopped some imports at the first); a Rider log that passes midnight goes on into the next day (legacy kept the first day); an entry's type N/A is no type. A day marker's two-figure year follows the entries' rule (after 80, 19xx).

What the analyst is asked, as legacy Debrief asked, before a document is read into the open plot (debrief/preview_narrative says what the file holds, changing nothing):

  • which types of entry to read, with how many of each, all ticked, when there are several;
  • all entries, or only those within the plot's period (its tracks' first to last fix), when some fall outside;
  • which of the plot's tracks a platform is, for each of up to five platforms with no track of their name (legacy Debrief's prefixes HMS, Hms, USS, RNAS and HNLMS are skipped before matching: HMS BLUE ONE is BLUE ONE's).

An entry whose platform is matched to a track, by its name or by the analyst's answer, has the track's name as its source, and so its colour (product owner, 15 Oct 2026): HMS BLUE ONE's entries are BLUE ONE's. The name as the document wrote it is kept in the step's record (9 entries written as from HMS BLUE ONE are BLUE ONE's). A platform matched to no track keeps its name as written.

The answers are remembered, for each dialect, as the analyst's own setting (product owner, 15 Oct 2026): the types not read, whether only within the period, and the track (by name) each platform was said to be. In VS Code they are kept in the user's configuration file (debrief-config's narrative_import, configuration version 3), in the playground in the page's settings; never in a plot or a catalogue, and the importer is only given the answers. Next time a document of that dialect is read, they are offered: in VS Code a first Quick Pick, Read as last time with the answers in a line, chosen by Enter, or Choose again; in the playground the form comes filled in, the answers said above it, with Read taking the keyboard. A type not seen before is read; a platform not remembered, or whose track the plot has not, is asked about.

VS Code asks in Quick Picks, one after another; the playground in one form. An agent passes the answers to debrief/import_narrative (types, within_period, tracks, platform, and duplicates for a file in the plot already) or reads everything. A PDF of a log names no platform (its metadata was hidden text, not printed): its entries' source is the plot's one track, as legacy Debrief took it, or else the document's name, or platform where an agent gives it.

Reading the files. Documents come from elsewhere, so each reader has hard limits and refuses, saying which, what passes them rather than exhaust the host's memory or time: a file over 200 MB (before it is read into memory); a .docx whose zip directory is over 4 MB, whose text part unpacks to over 64 MB, or whose XML nests over 1,000 deep; a .doc claiming more text than its stream holds, or whose piece table is out of order; a PDF of over 10,000 pages, a page drawing over 4 MB of instructions or showing text over 20,000 times, a stream unpacking to over 32 MB, over 5 million operations in all, or taking over 60 seconds; and, for all, over 500,000 paragraphs or 20 million characters, far more than any narrative. .docx with the standard library (zip and expat, refusing document type declarations, as the .dpf reader does); .doc with olefile (pure Python, for the compound file), its text from the piece table and its tables' rows from the paragraph properties, read in debrief_io.documents; PDF with pypdf (pure Python), a line of text a line. A file is known by its first bytes, not its name: legacy Debrief met .docx files named .doc. All three run in Pyodide, so the playground reads Word and PDF too, in the browser; the Pyodide spike holds the browser's reading to the desktop's. A Word 6 or 95 document, a password-protected one, a damaged one, and a PDF with no text (a scan, which needs text recognition first) are refused, saying which. python-docx is used only to build the tests' synthetic documents.

docs.text:
• Model and Python: schema 0.0.19's NarrativeFeature, NarrativeProperties and NarrativeSpec in schemas/linkml/features.yaml, the Timeline's messages and TimelineEntry in schemas/linkml/messages.yaml; debrief_stac.narrative (order, query, build, describe) and Catalogue.add_narrative, edit_narrative, delete_narrative, add_narrative_entries; debrief_io.rep.parse_narrative and debrief_io.narrative.import_narrative (with Choices, preview_narrative, and earlier_reads and already_in_plot for a file read in before); debrief_io.word.out_of_order (a number at the start of a line); Word and PDF in debrief_io.documents (reading the files), debrief_io.word (the dialects) and debrief_io.document_import (a document as a plot); the service methods debrief/narrative, debrief/add_narrative, debrief/edit_narrative, debrief/delete_narrative, debrief/import_narrative and debrief/preview_narrative.
  • The Timeline: vscode/webview/timelinecontrol.ts (the component), vscode/webview/timelinelogic.ts (filter, current entry, rows, layout, following, which keys undo and where they are left to the text; the reader's view: highlights, text sizes, columns), vscode/src/narrativeimport.ts (what to ask before reading a document in, shared by both hosts), vscode/src/timeline.ts (the entries from a plot, in order; the entry on the map), vscode/src/panels/timelineview.ts (VS Code's view), vscode/play/host.ts and narrative in vscode/play/play.py (the playground).
  • Tests: python/debrief-stac/tests/test_narrative.py, python/debrief-io/tests/test_rep_narrative.py, the dialects' test_word.py, test_narrative_documents.py and (with DEBRIEF_LEGACY) test_word_legacy_samples.py, on the synthetic documents of synthetic_docs.py and tests/data; the service's in python/debrief-tools/tests/test_service.py; Pyodide's reading held to CPython's in spikes/pyodide; vscode/test/unit/timeline.test.ts and timelineview.test.ts; the playground's vscode/test/play/narrative.mjs and narrativeword.mjs, played by vscode/test/play/play.mjs; the narrative steps of vscode/test/integration/suite.ts.

docs.title: TMA solutions
docs.text:
How an analyst makes a target motion analysis (TMA) solution from a run of bearing cuts, reads its bearing residuals in the Bearings view, drags it on the map with the residuals following, leaves wild cuts out of the RMS, and splits it into legs. How legacy plots' solutions come in. Decisions of the product owner, 24 Oct 2026, unless said otherwise; hidden cuts, independent legs and both bearings of an ambiguous cut, 25 Oct 2026; the Bearings view as legacy's Bearing Residuals (Stacked Dots) laid it out, and the way of fitting a leg it serves, 25 Oct 2026; the cuts, legs and positions in the Outline, the operations in the Tools, and Bearings without lists, following the Outline's selection, 27 Oct 2026 (The Outline and the Tools).

A newcomer learns it from the walkthrough Bearings and TMA (walkthroughs), on the sample's towed array, fitted as legacy's tutorial teaches (product owner, 25 Oct 2026, "fit properly"): a side kept, a first guess, its start moved along the first bearing to the target's range, the first leg sheared to fit, a wild bearing left out, a split at the turn and the second leg fitted the same way, to an RMS of 1.8°, near the bearings' own accuracy.
