Its buttons choose in the Outline (debrief.chooseInOutline: a cut at a time, a period's cuts and the first guess's form, or a solution's position), and the reader acts in the Tools.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-21 A TMA solution is rooted in a selected period of bearing data, its positions at the sensor's observation times in that period, with live bearing residuals while it is dragged. Solutions generated automatically (SATC) are out of scope. CAP-22 Bearings and ambiguous bearings, resolved to one side by the analyst: what a solution is rooted in (sensors and bearings). CAP-01, CAP-28 Tracks and their manipulation; the time window. PRN-08 Analysts work from bearings over time, as legacy Debrief's Stacked Dots showed them. SUB-22, SUB-24 Every change is one recorded, undoable step with its parameters. EXT-14 Legacy plots are read as legacy Debrief read them, and what is not imported is listed. NFR-04 The drag budget: the map follows the pointer smoothly, and what depends on the drag within 100 ms. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. A solution is a track. A TMA solution is an ordinary track plotted by dead reckoning (DR), so every track operation works on it unchanged: move, rotate, shear, stretch, split, merge, colour, hide, the Tote. What makes it a solution is its tma tag (TmaSolution, schema 0.0.24): the contact it is a solution of (Contact 1), the sensors whose cuts it was made from, its period, the cut ids it is rooted in, the times its legs start, and the cuts left out of its RMS. Its sensors are always those of the cuts it is rooted in: when a sensor's track is split and its later cuts become another sensor's, the solution names that sensor too. The Outline tags it TMA (in VS Code, TMA · Contact 1).
  2. Rooted by cut ids. A solution remembers which cuts it was made from by their ids, not by sensor and period, so it keeps them when its sensor's track is split (and the later cuts become another sensor's) or merged. Its fixes are at the observation times of the cuts shown on the map, one at each distinct time, in the period chosen; its courses and speeds are those of its DR legs, in knots. It has no logged courses or speeds of its own.

  3. Made in one step, from a run of cuts selected in the Outline (or a sensor, for its cuts in the time window) with TMA solution from cuts… in the Tools, rooted in exactly those cuts, and a first guess, either way (the form opens in Bearings):

    • By form. The range along the first cut's bearing, the course and the speed. Debrief's defaults: 10,000 yd (said in the analyst's length unit: 4.94 nmi), a course across the bearing (the bearing plus 90°), 8 kn. A towed array's unresolved first cut asks which of its two bearings to start on.
    • By two clicks on the map. The first cut's line and the last cut's are drawn on the map; click on the first, then on the last. Each click is taken onto its line (the nearest point on it, from the cut's origin outwards); the course and speed follow from the two points and the cuts' times. A click behind the sensor is on no line, and the map says so. Escape stops.

    The step is named so the History reads it: Contact 1 solution made: 60 Bow sonar cuts 12:24:00Z–13:08:30Z. Its notes say the first guess as given (First guess: 5.00 nmi along 257.5°T from where the first cut was taken, then 347.5°T 6.0 kn), and its record holds the request. The next contact's number is the first not in use. 4. Which cuts count. Every cut of the period on the sensors chosen, except those hidden on the map, as legacy Debrief's default (Only plot visible data; product owner, 25 Oct 2026). A hidden cut in the period is still rooted, so shown again it counts again, with nothing else to do; while hidden it is listed, marked ⊘, its residual given but neither drawn nor counted, and the view says how many (3 hidden cuts left out: they are hidden on the map, and count again once shown.). A legacy plot's Visible="false" cuts come in hidden, so its RMS is legacy's. A solution of hidden cuts alone is refused. Each cut's bearing is measured from where the cut was taken: its sensor's array astern of the ship, or its own origin; a cut whose origin Debrief worked out when its track was split (origin_derived) is counted and marked ◇. A cut outside its host's fixes or the solution's gives no residual, and the view says how many. 5. Residuals. For each rooted cut: the measured bearing less the calculated one, the bearing from the cut's origin to the solution's position at the cut's time (along the geodesic between its fixes, the later fix where two share a time), wrapped to −180° to 180°. A resolved cut is measured by the bearing kept. An unresolved ambiguous cut is measured by whichever of its two bearings is nearer the solution, and the view says so (12 ambiguous cuts not yet resolved: each is measured by the bearing nearer the solution (marked ≈)), so the analyst knows the RMS assumed a side. Its other bearing is drawn too, faint, with its residual (other_residual), and never counted, as legacy drew both, so the analyst can pick a side from the plot (product owner, 25 Oct 2026). The RMS is over the cuts counted: those with a residual, shown on the map, not left out. 6. Left out of the RMS. A wild bearing is left out of the RMS, and counted again, as one step each (Leave out of Contact 1 solution and Count in Contact 1 solution in the Tools, for the cuts selected in the Outline, against the solution Bearings shows, or chosen when they are rooted in several; or Space in the plot): Contact 1 solution: cut at 12:24:30Z left out of the RMS, its notes saying the RMS before and after. Several cuts at once are one step. Only rooted cuts can be left out. A cut left out keeps its residual, drawn as a dotted ring and struck through in the list. 7. Legs. A solution is split into legs, one step: by a position in the Outline (product owner, 27 Oct 2026), Split before making it the first position of a new leg, Split after the last of the earlier leg (Contact 1 solution split into legs before its fix at 12:53:30Z); or at a time, S in the plot at the cut chosen there (a manoeuvre picked in the bearings), or current time (Contact 1 solution split into legs at 12:53:30Z). The legs already there keep their positions: nothing moves. Each leg needs two fixes or more. It stays one track: its legs are periods of it, each starting at a fix (leg_starts). On the map, This leg (beside Whole track and Time window under What changes) drags the leg the analyst clicks on the map, at first the one current time is in, by any of the track drags; the note says which (Contact 1 solution, leg 2 of 3). A split is offered only where the leg there keeps two fixes or more either side, as Debrief accepts it.

    How the join behaves (product owner, 25 Oct 2026). Each leg is independent, as in legacy Debrief. The legs are joined by the stretch from one leg's last fix to the next leg's first. Dragging a leg moves only that leg: the legs before and after it, already fitted, never move. The two joins next to it are solved again: the leg before's last fix takes the course and speed that reach the dragged leg's new first fix, and the dragged leg's last fix takes the course and speed that reach the next leg's first fix, so dead reckoning from the first fix still puts every fix where it is. The map's preview shows the same while the drag goes on. Dragging the whole solution moves every leg together. The step's notes say The other legs stay where they are: the joins either side of the leg are solved again.

    Split track, the ordinary track operation, still splits a solution into two tracks: each is then a solution of its own, rooted in its own cuts. Merge joins solutions back into one, each later solution a leg of it, its cuts and exclusions together; each earlier solution's last fix is aimed at the next one's first fix, as a legacy plot's legs are joined, so merging moves nothing. A solution is merged only with other solutions: merged with a track that is not one, Debrief refuses and says why. 8. Legacy plots' solutions (.dpf, EXT-14). A legacy TMA track comes in as a solution track: its absolute legs as legacy saved them (origin, course, speed); its relative legs converted at import to positions, from where the host's sensor array was at the leg's start plus the saved offset, along the geodesic, and the notes say so, with the most any fix is from where legacy drew it. On legacy's sample plots that is mostly within 0.07 nmi, for two reasons where it is more: midflow2's 0.22 nmi is because its saved positions leave out its sensors' plain arrays, 300 and 400 m astern, which v4 applies, as current legacy Debrief does on load; 2648_tx (0.56 nmi over a 16.6 h leg) and Ambig_tracks3 (0.15 nmi at 60°N) are legacy's flat earth, where v4 works along geodesics. Each fix is worked out by DR from the leg's course and speed; the legs are joined by their joins; a dynamic infill between legs is not a fix of the solution (the join takes its place), said in the notes. It is rooted in its host sensor's cuts within its legs; a solution of absolute legs alone names no sensor, so it is rooted in the cuts of the sensors of the legacy tote's primary track within its period, as legacy Stacked Dots measured it, and the notes say so. TMA tracks are no longer listed as not imported; legacy's TMA solution set (contact ellipses) still is. 9. For agents. debrief/tma_create (writing) makes a solution from sensor_ids and a period (or cut_ids), a contact name, and the first guess (range, course, speed, first_bearing, or first_position and last_position; none for Debrief's defaults). It answers the feature, the notes and its residuals. debrief/tma_residuals (reading) answers a solution's residuals (TmaResiduals: a row per rooted cut, with the other bearing's residual of an unresolved ambiguous cut; the RMS, how many counted, left out, hidden, without a residual, measured by the nearer side, from a derived origin). debrief/tma_exclude_cut leaves cuts out of the RMS or counts them again; debrief/tma_split_leg splits a solution into legs at a time, or with side (before or after) by its fix at that time, or with join joins a leg to the one before; debrief/delete_cuts deletes cuts, the solutions rooted in them dropping them; debrief/set_hidden hides cuts, or shows them, saying which solutions they leave or join again; debrief/resolve_ambiguity keeps a side of the cuts named. Each writing method is one step. Held to schemas/vectors/tma-residuals.json and schemas/vectors/tma-legs.json in both languages.

sequenceDiagram
  actor Analyst
  participant View as Bearings view
  participant Map
  participant Host as Host (VS Code or playground)
  participant Python as debrief/tma_*
  Analyst->>Host: the Outline: a sensor's cuts; Shift+Down to the run's last cut
  Analyst->>Host: the Tools: TMA solution from 60 cuts…
  Host->>View: show_tma, focus {make, cut_ids}: the first guess's form (10,000 yd, across, 8 kn)
  View->>Host: tma_create {cut_ids, range, course, speed}
  Host->>Python: debrief/tma_create
  Python-->>Host: one step: "Contact 1 solution made: 60 Bow sonar cuts 12:24:00Z–13:08:30Z"
  Host->>View: the solution's residuals, RMS
  Analyst->>Map: drag the solution's end (shear)
  loop each frame of the drag
    Map->>Host: tma_preview {feature_id, coordinates}
    Host->>View: preview: residuals worked out again, RMS "(while dragging)"
  end
  Analyst->>Map: let go
  Map->>Host: one step: "Contact 1 solution (DR) sheared: 353.9°T 7.0 kn"
  Host->>Python: debrief/tma_residuals
  Python-->>View: the residuals, exact again

docs.title: The Bearings view
docs.text:
The view works as legacy Debrief's Bearing Residuals view (its Stacked Dots) does: its orientation and its way of working, not its pixels (product owner, 25 Oct 2026).

Where it is. In VS Code, Bearings is in the panel below the editor, beside the Terminal and Problems, a view container of its own (product owner, 25 Oct 2026; Show bearings on a sensor's or a solution's menu in the Outline, and the Bearings and TMA walkthrough, open it there): wide and short, so its panes sit side by side with room each and the time axis takes the panel's height. In Debrief's side bar, as a seventh view, its panes were about 100 px wide. Drag the panel taller for a longer time axis, or move the view where you like, as with any VS Code view. The controls are on top of the plot at any size (product owner, 26 Oct 2026), except where on top they would leave the plot under 220 px, as VS Code's default bottom panel would (about 126 px measured): then, the view wide, the plot takes the whole height on the left and the title, the toolbar and the status line stack in a column beside it (in a 1440 × 900 window the plot about 218 px tall, each pane about 340 px wide). They go back on top once on top would leave 250 px, so a resize never flickers between the two. The same in the playground. In the playground, right of the map, on top of the right-hand column with about 62% of its height, the walkthroughs beneath it (product owner, 25 Oct 2026), so a walkthrough's words stay in sight while working in Bearings; the map is as wide as before. While a solution is open in Bearings the column widens, to about 40% of the window, so each of two panes is 160 px or more, and the map narrows (to 40% of the window, the one time it keeps less than half from 1280 px); with no solution it goes back, and a column the reader has sized is left as they made it. The walkthroughs collapse to their tab from the tab's menu (Collapse to its tabs), giving Bearings the whole column. Shorter than 640 px, the view drops its key and lays the readout over the panes' names; what does not fit scrolls. Dragged elsewhere (under the map, say) it still works. On a phone, and below 900 px, it is a section of the one column, as tall as its plot needs.

It follows the Outline's selection (product owner, 27 Oct 2026): a TMA solution, one of its legs or one of its positions shows that solution (a position ringed in the plot, and current time moved to it); a sensor, or some of its cuts, shows that sensor's coverage (the last cut ringed); a cut of the sensors the solution shown is rooted in keeps the solution shown, as a dot clicked does; something unrelated (another track, an annotation) keeps what is shown. A one-line title says what is shown: Contact 1 solution · leg 2 of 3 · fix at 10:38:00Z, Towed array on BLUE ONE · 132 cuts, 132 ambiguous. It has no lists of its own: no cut list, and no Sensor or Solution pickers, which wasted space (they were the 24 and 25 Oct design); the Outline lists the cuts, legs and positions, and the Tools do what the list's buttons did.

  • The title, one line, what is shown (above).
  • The toolbar, one row: the panes shown (Bearing, Error, Course/Speed, each a toggle), Select bearings (a toggle, below), Hold (Hold scale), Reset (Reset zoom) and ⋯, which shows the Cut-off, the key, the Course/Speed pane's legend (each track named in its colour) and the notes on what the RMS assumed beneath the row.
  • A sensor's coverage, with no solution shown: every bearing of the sensor shown on the map over its whole coverage in the Bearing pane (an unresolved pair both faint), ownship's course and speed if Course/Speed is on; no Error pane, which needs a solution (132 cuts plotted, 132 ambiguous (both bearings, faint). No solution: no errors.). This is where an analyst resolves a towed array's ambiguity, before any solution: BLUE ONE's legs in the Course/Speed pane beside the bearings, and Select bearings to box the run that is the contact.

  • The plot. Time runs up the left, the latest at the top, as legacy's did. Beside each other, sharing that time axis:

    • Bearing (°): every measured bearing of the solution's sensors shown on the map, over their whole period, not only the solution's (each in the cut's colour; an unresolved pair outside the solution both faint); within the solution, a ring for one measured by the nearer of two bearings, its other bearing faint and never counted, a dotted ring for one left out; the solution's calculated bearings as a line in its colour, only where the solution is, and again as small triangles (▲) drawn over the dots, edged in the background colour, so where the measured bearings lie on the line (a solution fitted) it stays in sight beneath them, as legacy's triangles did. Bearings are unwrapped about the calculated ones, so a contact passing north stays one line: legacy's Centre bearing axis on North (0–360° to ±180°) is never needed.
    • Error (°): each residual, only where the solution is, against a strong zero line. Its background is green while every error counted is within the cut-off, pink otherwise, as legacy's calculateErrorShadeFor shaded it: counted as the RMS counts (a residual of a cut shown on the map, not left out; never an unresolved pair's other bearing). Never colour alone: beside it a mark and words say the same, and how many are beyond (product owner, 25 Oct 2026): ✓ Every error within 3.0°; ✗ 2 of 60 beyond 3.0°, the largest 4.4°; a screen reader hears the same words. Its axis fits the errors counted, zero included: an unresolved pair's other bearing and a cut left out are drawn (faint, or a dotted ring) where they fall inside it, and when some fall outside a note says so beside the cue (3 other bearings off scale, 1 left out off scale), never a dot pinned at an edge. Hold scale widens only for the errors counted. A deliberate departure from legacy: legacy's pass/fail shading counted an unresolved pair's other error too (its ambiguous series was in the shaded plot); here it does not, as the RMS does not. The shades are the theme's (VS Code's for lines added and removed); a high-contrast theme, which has none, borders the pane in its passed or failed colour instead.
    • Course/Speed (product owner, 28 Oct 2026): ownship's and the target's course and speed, each in its own track's colour, as on the map. Ownship (the sensor's host, BLUE ONE) always, with or without a solution: its course and speed as logged at its fixes, or as its fixes imply where nothing is logged. The target (the solution's DR legs) when a solution is shown, a little wider. Course solid on the Course (°) axis above, speed dashed on a Speed axis of its own beneath, in the analyst's speed unit, its ticks to the decimals their step needs. Where the two tracks' colours are too near to tell apart, the target is also marked at each fix, so they differ by more than colour; the legend in ⋯ names each (BLUE ONE (ownship): course solid, speed dashed). The course axis fits the courses shown, unwrapped through north as the bearings are; the speed axis fits the speeds from zero; with nothing to plot the pane says No course or speed to plot rather than draw empty axes. Ownship's line is thinned to 2,000 points, each stretch's least and most course and slowest and fastest speed kept, so no turn or sprint is smoothed away. Off by default: at the side column's 270 to 380 px two panes keep about 120 px each to read dots in, and three would leave 80. Turn it on for a manoeuvre, and to resolve a towed array's ambiguity.

    Which panes show is the analyst's, remembered in this browser (the playground) or as the view's state (VS Code); one at least always shows. Legs' starts are dashed across every pane, current time a line. A crosshair follows the pointer and a readout above the plot says the time and value under it (12:53:30Z · Error +1.6°). The plot is described for a screen reader (Bearings and residuals of Contact 1 solution, time upward from 12:00:00Z to 17:00:00Z; panes Bearing, Error: RMS 1.6° over 60 cuts. Every error within 5.0°.). - Zoom. Drag a box in any pane: time zooms to its height in every pane, and that pane's values to its width. A double-click, Reset zoom, or 0 undoes it. A zoom stays while the solution is dragged, so the fine tuning is done zoomed in. - Select bearings (product owner, 28 Oct 2026): a toggle (aria-pressed). On, the pointer is a cell cross, a line beneath the plot says so, and a box dragged in the Bearing pane resolves instead of zooming (a box in another pane still zooms): the box toggles each cut it takes in (product owner, 28 Oct 2026), all at once, as one step with its provenance, named for what it did: an unresolved cut with a dot inside keeps the side whose dot was boxed, its first bearing or its twin, the faint other dot going (Kept 27 Towed array cuts to starboard, 09:46:00Z–10:13:00Z); a resolved cut whose kept dot is inside is made ambiguous again, both its faint dots back (Made 27 Towed array cuts ambiguous again, 09:46:00Z–10:13:00Z); both in one box, Kept 14 cuts to starboard and made 13 ambiguous again (the period, and the sensor where the name would be too long for the History, in the step's next note). An unresolved cut with dots inside on both sides is left as it was, and the step says so (1 cut boxed on both sides, left as they were.); a cut never ambiguous (one bearing, as a bow sonar's) is untouched; hidden cuts are never boxed (they are not drawn). Nothing to change, no step: the status line says why (Nothing to change: 4 cuts boxed on both sides, left as they were.). The zoom stays as it was, during and after, through undo and redo. It works with a sensor's coverage shown (the usual case, before any solution) and with a solution shown. The result is said in the status line, read aloud. It is the same step the Tools' Keep port, Keep starboard and Make ambiguous again take (debrief/resolve_ambiguity, with other_cut_ids for the cuts boxed on their twin and clear_cut_ids for those made ambiguous again), in both hosts, so agents can ask for it too. Only the dots drawn can be boxed: an unresolved pair's both are drawn inside the Bearing axis, which fits both; one beyond a zoom is outside the box's reach until the zoom is reset. - A dot clicked selects its cut, in the Outline (its sensor opened to it) and on the map, and moves current time to it, as legacy's did; the plot rings it. A click on the solution's calculated line or its course or speed selects the solution's position there, in the Outline too: the solution selected, current time at the fix. A click away from any dot moves current time. - The cue and the RMS, one status line beneath the plot, and what the RMS assumed (ambiguous cuts by the nearer side, cuts without a residual, derived origins, hidden cuts left out). While a solution is dragged it says (while dragging). - The first guess's form, beneath the status line when TMA solution from cuts… is chosen in the Tools: for exactly the cuts selected in the Outline, or a sensor's in the time window.

docs.title: The Outline and the Tools
docs.text:
Decisions of the product owner, 27 Oct 2026.

  1. A TMA solution is a tree in the Outline. It expands to its legs (Leg 2 10:38:00Z–12:00:00Z · 44 fixes · 200.0°T 5.2 kn), and each leg to its positions (fixes: 10:38:00Z 200.0°T 5.2 kn), its course and speed those of its DR legs. Selecting a position selects the solution on the map, shows it in Bearings with the position ringed, and moves current time to it; a leg or a position stands for its solution wherever a feature is wanted (the map, the analysis tools).
  2. A sensor expands to its cuts, under its track: time; bearing, with the other side for an ambiguous pair not yet resolved, marked ≈ as Bearings measures it by the nearer (≈ 236.3° stbd / 142.3° port), or the side kept (236.3° stbd kept); its range if it has one; hidden on map if hidden, the row greyed. A screen reader hears Cut at 09:46:00Z, 236.3° to starboard or 142.3° to port, not yet resolved. Selecting cuts selects them on the map; click, Shift-click a range, Ctrl-click to add or take away.
  3. Thousands of rows. In the playground the tree is virtualised: drawn whole up to 600 rows (a plot's features and a sensor or two of a few hundred cuts), and beyond only the rows in sight and some either side, the rest stood in for by spacers, so a sensor of 10,000 cuts opens and scrolls at once. In VS Code the native tree draws only the rows in sight, and children are made only as a branch opens; a sensor of more than 500 cuts opens to pages of 500 by time (09:00:00Z–09:41:30Z, cuts 1–500 of 1,840).

  4. The Tools' entries for the selection are above the analysis tools in the Tools (playground) and in the Tools view's For the Outline's selection (VS Code, where each is also a command and on the tree's menus). Each is one undoable step with its provenance; each shows when the selection has what it acts on, and when it cannot act it is disabled with the reason beside it:

    Entry For Does Disabled when Split before 10:38:00Z one position of a leg The position becomes the first of a new leg (leg_starts); the other legs keep their positions: nothing moves it already starts a leg; a leg would keep fewer than two positions either side; not one position Split after 10:37:30Z one position of a leg The position becomes the last of its leg, the next starting the new one it already ends a leg, or is the solution's last; as above Keep port, Keep starboard cuts The bearing on that side of the course where each cut's sensor was, for every cut selected at once (a whole period resolved in one step) none of them has two bearings Make ambiguous again cuts Both bearings drawn again none has a side kept Leave out of Contact 1 solution, Count in Contact 1 solution cuts The cuts left out of the RMS, or counted again, of the solution Bearings shows if they are rooted in it, else the only one; rooted in several and none shown, the analyst chooses none is rooted in a solution; all left out, or all counted, already Hide 12 cuts, Show 12 cuts cuts Off the map and out of every solution's residuals (legacy's Visible=false), or back; the notes say which solutions they leave (Contact 1 solution: 3 of its cuts left out of its residuals until shown again) all hidden, or none hidden, already Delete 12 cuts cuts Deleted from the plot; the solutions rooted in them drop those ids, and the notes say so (Contact 1 solution drops the 3 cuts deleted it was rooted in: rooted in 28 cuts now, its fixes where they were). Undo brings them back never (but read-only) TMA solution from 60 cuts 12:24:00Z–12:53:30Z… cuts, or a sensor The first guess's form in Bearings, the solution rooted in exactly the cuts selected; with only a sensor selected, its cuts shown on the map in the time window. Two clicks on the map stay, from the form all hidden; fewer than two times

    An earlier revision shown read-only disables them all, saying so. The Outline's toolbar (product owner, 28 Oct 2026) also hides and shows cuts, with tracks, solutions and sensors in the same selection, through the same operation, and its Select children turns a sensor selected into all its cuts, a solution into its legs and a leg into its positions (selection). 5. The plot keeps its actions (Keyboard and touch): a dot clicked selects its cut, now in the Outline too; Space and Delete leave it out; S splits; 1 and 2 keep a side. The map's cut popover stays. Bearings' own Split, Keep, Leave out and Previous and Next ambiguous buttons are gone: the Tools have them, for one cut or many.

The cut-off is the analyst's setting, like their other preferences: 3° unless they set another, kept in their Debrief configuration (tma_error_cut_off, configuration version 4), never in a plot. Set it under ⋯ in the view, or in VS Code's Settings (debrief.tma.errorCutOff); the two agree, and both take 0.01° to 180°.

docs.title: Fitting a leg, as legacy's tutorial teaches it
docs.text:
1. Pin the leg's start on the first bearing. Make the solution with its first guess's range along the first cut's bearing (the form), so the first error is zero. Early in the fit the errors ramp away from it, and the Error pane is pink. Bearings never give range: to try another, move the whole solution along that bearing (Move… with the distance and the bearing's reciprocal, or its Move handle with the lowest error kept on zero), then shear again; the RMS may rise on the move before the shear brings it down.
  2. Drag the leg's end (a shear: the start held) and watch the Error pane. Its axis fits the errors every frame, so as they shrink they still fill the pane: a ramp that tilts one way or the other says which way to drag. Drag until the errors flatten about zero and the pane turns green.
  3. Zoom in for the fine tuning: a box round the leg's errors, then small drags (or the arrow keys on the handle). The zoom stays while dragging. Hold scale keeps the Error axis still if the moving scale distracts; it widens rather than hide an error.
  4. The next leg: split at the manoeuvre (Split before in the Tools, on the position in the Outline where the errors start to run away, or S in the plot at the cut chosen there), choose This leg on the map (the leg current time is in; a click picks another), pin its start on its own first bearing (its Move handle, or Move… with This leg), and shear its end the same way; the leg already fitted stays where it is.
  5. When it is done. The cue counts every error of the solution, so it stays pink until every leg is fitted. With noisy bearings it may never turn green: a 1.5° sonar over a hundred cuts leaves a few beyond a 3° cut-off whatever the fit (on the walkthrough's sample, RED ONE's true track leaves 8 of 101). Aim for an RMS near the bearings' own accuracy and only a handful beyond, the largest not far past the cut-off; one far out is a wild bearing to leave out.

docs.title: Live residuals while dragging
docs.text:
The map previews a drag as it always has (a drag is one step only when let go). For a solution, each frame's positions go to the Bearings view, which works the residuals out again in the browser (the same geodesic and the same rules as Python, held to the same vectors) at most once a frame. Let go, and Python's residuals for the saved step replace them. A drag put back (Escape) puts the residuals back.

The axes while dragging (product owner, 25 Oct 2026). The Error axis fits the errors every frame, as legacy's auto-resize did (BaseStackedDotsView.wrappedUpdateStackedDots); with Hold scale it stays as it was, and widens on the side an error falls outside, never shrinking until let go. No dot is ever drawn at an edge it is not at: the held axis of the first TMA pull request clamped them there, and that is superseded. The Bearing axis keeps its range during a drag, as legacy's did, widened the same way if the calculated bearings leave it. The Course/Speed pane fits its courses and speeds every frame, the solution's worked out from the dragged fixes with the WGS84 ellipsoid's local radii at each leg's middle latitude (localCourse), measured against geographiclib's geodesic: within 0.0001° and 0.0001% for legs to 10 km at latitudes to 70°, at worst 0.0002° and 0.0006% for a 20 km leg at 75°. A zoom wins over all of them.

A frame does only what changes: the residuals worked out again (each row's cut and time parsed once, before the drag begins, and the rows written again in place), the RMS and the cue, and the plot (its size read once a drag, dots of one kind and colour drawn as one path, a dot where its like is already drawn left out, the crosshair on a canvas of its own). The whole frame is timed. Measured in headless Chromium on a shared four-core machine, sixty frames each, all three panes shown, the sensor's other cuts half as many again and ownship's course 2,000 fixes: 600 cuts, median 3 to 4 ms; 1,000 cuts, 5 to 6 ms; 2,000 cuts, 7 to 11 ms, its 95th percentile 12 to 17 ms; the worst single frame at 2,000 cuts 18 to 30 ms, from the machine's pauses rather than the work (NFR-04's 100 ms either way). The playground's test drags a solution of 600, 1,000 and 2,000 cuts and holds each median within a frame.

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text:
The Outline is a tree (role="tree"), one tab stop. Up and Down move the keyboard, Right opens a row or goes into it, Left closes it or goes to its parent; Home, End, Page Up and Page Down as usual; Shift with the arrows extends the selection from where it started (a run of cuts); Enter or Space selects the row, Ctrl with them adds or takes it away, Shift with them selects from the anchor; Ctrl+A selects every row shown. Each row says its level, its place and how many share it (aria-level, aria-posinset, aria-setsize, aria-expanded), kept so while virtualised, as the row with the keyboard is always in the page. In VS Code the native tree does the same. The Tools' entries are buttons (a disabled one stays reachable, aria-disabled, its reason beside it and read with it); in VS Code, items of the Tools view, commands in the Command Palette, and items on the tree's menus (Shift+F10).

The plot is a tab stop too, the keyboard's way to everything the pointer does there:

Key In the plot Up, Down The next later or earlier cut (time runs up), ringed in each pane, read above the plot and said to a screen reader Enter Select the cut, in the Outline and on the map Space, Delete Leave the cut chosen out of the RMS, or count it again (as Leave out and Count in in the Tools), one step S Split the solution into legs at the cut chosen, one step (where each leg keeps two fixes) 1, 2 Keep an unresolved ambiguous cut's first or second bearing, one step (as Keep port or Keep starboard in the Tools) +, − Zoom time in or out about the cut chosen ], [ Zoom the Error pane's values in or out Page Up, Page Down Move a zoom later or earlier 0 Reset the zoom (as a double-click, or Reset zoom)

What the plot's keys do is said in the view's live region as well as drawn: the cut chosen (12:41:30Z, Bearing 263.4°, Error +1.2°) and the zoom (Zoomed: 12:20:00Z to 13:10:00Z). Time zooms in to ten seconds at the least.

Select bearings from the keyboard needs no keys of its own: select the run of cuts in the Outline (a sensor opened, Shift with the arrows), then Keep port or Keep starboard in the Tools, or Make ambiguous again to take a side back, the same step (The Outline and the Tools).

The toolbar's toggles are buttons (aria-pressed; in Windows' forced colours a pressed one is drawn in the system's Highlight); ⋯ is a disclosure (aria-expanded), and Escape closes it and puts the keyboard back on it; the cut-off is a number field. The plot's keys choose, select, leave out, split and keep; the Tools do the same for the Outline's selection. The first guess's form takes the keyboard first, at the range; each field says what it means beneath it as it is typed (Means 5.00 nmi.), and a mistake before anything is sent. Two clicks on the map instead has no keyboard way of its own: the form is the keyboard's. On the map, This leg is a button like Whole track, and the drags are the track's, with their keys (track operations); from the keyboard, the leg dragged is the one current time is in (a position chosen in the Outline moves current time to it), and a click or tap on the solution's line picks another. The forms Move…, Rotate…, Shear… and Stretch… offer This leg under What changes too, the leg current time is in, so a leg is fitted by typing (26 Oct 2026). A tap is a click; a box is dragged with a finger as with a mouse (the plot takes the touch, so the page scrolls from beside it).

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Generated solutions (SATC, or a solution fitted to the bearings): out of scope (CAP-21).
  • Residuals while ownship is dragged: ownship moves the cuts' origins; the residuals are worked out again when the drag is saved, not while it goes.
  • Boxing dots off scale: Select bearings boxes the dots drawn. With a zoom, a pair's other side beyond the zoomed Bearing axis is out of the box's reach until the zoom is reset or moved.
  • Several sensors' cuts in one run: cuts of several sensors can be selected in the Outline and a solution made of them, but Bearings shows one sensor's coverage at a time without a solution (the plot of a solution shows every cut of its sensors).
  • Legacy's TMA solution set (contact ellipses): still listed as not imported.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Model: TmaSolution, TmaRequest in schemas/linkml/features.yaml; schemas/linkml/tma.yaml (the view's rows and the residuals; the sensors' other cuts, ownship's courses and the cut-off it plots with); tma_error_cut_off in schemas/linkml/config.yaml (the analyst's cut-off, debrief_config.tma_error_cut_off and @debrief/config's tmaErrorCutOff); the rules in debrief_schemas.documents (a contact named, the period in order, cuts rooted once, cuts left out only of those rooted, legs in order; a request by form or by clicks, not both).
  • Python: debrief_kernel.tma (residuals, vectorised; the first guess; a click onto a cut's line); debrief_stac.tma and Catalogue.create_tma, tma_residuals, tma_exclude, tma_split_leg, with split_track and merge_tracks; debrief_io.dpf_tma (legacy solutions); debrief_stac.tma.split_at_fix_index, split_at_fix, without_cuts and hidden_notes, with Catalogue.delete_cuts and set_hidden; debrief/tma_create, debrief/tma_residuals, debrief/tma_exclude_cut, debrief/tma_split_leg (with side), debrief/delete_cuts and debrief/set_hidden in debrief_tools.service.
  • Hosts: vscode/webview/tma.ts (residuals while dragging, words; the coverage and ownship sent to the view), vscode/webview/stackeddots.ts (the plot's axes, fit and hold, cut-off, zoom, pointing, course and speed, panes), vscode/webview/tmacontrol.ts (the view), vscode/webview/tmamap.ts (two clicks), vscode/webview/trackmap.ts (This leg); vscode/webview/outlinemodel.ts (the Outline's legs, positions and cuts, the Tools' entries, what Bearings shows) and vscode/webview/outlinetree.ts (the tree's rows and keys); vscode/src/views/outline.ts (VS Code's tree) and vscode/src/views/tools.ts (its Tools view); vscode/src/panels/bearingsview.ts and the commands debrief.tmaCreate, debrief.tmaSplitLeg, debrief.tmaExclude, debrief.showBearings, debrief.chooseInOutline, and the Tools' debrief.splitBeforeFix, debrief.splitAfterFix, debrief.hideCuts, debrief.showCuts, debrief.deleteCuts, debrief.tmaLeaveOut, debrief.tmaCountIn, debrief.keepPort, debrief.keepStarboard, debrief.makeAmbiguous and debrief.tmaFromCuts; the playground's in vscode/play/host.ts and vscode/play/outline.ts.
  • Tests: python/debrief-kernel/tests/test_tma.py, python/debrief-stac/tests/test_tma.py, python/debrief-io/tests/test_dpf_tma.py, python/debrief-tools/tests/test_tma_service.py, vscode/test/unit/tma.test.ts, vscode/test/unit/stackeddots.test.ts, vscode/test/unit/outline.test.ts, vscode/test/play/tma.mjs, and two steps of vscode/test/integration/suite.ts; vectors schemas/vectors/tma-residuals.json and schemas/vectors/tma-legs.json.

docs.title: Tool invocation and forms
docs.text:
How an analyst runs a tool: the generated parameter form, its explanation, running it, and where the result goes.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement TL-07 Debrief generates the parameter form from the tool's declaration. CAP-24 The form shows the tool's explanation, and any judgement it involves. SUB-04 Values on the form use the analyst's units and notation. TL-11, TL-13 Results may be features, changes, deletions, non-spatial results, named sets or changes to shared state; non-spatial results appear in a temporary panel and can be saved. TL-14 Agents invoke the same tools with the same permissions. SUB-19, SUB-24 Every run is recorded, with the tool's version.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Choose. The analyst picks a tool under For this selection.
  2. Form. The tool's form opens beside the map. Debrief builds it from the declaration (TL-07):
  3. the title and explanation, then any judgement, set apart so it is read (CAP-24);
  4. what the tool will act on ("Applies to: NELSON, BLUE");
  5. one field per parameter, with its explanation and default. A quantity has a unit picker, starting at the default's unit (SUB-04).
  6. Times are typed as the language guide writes them: 09:30Z (on the plot's day), 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, a date-time group such as 150930Z JUN 23, or ISO. Under the field the form says what it understood ("Means 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z"), so a mistaken day is caught before the run.
  7. Run. Run sends the values; Cancel closes the form and changes nothing. While the tool runs, the form shows Running… and can't be sent twice.
  8. Refused. If a value is wrong, or the tool fails, the form stays open with the reason above the buttons, in the analyst's words. The plot is untouched (TL-03).
  9. Done. The form closes.
  10. Features. New or changed features appear on the map and in the outline at once. A notification says what changed ("Range rings added 3 features").
  11. Numbers and tables. These open in a Results panel beside the map (TL-13). The panel:
    • repeats the tool's judgement, so a figure is never read without its caveat (CAP-24);
    • says what was added to the plot;
    • says that the figures themselves are not saved;
    • offers Copy for each table, as tab-separated text for a report or spreadsheet.
  12. History. Every run that changes the plot is recorded with the tool, its version, who ran it, the selection and every value (SUB-19, SUB-24). A run that only returns a number or table changes nothing and records nothing.

Agents and keyboard users run the same tools through the Run tool command, without the form. The checks and the records are the same (TL-14).

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Form as Tool form (webview)
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Worker as Tool worker
    participant Cat as Catalogue
    Analyst->>Form: Run (spacing 1.5 nmi, 3 rings)
    Form->>Host: run_tool
    Host->>Form: form_busy
    Host->>Service: tools/call (store, plot, selection, values, agent)
    Service->>Worker: run on a copy of the plot
    Worker->>Cat: check result, record history, save atomically
    Worker-->>Service: result, changed
    Service-->>Host: result
    Host->>Host: reload plot; show results if any
    Host->>Form: close

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• The form: vscode/webview/form.tsx, built from vscrui components behind vscode/webview/ui.tsx.
  • Running from the host: vscode/src/extension.ts (runTool).
  • Results panel: vscode/webview/results.tsx.
  • The service side: debrief_tools.service and debrief_tools.run.

Not yet: echoing values other than times back to the analyst, progress and cancelling a run that's under way (long-running operations, Phase 2), undo (Phase 2), graphs (shown as tables until then), and saving a result.

docs.title: Tote
docs.text: How an analyst compares one primary track with several secondaries at current time: the Tote, what it measures, how tracks are chosen, and what is saved where.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-06 The Tote shows relative geometry between one primary and several secondaries, updated with current time. CAP-07 The Tote is a view onto a measure group: a named, reusable set of measures for a mode of analysis, extending a shared core, defined by a study's lead analyst and kept in the study catalogue. NFR-04 Tote values update within 100 ms of a change to current time. Per-call requests meet it (Phase 0 spike); the dense-sampling fallback stays a contingency. PRN-03 Measures are worked out in Python. Views only format them. SUB-03 Range and bearing are geodesic on WGS84. SUB-04 Values are written with the analyst's units and decimals, by the formatting service. SUB-22 View state in the island is neither undoable nor recorded; two analysts changing it at once are told, not overwritten. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, and by touch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. One component, every host. VS Code shows the Tote as a view in the Debrief sidebar, below Time, folded until it is first used: the commands that choose its tracks open it. The playground shows the same component under the time controller, in a panel that folds away by its heading, as every panel in the playground's side column does (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026): the heading stays a heading for screen readers, with a button in it that says whether the panel is open, and which panels are folded is remembered in that browser (an embedded demo starts with its panels open). The map draws a thin, muted, dashed line from the primary's square to each secondary's at current time (see 9).

  2. One primary, several secondaries. The primary is the track the others are measured from: usually ownship. Choose it from Primary at the top of the Tote. Add secondaries from Add below the table, in the order they should be listed. A track is never both: choosing a secondary as the primary takes it out of the secondaries. Each secondary has × in its column's heading, after its name, to remove it; Delete or Backspace on the × does the same.

    From the outline, a track's menu (right-click; press and hold on a touch screen; Shift+F10 or the menu key from the keyboard) has Set as Tote primary, Add to Tote and Remove from Tote. In VS Code these act on every selected track, so several can be added at once. 3. The core measures. The Tote is a view onto a measure group (CAP-07). The only group so far is core, the measures legacy Debrief's Tote showed, its optional angle on the bow and bearing rate included (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026), in this order:

    Measure Row heading (default units) Of Worked out as Range Range nmi primary to secondary Geodesic distance on WGS84; where the analyst's lengths are nautical miles, under 1 nmi in whole yards, 60 yd, and from 1 nmi in nautical miles, 1.00 nmi Bearing Brg °T primary to secondary True bearing along the geodesic, three figures: 304.0°T; a dash where the two are in one place Relative bearing Rel ° primary to secondary The bearing less the primary's course: red to port, green to starboard, R045.0°, G120.0°; dead ahead 000.0°, dead astern 180.0°; a dash where the primary has no course, or the two are in one place Angle on the bow AOB ° primary to secondary The bearing from the secondary to the primary less the secondary's course: the secondary's aspect as the primary sees it, written as relative bearing is, R030.0° (the primary on its port bow, so its port side is seen), G135.0°; 000.0° bows on, 180.0° stern on; a dash where the secondary has no course Bearing rate Brg rate °/min primary to secondary How fast the true bearing from the primary changes, from both tracks' courses and speeds at that instant (each moved a second either way along its course, on the geodesic): positive drawing right (clockwise), negative drawing left, in degrees per minute (the angular-rate kind, 0.5°/min, to the analyst's angle decimals); a dash without both courses and speeds Course Crse °T each track Recorded course at the fixes either side, interpolated the shorter way round through 360°; where they are opposite (within 0.5°), a reversal with no shorter way round, the nearer fix's course, not one half way that the track never steered (half way, the later fix's); a track with no recorded courses, the geodesic's direction there Speed Spd kn each track Recorded speed, interpolated; else the leg's length over its duration Depth Depth m each track Recorded depth, interpolated; a dash where none is recorded

    Units and decimals are the analyst's display settings (SUB-04): ranges in their length unit, speeds in theirs, angles to their decimals, bearing rate included (0.5°/min at the default one decimal). Close ranges are in yards, as analysts call them: where lengths are in nautical miles, a range under 1 nmi is in whole yards (60 yd, 1350 yd), from 1 nmi in nautical miles to the analyst's decimals; any other length unit is used as it is (decisions, product owner, 14 Oct 2026). Only the Tote's range does this: other distances on the map, such as a move's readout, stay in the analyst's length unit. Depths are in metres, or feet where lengths are in feet or yards, to one decimal: there is no depth setting yet. Relative bearing uses the primary's course as its head, as legacy Debrief did; a heading separate from course would change it only for a platform crabbing across a current.

  3. The table: a row a measure, a column a track. Legacy Debrief's Tote, as the product owner chose it (decision, 14 Oct 2026; it replaced a layout of labelled values, which read badly on a phone).

    ● BLUE ONE ● RED ONE × ● Cargo 01 × Range nmi 4.04 30.91 Brg °T 283.5 230.7 Rel ° R012.2 R065.0 AOB ° R121.2 G176.2 Brg rate °/min -1.5 -0.3 Crse °T 295.7 224.6 234.2 Spd kn 10.0 5.1 0.3 Depth m 0.0 20.0 —
    • Row headings name each measure with the unit its values are in, as the analyst's settings write it (Range km, Spd m/s, Depth ft with other settings). The unit is taken from the formatting service itself, so a heading and its values cannot disagree. Hover a heading for the measure's full name.
    • Cells hold figures only, right-aligned in tabular figures; hover one for the value with its unit. A value in another unit than its heading's keeps its own: a close range is 1070 yd in the row headed nmi, the only cell where a unit appears.
    • The primary's column comes first, its name in bold; it is blank for the measures between tracks (its range from itself), and gives its own course, speed and depth.
    • A column a secondary, in the order added, headed by its colour on the map, its name and its ×. Where room is short, a name breaks at its spaces onto a second line (Cargo over 01), so a column is no wider than its values; a longer one is cut short, in full on hover.
    • A quiet rule divides the measures between tracks from each track's own.
    • One layout at every width. Where the columns do not fit, as in VS Code's sidebar, the playground's side column, a demo in a blog post or on a phone, the row headings stay put and the tracks scroll sideways inside the table; the page never scrolls sideways.
    • It is a real table for screen readers: named Tote, each value read with its measure's heading and its track's name.
    • Where tracks are at current time. Exactly where the map draws each track's square at current time: along the geodesic between the fixes either side, in proportion to time. The Tote and the map are held to the same shared test vectors (schemas/vectors/track-positions.json), so the range read off the Tote is the range between the two squares.
    • No data at current time. A track that has not started, or has ended, has a column of dashes, its name greyed, and says why under the table: Cargo 04 Starts 08:28:48Z or Tug 01 Ended 10:35:17Z (and on hover, over its column). Without the primary at current time, only each secondary's own measures show. A track chosen that the plot no longer has (merged or deleted since) says No longer in the plot; remove it, or undo the change that removed it.
    • Values follow current time. Dragging current time, stepping it, playing or a tool moving it all update the Tote. It asks Python once for each time: one request at a time, and when the answer comes, one more for the latest time if current time has moved on. Times passed over meanwhile are never asked for, so playing never builds a queue, and the Tote is never more than one answer behind (decision 11 Oct, from the Phase 0 spike). Only a Tote that is showing asks.
    • What is saved where.
    Where Undoable In the history The primary, the secondaries, the measure group, the map's lines on or off The plot file, in its island No No Current time Shared state, not saved No No Measure groups of a study (part B) The study catalogue

    Choosing tracks is how the plot is being looked at, not a change to it, so it is view state, like the time window: it travels with the plot, so a colleague given the plot file sees the same Tote, but Ctrl+Z never changes it and choosing never conflicts with a change to the plot's content. Legacy Debrief kept its Tote's tracks in the GUI part of a .dpf file, beside the plot's data, for the same reason. Each choice is saved at once, through the same path as the window. A colleague's choice made meanwhile is shown, never overwritten: Someone else changed this plot's view, so your choice of Tote tracks was not saved (SUB-28).

  4. The Tote on the map. A thin dashed line in a muted theme colour (the theme's description colour, never a fixed one) runs from the primary's square to each secondary's at current time, along the geodesic, so the range read off the Tote is the line's length. It moves with current time, and a secondary with no data then has none. Lines on the map, a box under Add, turns them off and on for the plot: island state like the choice of tracks, never a step (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026). The lines are never in the way: they take no clicks.

docs.title: Keyboard and touch
docs.text:
Where Key or gesture Does Primary, Add ↑ ↓ (or Alt+↓ to open the list) Choose the primary; add a secondary The table Tab Reaches each secondary's ×, in its column's heading, named for screen readers (Remove Cargo 01 from the Tote) × Enter, Space, Delete, Backspace Removes that secondary; the keyboard moves to the next one's ×, else the one before, else Add The table, too wide for its place Scroll sideways (trackpad, Shift+wheel, swipe) Moves the tracks under the row headings; Tab to a × brings its column into view A track in the outline Shift+F10, menu key Its menu: Set as Tote primary, Add to Tote or Remove from Tote; ↑ ↓ move, Enter chooses, Escape closes A track in the outline (touch) Press and hold The same menu Lines on the map Space Turns the map's lines from the primary off, and on The playground's Tote heading Enter, Space Folds the panel away, and back

Values arriving many times a second while playing never move the keyboard: they are written into the cells already there, so the × that had it keeps it, and nothing shifts.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Tote
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Plot as Plot file
    Analyst->>Tote: Add RED ONE
    Tote->>Host: tote_changed (primary, secondaries)
    Host->>Service: debrief/set_view (view with tote, hash last read)
    Service->>Plot: rewrite the island only
    loop each change of current time
        Host->>Service: debrief/tote (time, tote) if none is out
        Service-->>Host: ToteResult (values in m, deg, m/s)
        Host->>Tote: show_tote (values)
        Note over Host,Service: a time passed over meanwhile is never asked for
    end

docs.title: Latency (NFR-04)
docs.text:
Measured on the development container on 14 Oct 2026, serial 1 of the sample exercise, BLUE ONE against every other track, with all eight core measures (bearing rate is the dearest: each track is moved a second either way and the bearing measured again):

Host Measured from p50 p95 max Tool service, in process (pytest, 9 secondaries, 400 slider positions) request to reply 7.8 ms 10.4 ms 16 ms Python alone, the same call to return 4.4 ms 6.2 ms 8.5 ms VS Code, real service (integration test, 3 secondaries, 300 times at 60 a second) asking to showing 5.2 ms 10.4 ms 33 ms Playground, Pyodide in Chromium (playground test, 4 secondaries, playing) asking to showing 6.4 to 7.2 ms 15 to 20 ms (three runs) 30 to 71 ms Pyodide in Node (spikes/pyodide/run.sh, 2 secondaries) Python alone, mean 2.2 ms

Every measurement is well inside 100 ms, so the Tote stays on the architecture the Phase 0 spike chose: one request per time. The dense-sampling fallback is not built. Each check reports its numbers and asserts generously (three times the budget at p95), so a slow CI machine does not fail it: python/debrief-tools/tests/test_tote_latency.py, the integration test's Tote steps and vscode/test/play/tote.mjs.

docs.title: Measure groups: what part B adds
docs.text:
The schema and the service are ready for groups beyond core:

  • MeasureDefinition (id, title, heading label, subject relative or own, quantity kind, how it is shown) and MeasureGroup (id, title, extends, measure ids in order) are LinkML types; ToteView.measure_group names the group a plot's Tote shows; ToteResult carries the group and its definitions with the values, so a view shows any group without knowing it in advance.
  • debrief/measure_groups lists the groups and measures available; debrief/tote takes the group in its tote parameter. A group a plot names that its study does not have is shown as core, with a note saying so.

Part B needs: a study catalogue item holding the study's groups, written by its lead analyst and read by every plot in the study (CAP-07); measures beyond core declared by Python tool libraries, as tools are, and evaluated by debrief_stac.tote; a choice of group in the Tote; and rules for a group whose measure a library no longer provides.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Measures: python/debrief-kernel/src/debrief_kernel/measures.py (TrackMotion, measure, CORE_GROUP), positions from geodesy.TrackPath, tested in tests/test_measures.py (geodesic range and bearing, relative bearing across 360°, angle on the bow, bearing rate against crossing speed over range, far north, the antimeridian, missing data, interpolation). Formatting: format_range, format_relative_bearing and format_depth in debrief_kernel.formatting and formatRange, formatRelativeBearing, formatDepth in ts/kernel, held to schemas/vectors/formatting.json. Course across a reversal: TrackMotion and the course samples in schemas/vectors/track-positions.json. The playground's folding panels: vscode/play/fold.ts, played in vscode/test/play/tote.mjs.
  • Over a plot: python/debrief-stac/src/debrief_stac/tote.py (tote, tote_tracks, measure_groups): tracks prepared once and kept while the plot file is unchanged, or only its island; tested in tests/test_tote.py.
  • The service: debrief/tote and debrief/measure_groups; the choice through debrief/set_view.
  • The component: vscode/webview/totecontrol.ts and tote.css; its rules, free of the page, in vscode/webview/totelogic.ts (withPrimary, withSecondaries, withoutSecondary, withMapLines, toteMapLines, formatMeasure, toteHeadings and measureUnit for the row headings' units, cellText for figures alone, toteLines, ToteRequests), tested in vscode/test/unit/tote.test.ts, with the map's positionAt (vscode/webview/geodesic.ts) held to the shared position vectors.
  • The map: drawToteLines in vscode/webview/map.ts, from the island on show_plot and from set_tote when the choice changes.
  • VS Code: the Tote view, vscode/src/panels/toteview.ts and vscode/webview/tote.ts; saving the choice in vscode/src/extension.ts (saveTote, through saveView). Commands debrief.tote.setPrimary, debrief.tote.add, debrief.tote.remove (the outline's menu) and debrief.setTote (agents and keyboard macros).
  • The playground: vscode/play/host.ts (refreshTote, chooseTote, trackMenu) and tote in vscode/play/play.py.
  • Schema: schemas/linkml/measures.yaml (0.0.18); PlotView.tote (with map_lines); messages show_tote, tote_changed and set_tote.

Not yet: study measure groups and measures beyond core (part B); a heading separate from course for relative bearing; a depth unit setting.

docs.title: Track operations
docs.text: How an analyst moves a track, or a period of it, rotates it about a point, shears or stretches it from one end, splits it at a time and merges tracks into one; and how they clean it: removing jumps, smoothing it, and giving single fixes a colour, a label or a comment of their own. Part A: moving, rotating, splitting and merging (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026). Part B1: shearing and stretching, shear first as the operation analysts use most with TMA legs (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026; see Shearing and stretching). Cleaning tracks (part B2, 14 Oct 2026): jump removal, smoothing and marked fixes. Single fixes, and dead reckoning (part B3, 14 Oct 2026): one fix dragged on its own, and the legacy OTG and DR modes, asked of each track imported. Editing a track plotted by dead reckoning (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026): every operation on a DR track changes where it starts, or its courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-01 Dragging, splitting, merging, jump removal and smoothing of tracks; single fixes dragged on their own; the legacy OTG and DR modes. CAP-02 Track edits are destructive in the working plot, each recorded as a delta. CAP-21 The TMA module's manual dragging of a solution: translate, rotate, stretch, shear. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; undo is replay to a point, never an inverse operation. SUB-24 Provenance records who made each change, and what they asked for. SUB-03, SUB-04 Measured along geodesics; read and shown in the analyst's units and notation. SUB-26, SUB-28 Moving a track changes neither current time, the window nor the selection; a change made elsewhere is never overwritten. NFR-13 Dragging a track has a keyboard and a form-based equivalent. PRN-08 The analyst owns the data: a track is moved where the analyst says, without second-guessing; nothing is removed or moved without the analyst seeing it first. EXT-14, EXT-15 A legacy plot's per-fix colours, labels and comments are imported, not listed as left out; a leg it plotted by dead reckoning is said to be.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. What moves: the whole track, or a period of it. Legacy Debrief dragged a whole track, or a selected time period of it, to line it up with a reference: that is kept (decision, 13 Oct 2026). On the map, a small control below the drawing toolbar, What changes, says which (for moving, rotating, shearing and stretching alike): Whole track (the default) or Time window, the fixes in the time window shown. The forms offer the same choice; for a TMA solution split into legs, they also offer This leg, the leg current time is in, as the map's This leg drags it (TMA solutions; 26 Oct 2026). An agent may give any period. Fixes whose times fall in the period, ends included, move; the rest stay where they are.

  2. The joins jump. Moving a period moves only its fixes, so the track jumps where they meet the rest: the track is not stretched or smoothed to keep it continuous. (That is over the ground. On a track plotted by dead reckoning the fixes after follow on, with no jump: see Editing a track plotted by dead reckoning.) The map shows the jump while the analyst drags, and says so: only the fixes in the time window move, so the track jumps where they meet the rest. Jump removal (part B) will tidy a join an analyst does not want.

  3. Moving is geodesic. A move takes every fix the same range along the same true bearing, each along its own geodesic, as legacy Debrief offset each fix: not a change of latitude and longitude, as an annotation's whole-shape move is. Courses and speeds over ground are kept as they were. On a curved earth no move of every fix by the same range and bearing keeps a track's shape exactly: as meridians converge, a track far north moved north is squeezed east-west a little, and one moved east turns a little. For the moves an analyst makes the difference is small (a track at 60°N moved 5 nmi north is 0.25% shorter; at 70°N moved 20 nmi, 1.6% shorter; a track steering 000 at 70°N moved 20 nmi east then steers 000.9), so the recorded speeds and courses are kept rather than worked out again from the moved positions.

  4. Rotating is geodesic. A rotation keeps each fix's range from the pivot and turns its bearing from the pivot by the angle; clockwise is positive. Courses over ground of the fixes turned turn with the track: by the angle, near the pivot; far from it, or far north, by a little more or less, as the meridians converge, so that each course is still the track's direction as drawn (turned about the North Pole, a ship steering 090 still steers 090). The pivot is, unless the analyst chooses, the fix nearest current time, when current time is within what moves; otherwise the first fix of what moves. On the map the pivot is a handle of its own: drag it (or move it with the arrow keys) to turn about somewhere else. Moving the pivot records nothing; it says where the next rotation turns about.

  5. Handles. A track selected on its own, and drawn on the map, shows three handles in the theme's focus colour, each named for a screen reader:

    Handle Looks like Does Move a filled square on a fix in the middle of what moves drag it, and the track follows it Rotate a ring beyond the fix farthest from the pivot, on a dashed arm from it drag it round the pivot, and the track turns with it Pivot a dotted ring, by default on the fix nearest current time drag it to choose where the track turns about Ends a diamond beside the first fix and one beside the last fix of what moves (a double edge when Stretch is chosen) drag one to shear the track, or stretch it, holding the other end (below)

    Dragging the move or rotate handle draws the track moved or turned as the pointer goes, the track as it was dashed beneath it, and the note at the top of the map says by how much: BLUE ONE: moving 1.20 nmi 045.0°T, BLUE ONE: rotating 12.0° clockwise about 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W. Letting go saves it as one step. Escape before letting go puts it back, and nothing is recorded. What is saved is what the note said: the distance in the analyst's length unit and the bearing or angle, each to the decimals shown.

  6. Steps, named for what was done. Each operation is one step in the History view, its first note naming it and later notes saying the rest:

    Operation Named Further notes Move the whole track BLUE ONE moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T Move a period BLUE ONE part moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T Only the fixes from 09:30:00Z to 10:15:00Z Rotate BLUE ONE rotated 12.0° clockwise (or part rotated) About 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W, and the period Split BLUE ONE split at 09:30:00Z Into BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2) Merge BLUE ONE and BLUE TWO merged (or 3 tracks merged) Into BLUE ONE, and any series not kept Shear BLUE ONE sheared: 087.2°T 12.4 kn (or part sheared) Held at the start, 09:30:00Z, Was 090.0°T 10.0 kn, and the period Stretch BLUE ONE stretched: 12.4 kn (or part stretched) Held at the end, 10:15:00Z, Was 10.0 kn, and the period

    Each step's provenance record holds who made it, the track or tracks it chose (selected), and what was asked (parameters): the distance and bearing, or the angle and the pivot's latitude and longitude, the period's start and end, the time of a split and the names of its parts, or the merged track's name (SUB-24). Undo is replay to the step before, as for any step (SUB-21).

  7. Splitting at a time. Split track at current time… splits the selected track at current time into two: the fixes before it, and the fixes from it on (a fix exactly at the time starts the second part). The parts are offered as BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2), which the analyst may change. Each keeps the track's colour, platform class, hiding and provenance. The first keeps the track's identity, so a named set or a tool result that refers to the track still does; the second is a new track, listed straight after it, and named sets that held the track hold both. Sensor observations that start at or after the time go with the second part. Observations that run across the time are not cut in two: they stay with the first part, and the step's notes say so (2087 bearings runs past the split and stays with BLUE ONE (1)), since those after the time now have a host track that has ended. Each part needs at least two fixes, or nothing is split and the message says how many each side has. Both parts are selected afterwards.

  8. Merging. Merge selected tracks joins two or more selected tracks into one, in time order, whatever order they were selected in. The merged track keeps the earliest's identity, colour and platform class, and is named as the analyst says: offered the earliest's name, or, for the parts of one split track (BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2)), the track's own (BLUE ONE); the others go, and sensor observations and named sets that referred to them refer to it. Tracks that overlap in time are not merged, and the message says where: The tracks were not merged: they overlap in time (BLUE ONE and RED ONE from 09:00:00Z to 09:40:00Z). Split or move one so they no longer overlap, then merge them. (Choosing which track wins where they overlap was considered and left out, to keep merging predictable.) Tracks that only meet, one ending as the next starts, merge. Speeds, courses or depths are kept only if every track has them. Before merging tracks where some have none, Debrief asks (Merging BLUE ONE, BLUE TWO keeps only what every track has. Courses not kept: BLUE TWO had none. Undo puts them back., with Merge anyway); the step's notes say which were not kept, and why, and the tool service returns the same in notes. The merged track is selected afterwards.

  9. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Letting go of the move or rotate handle Yes, one Yes A run of arrow keys on the move or rotate handle Yes, one for the run Yes Letting go of an end, to shear or stretch Yes, one Yes A run of arrow keys on an end Yes, one for the run Yes Move…, Rotate…, Shear…, Stretch…, Split…, Merge Yes, one each Yes Dragging or nudging the pivot No No Choosing Whole track or Time window, or Shear or Stretch No No Escape during a drag; a move of nothing No No

  10. The keyboard. Tab to a handle. On the move handle the arrow keys move it 5 pixels, 25 with Shift; on the rotate handle Right and Up turn it 1° clockwise, Left and Down 1° anticlockwise, 10° with Shift; on the pivot the arrow keys move it 5 pixels (25 with Shift). A run of presses on the move or rotate handle is saved as one step once they stop (under a second), on Enter, or when the keyboard moves on; Escape first puts it back. Presses made while that step is being saved are not lost: they are made as the next step. Whole track and Time window are buttons on the map, reached with Tab, as are Shear and Stretch. The ends are described below.

  11. The forms. For an exact change, or without the map:

    • Move track… (the outline's context menu on a track; Move… under Track, below the outline, in the playground): what moves (Whole track or Current time window, with how many fixes it holds), the distance (1.2 nmi, 2000 yd, 3 km, or a number in the analyst's unit) and the bearing in degrees true (045). Each field says what it understood (Means 1.20 nmi) or what is wrong.
    • Rotate track…: what turns; the pivot (Fix nearest current time, First fix, Last fix, or in VS Code a position typed in any notation Debrief reads); and the angle (12, 12 clockwise, -12 or 12 anticlockwise).
    • Split track at current time…: the names of the two parts, offered as X (1) and X (2).
    • Merge selected tracks: the merged track's name, offered as above; first, if speeds, courses or depths would not be kept, whether to merge anyway.
    • Shear track… and Stretch track…: below.

  12. Shared state and conflicts. Moving, rotating, splitting and merging change neither current time nor the time window. The selection is kept, except that a split selects both parts and a merge the merged track. If the plot changes elsewhere during a drag (a colleague, an agent), the map shows the latest at once, drops the drag and says The plot was changed elsewhere, so your change was not made. Debrief is showing the latest; try again if you still want to. A change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused the same way (SUB-28): track operations are never merged with a change made meanwhile. Context tracks follow the track: the whole moved track is drawn as context outside the window. A hidden track is not drawn, so it has no handles, but it can still be moved, rotated, split and merged from the outline.

  13. For agents. The same steps through the tool service: debrief/edit_track (feature, edit: a TrackEdit, {"action": "move", "distance": {"value": 1.2, "unit": "[nmi_i]"}, "bearing": {"value": 45, "unit": "deg"}} or {"action": "rotate", "angle": {"value": -10, "unit": "deg"}, "pivot": [-4.12, 50.33]}, with a period to move or turn only that; for a rotation with no pivot, current_time chooses the default), debrief/split_track (feature, at, and names if wanted) and debrief/merge_tracks (features, and name if wanted), each with base as for any change. Shears and stretches go through debrief/edit_track too (below). In VS Code the commands debrief.moveTrack, debrief.rotateTrack, debrief.shearTrack and debrief.stretchTrack take the track and the edit, debrief.splitTrack the track and {at, names}, and debrief.mergeTracks the tracks' ids and {name}, instead of asking.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Map
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Plot as Plot file
    Analyst->>Map: select BLUE ONE
    Map->>Map: move, rotate and pivot handles
    Analyst->>Map: drag the move handle
    Map->>Map: draw the track moved (geodesic), the old one dashed; "moving 1.20 nmi 045.0°T"
    Analyst->>Map: let go
    Map->>Host: edit_track (feature_id, track_edit: move, distance, bearing, period?)
    Host->>Service: debrief/edit_track (edit, base)
    alt changed elsewhere since base
        Service-->>Host: CONFLICT
        Host->>Map: show_plot (the latest); nothing was changed
    else
        Service->>Plot: one step: "BLUE ONE moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T", with its parameters
        Service-->>Host: new base
        Host->>Map: show_plot (handles where the track now is)
    end
sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    Analyst->>Host: Split track at current time… (names offered)
    Host->>Service: debrief/split_track (feature, at, names, base)
    Service-->>Host: one step: "BLUE ONE split at 09:30:00Z"; the two parts
    Host->>Host: reload; select both parts
    Analyst->>Host: Merge selected tracks (name offered: BLUE ONE)
    Host->>Service: debrief/merge_tracks (features, name, base)
    alt the tracks overlap in time
        Service-->>Host: refused, saying where they overlap; nothing changed
    else
        Service-->>Host: one step: "BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2) merged"
    end

docs.title: Shearing and stretching
docs.text:
Part B1 (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026): shear is the operation analysts use most when working with TMA legs, so it comes first, with stretch beside it. A target's leg is a straight line run at a steady speed; the analyst keeps one end where the bearings put it and changes the course and speed of the rest. Both are legacy Debrief's TMA drags (CAP-21), here on any track.

  1. One end is held. What changes is the whole track or only its fixes in the time window, chosen with the same Whole track and Time window control. One end of it, its first fix or its last, is held (the anchor) and does not move; the analyst drags the other end. Dragging the end at the start holds the end, and the other way round.

  2. Shear: every fix moves in proportion to its time from the held end. Say the held fix is A, at time tA, and the dragged end E, at time tE, is dragged to E′. A fix at time t moves by the fraction f = (t − tA) / (tE − tA) of the end's move: not at all at the held end, the whole of it at the dragged end, half of it halfway in time. A straight leg at a steady speed stays a straight leg at a steady speed, with a new course and a new speed: they change together, as in legacy Debrief's TMA shear.

    A, held E E′ ⅓ of the move ⅔

    Dashed: the leg as it was. Solid: sheared. Each fix moves the part of E's move that its time is of the leg's.

  3. Measured on the earth, from the held end. The move is taken in the frame centred on the held fix in which each position is placed by its range and true bearing from it (an azimuthal equidistant projection): there, a geodesic through the held fix is a straight line, and ranges from it are exact. So a straight leg through the held end (a geodesic, run at a steady speed) stays exactly straight after a shear, at any latitude and across the antimeridian. We considered moving each fix the fraction f of the end's range along the end's bearing, as a move does; but over a leg the meridians close in, the same bearing points slightly differently at each fix, and the sheared leg would bend (by tens of metres over a 10 nmi leg at 50° north). The tests check legs at 50°N, at 84°N and across the antimeridian.

  4. Stretch: only the speed changes. With Stretch chosen, only how far the end is dragged along the line from the held end counts: the drag is taken onto that line. Every fix keeps its bearing from the held end and its range from it is multiplied by one factor, the new range of the dragged end over its old one. A straight leg stays on its line, at the new speed, on the same course; a track that turns keeps its shape, larger or smaller about the held end, and every speed changes by the same factor. A stretch never goes to nothing or past the held end: the slowest it offers is one step of speed (0.1 kn).

  5. Recorded courses and speeds go with the fixes. Each fix's recorded course and speed are carried through the same change rather than worked out again from the new positions: Debrief follows the fix's recorded course and speed for ten seconds, changes that point as a fix at that time would be changed, and takes the new course and speed from the changed fix to it. So a shear adds the leg's change of velocity to each fix's own (a fix logged at 000 at 10 kn on a leg that gains 10 kn east is now 045 at 14.1 kn), and a stretch multiplies each speed by the factor and keeps each course. On a straight steady leg every fix's course and speed become exactly the leg's new ones; on a real track the detail recorded at each fix survives instead of being replaced by the jitter of the positions. A track that records courses but not speeds, or speeds but not courses, has the missing one taken from its positions for the purpose; what it does not record stays unrecorded.

  6. Course and speed made good. What the map and the step say: the true bearing, at the first fix of what changes, of the geodesic from it to the last fix, and the range between them over the time between. For a straight steady leg these are its course and speed.

  7. The ends on the map. A track selected on its own shows a diamond beside its first and last fixes of what changes, in the theme's focus colour, drawn to the left of the way the track goes so they are clear of the pivot (often on an end) and the rotate handle (beyond the far end, on the line of a straight leg). Beside What changes, so the control stays short on a short map, its Drag the ends says what dragging one does: Shear (the default) or Stretch, which gives the diamonds a double edge. Each is named for a screen reader: BLUE ONE: shear from the end, holding the start; drag it, or use the arrow keys; BLUE ONE: stretch from the start, holding the end; drag it along the track, or use Up and Down to change speed. We chose a switch on the map over a modifier key (Shift-drag), which nobody can see and which is awkward from the keyboard, and over separate stretch handles, which would put four diamonds on a short leg; legacy Debrief, too, chose the drag first and then dragged.

  8. What the map says.
